passages.title: Allah's decree is coming; angels bring revelation
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Sūrah al-Naḥl opens with a thunderclap. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the surah begins without any particular introduction — with a direct, stern and awesome note of warning. The first words announce that the command of Allah has come, and rebuke the people who had been daring it to hurry up. Ayah 2 is the ground beneath that announcement: the same Allah who issued that command is the One who sends angels down with revelation to servants of His choosing, and the message they carry is one sentence — none has the right to be worshipped but Him, so have taqwā of Him.

The two ayat lock together as warning and proof. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the essential message of the first ayah is to call people to belief in the Oneness of Allah (*tawḥīd*) through a stern warning; the second affirms that same belief through a *reported proof* — the testimony of the messengers, every one of whom preached it. The rational proof comes next, in ayat 3–8, where Allah turns the argument towards His blessings.

## The surah of the bee, the surah of blessings

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this surah is called al-Naḥl — the honey bee — because it mentions the bee as a unique Divine marvel. Another name for it, it adds citing Qurṭubī, is Sūrah al-Niʿam: *niʿam* is the plural of *niʿmah*, blessing, because the great blessings of Allah are particularly mentioned in this surah.

Hold that beside the opening line. A surah known for its catalogue of gifts begins with a command the deniers cannot outrun.

## The taunt that ayah 1 answers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the situation behind the abruptness. The polytheists were saying that Muḥammad ﷺ keeps warning them of the Day of Qiyāmah — the Day of Judgement — and of the punishment of Allah, and keeps telling them that Allah has promised him victory and promised his opponents punishment. All this, they challenged, they do not see coming upon them. Where is it? The surah's opening is the reply, delivered, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it, in a distinctly awesome tone:

> أَتَىٰ أَمْرُ ٱللَّهِ فَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلُوهُ
> "The Event ordained by Allah has indeed come, so do not seek to hasten it."

## "Has come" — the past tense of certainty

The most striking thing in ayah 1 is a matter of tense. *Atā* is a past-tense verb: **has come**, already, done. Yet the event it describes had not arrived in the deniers' experience — that was the whole basis of their mockery.

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah informs about the approach of the Hour in the past tense in Arabic precisely in order to confirm that it will undoubtedly come to pass. What Allah has decreed is as settled as what has already occurred; the only thing still outstanding is our arrival at it. He points to the same move elsewhere in the Qur'an, where the verbs likewise appear in the past tense in Arabic:

- **"Mankind's reckoning has drawn near them, while they turn away in heedlessness"** (21:1)
- **"The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has been cleft"** (54:1)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point about the wording, while admitting frankly that the nuance of the original expression does not survive translation: the sense is that *issued is the command of Allah* — it is bound to come, and you will soon see it. Not a forecast. A verdict already signed.

## What is "the command of Allah"?

The commentators give more than one answer, and the sources record the difference rather than settling it.

**The promise made to the Messenger ﷺ.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes *amrullāh* here to mean the promise Allah has made to His Rasūl — that his enemies will be made to surrender, and that the Muslims will be blessed with victory and honour. On this reading the ayah answers the specific taunt: you say you see no sign of what he promises; the command is issued, and you will soon see it.

**The Day of Qiyāmah.** Some commentators, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from *Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, take "the command of Allah" here to mean the Day of Qiyāmah, the Day of Judgement. Its being "bound to come" means that it is going to come soon — and set in the frame of the life of the entire world itself, its coming does not remain much distant. Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as a warning about the approach of the Hour.

Both are reported as the views of commentators. The sources set them side by side without ruling between them, and it is enough to receive them as such.

## "So do not seek to hasten it"

*Lā tastaʿjilūhu* — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it, do not ask for it to come sooner. The rebuke is aimed at a strange human habit: daring the very thing that will destroy you, as if speed of arrival were evidence of truth.

Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact and quietly devastating: **what was far is now near, so do not try to rush it.** You are already close enough. He brings the parallel where Allah says of the same demand:

> "And they ask you to hasten the torment, and had it not been for a term appointed, the torment would certainly have come to them. And surely, it will come upon them suddenly while they are unaware! They ask you to hasten on the torment. And verily! Hell, of a surety, will encompass the disbelievers." (29:53–54)

Two things stand out there. First, what stands between them and the torment is *a term appointed* — a fixed time set by Allah, and nothing else. Second, when it comes it comes **suddenly, while they are unaware**. The people demanding to see it are guaranteeing that they will not see it approaching.

## From the Sunnah: the three calls and the unfinished tasks

Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Abi Hatim reported from ʿUqbah bin ʿĀmir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that when the Hour approaches, a black cloud resembling a shield will emerge from the west and will continue rising in the sky. Then a voice will call out, "O mankind!" People will turn to one another — *did you hear that?* Some will say yes; others will doubt it. A second call comes: "O mankind!" Now they say to one another, yes, we heard it. Then a third call comes:

> "O mankind! The Event ordained by Allah has indeed come, so do not seek to hasten it."

The very words of our ayah, called out over the heads of humanity at the end. What was recited to the Makkans as a warning is heard at the last as an announcement.

Ibn Kathir then gives further words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, sworn upon: **by the One in Whose Hand is my soul**, two men will spread out a cloth but will never refold it; a man will prepare his trough but will never water his animals from it; a man will milk his camel but will never drink the milk. Then he said: the people will be distracted.

Notice what those images have in common. Not one of them is a sin. Spreading a cloth, filling a trough, milking a camel — these are the small, unglamorous, half-finished tasks of an ordinary afternoon. That is when it comes. The end does not wait for a dramatic moment; it interrupts one.

## Why "Glorified and Exalted is He" belongs here

The ayah closes: **"Glorified and Exalted be He above all that they associate as partners with Him."**

Ibn Kathir explains the join: Allah tells us that He is free from their allegations of partners, from their worship of idols, and from their making equals for Him — glorified and exalted be He far above that — and then adds the telling observation, *these are the people who deny the Hour.* The two go together. The one who denies the Day of accounting and the one who worships alongside Allah are named here as the same people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, again from *Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, presses this further: the act of these people in belying the promise of Allah is *itself* an act of *kufr* (disbelief) and *shirk* (ascribing partners to Allah), and Allah is absolutely free from it. So the answer to the taunt is not only "it is coming"; it is "your demand is itself the sin."

For a believer, *subḥānahu wa taʿālā* is also the right posture when facing a delay you do not understand. Allah is above needing to satisfy your timetable.

## Ayah 2: how any of this is known

> يُنَزِّلُ ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةَ بِٱلرُّوحِ مِنْ أَمْرِهِۦ عَلَىٰ مَن يَشَآءُ مِنْ عِبَادِهِۦ
> "He sends down the angels with the Rūḥ (revelation) of His command to those servants of His whom He wills: *Warn mankind that none has the right to be worshipped but I, so have taqwā of Me.*"

**"With the Rūḥ."** Ibn Kathir states plainly that *al-rūḥ* here refers to the revelation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Sayyidunā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that *rūḥ* here means *waḥy*, revelation, while noting that according to some commentators it means *hidāyah*, guidance. Either way, what descends comes from Allah; it is not produced by the one who receives it.

Ibn Kathir supports the reading with 42:52, where Allah says to the Prophet ﷺ: *"And thus We have sent to you a Rūḥ (revelation) by Our command. You knew not what is the Book, nor what is the faith. But We have made it a light by which We guide whomever We will among Our servants."* Note what that ayah says about the Prophet ﷺ himself: before the revelation he did not know the Book or faith. This was not something he produced. It was sent to him.

**"By His command."** The revelation is not the angels' own; they carry what is *min amrihi* — from His command.

**"To those servants of His whom He wills."** Ibn Kathir says this means the Prophets — prophethood is Allah's placing, never a human achievement. He cites *"Allah best knows where to place His Message"* (6:124) and *"Allah chooses Messengers from angels and from men"* (22:75). Notice also the word used for these chosen ones: not masters but *ʿibād*, **servants**. The men Allah selects to carry His speech are named by their servitude to Him.

Ibn Kathir adds a third parallel that carries ayah 1 and ayah 2 in a single breath: *"He sends the Rūḥ by His command to whoever among His servants He wills to, that he may warn of the Day of Meeting. The Day when they will all come out, nothing about them will be hidden from Allah. Whose is the kingdom this Day? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible!"* (40:15–16). Revelation descends *for* the warning; the warning is *about* the Day; the Day belongs to Allah alone.

## The content of every revelation ever sent

The commission given to the messengers comes in three short pieces.

**"Warn"** — Ibn Kathir: meaning that they should alert them. The commission opens with rousing people, not soothing them.

**"That none has the right to be worshipped but I"** — the whole content of the message, compressed into a sentence.

**"So have taqwā of Me"** — Ibn Kathir explains it as: *fear My punishment, if you go against My commands and worship anything other than Me.* Taqwā here is not an abstract feeling. It is the practical caution of someone who knows there is a real consequence and steers accordingly.

## Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's argument from the prophets' agreement

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why ayah 2 works as a *proof* and not merely a claim. Every messenger of Allah, from Sayyidunā Ādam (peace be upon him) to the Last of the Prophets ﷺ, came in different parts of the world at different times, and none of them knew anything of the life and work of the others, for obvious reasons. Yet every one of them preached this one belief in the Oneness of Allah.

Now just imagine, it says, at least one hundred and twenty thousand blessed, wise men, born in different ages, countries and regions, all believing in and adhering to one single principle. One is naturally compelled to accept that their saying so cannot be false. In order to have faith, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, this single proof is sufficient.

This is what the deniers had missed. They treated Muḥammad ﷺ as a novelty to be argued down. Ayah 2 places him at the end of a line reaching back to Sayyidunā Ādam (peace be upon him), every one of whom said the same thing.

## Living it

**Stop treating delay as evidence.** The Makkans reasoned: we do not see it coming upon us, therefore it is not true. Ayah 1 dismantles that. What stands between the command and its arrival is a term appointed by Allah — not a sign that nothing is coming.

**Do not dare Allah.** Demanding to see the proof of punishment, or of victory, on your own schedule is precisely the posture ayah 1 rebukes. Ask for readiness instead.

**Live as though the interruption is normal.** The report Ibn Kathir cites places the end in the middle of a spread cloth and a half-filled trough. Keep your accounts with Allah short enough that being interrupted mid-task costs you nothing.

**Recognise the size of what you carry.** The one sentence the angels descended with — *none has the right to be worshipped but I* — is the same sentence on your tongue. Say it as something delivered by revelation, not inherited by accident.

passages.title: Creation and cattle as favours — and the road Allah undertakes to show
passages.tafsir:
These ayat build a single argument for the Oneness of Allah out of things the first listeners could see and handle: the sky above them, their own origin, and the herds their whole economy rested on. Ma'arif ul Qur'an puts the logic plainly — the description of Allah's blessings in these verses is presented as *rational proof* of His Oneness. The passage moves outward and then inward: from the heavens and the earth, to man himself, to the animals made to serve man, and finally from the roads those animals carry you along to the road that carries you to Allah.

## The universe built with truth, and the creature who argues back — ayat 3–4

Ibn Kathir opens by noting that Allah is telling us of His creation of the upper realm, the heavens, and the lower realm, the earth, and everything in them. They were created, he says, **for a true purpose, not in vain** — and he anchors this in another ayah: so that Allah "may requite those who do evil with that which they have done, and reward those who do good, with what is best" (53:31). The universe is not decoration. If creation has a purpose, then life inside it has a reckoning.

Then comes the recoil: **ta'ala 'amma yushrikun** — "High is He, Exalted above all that they associate as partners with Him." Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion tightly: Allah declares Himself above the shirk of those who worship others besides Him; He is independent of His creation, alone with no partner or associate, and *for this reason* He deserves to be worshipped alone, without partners. The right to be worshipped is not one claim among several. It follows from being the One who made everything and needs nothing.

And then, immediately, the human being. Ayah 4's force is in the compression: created **min nutfah** — from a drop — *and then, behold*, **khasim mubin**.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an explains the word: **khasim** is derived from **khusumah** and means a quarrelsome person; Ma'arif renders the whole phrase as "a quarrelsome person expressing himself openly." And it catches the sting exactly: "when the elementally weak man was endowed with strength and speech, he turned into a critic of the Creator Himself disputing His Being and Attributes publicly."

Ibn Kathir traces the same arc. A nutfah is "something that is insignificant, weak and has no value" — but once man becomes independent and is able to fend for himself, "he begins to dispute with his Lord, may He be exalted, and disbelieves in Him and fights His Messengers." Then Ibn Kathir gives the line that should be written across the whole passage: **man was created to be a servant, not an opponent.** He supports it with 36:77–79, where this same phrase recurs and the disputant's own argument is quoted — *"Who will give life to these bones after they are rotten and have become dust?"* — and answered: "He will give life to them Who created them the first time! And He is the knower of every creature!"

The One who built the heavens for a true purpose is the same One who built you out of a drop. Deny the first and you have to explain away the second.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites a narration reported by Imam Ahmad and Ibn Majah from Busr bin Jahhash: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spat in his palm, then he said that Allah, may He be exalted, says: *"O son of Adam, how could you be more powerful than I when I have created you from something like this, and when I have fashioned you perfectly and made you complete, you walk wearing your two garments and the earth makes a sound (beneath your feet). You collect money but do not give anything to anyone, then when the soul of a dying person reaches the throat, you say, 'I want to give in charity', but it is too late for charity."*

## The long inventory of kindness — ayat 5–8

Ma'arif ul Qur'an explains why the animals come at this point and in this order — after human beings, Allah mentions the creation of things made specially for their benefit, and since the first addressees of the Qur'an were Arabs whose economic life depended on domestic cattle like camels, cows and goats, these were taken up first.

**Al-an'am** is the plural of *na'am*; Ma'arif, citing *Al-Mufradat* of Raghib al-Isfahani, glosses it as cattle such as the camel, the goat and the cow. Ibn Kathir says the term includes camels, cows and sheep, as was explained in detail in Surat al-An'am where the "eight pairs" are mentioned.

**Warmth.** **Difʼ**, Ma'arif explains, denotes what provides warmth — wool used to make warm clothing for winter. Ibn 'Abbas is reported by Ibn Kathir as saying simply that *difʼ* refers to clothing.

**Food.** **Wa minha ta'kulun** — "and of them you eat." Ma'arif includes both the slaughtering of these animals for their meat and, while they are alive, the milk taken from them, "which is fine food indeed," with butter, yoghurt, butter-oil and everything else falling under dairy.

**And then a word left deliberately open.** For the remainder, one word was considered sufficient: **manafiʼ**, other benefits. Ibn 'Abbas is reported as saying it refers to the ways in which people derive the benefits of food and drink from them. Ma'arif reads the brevity as intentional generosity: it signifies countless benefits tied to the meat, skin, bone and hair of animals, and within that brevity — even ambiguity — is a hint toward all modern innovations in the processing and use of food, dress, medicine and domestic articles, "innovations which have been made to date, or will be made right through the Last Day." Ibn Kathir gathers the same harvest concretely: wool and hair from which clothes and furnishings are made, milk which is drunk, young which are eaten.

**Beauty at dusk and dawn.** In ayah 6, after usefulness, Allah names **jamal** — beauty — and fixes it to two precise moments of the day. Ma'arif explains the two verbs: **turihun** is a derivation from *rawah*, and **tasrahun** from *sarh*; when the cattle are sent out to graze it is called *sarah*, and when they return home it is called *rawah*. Ibn Kathir explains what makes the evening return beautiful: that is when they are brought back from the pasture, and it is a reference to how "their flanks become fat, their udders fill with milk and their humps become bigger." It is the beauty of a herd that has been fed — visible prosperity walking home in the dust of sunset. Ma'arif adds the human dimension, in terms of the contemporary Arab taste of the time: at those moments these animals "become silent spokesmen of the strength and pride of their owners."

**Distance.** Ayah 7 moves to what these animals make possible that nothing else could: they carry your heavy loads to a land you could not reach **illa bi-shiqq al-anfus** — an expression Ma'arif glosses as personal hardship. Ibn Kathir explains "your loads" as the heavy burdens that you cannot move or carry by yourselves, and the destination as journeys "for Hajj, 'Umrah, military campaigns, and journeys for the purpose of trading, and so on." Ma'arif notes that camels and oxen especially have been harnessed into this service on a large scale, and that even in our day of trains, trucks and cargo planes human beings cannot universally claim to have become free of the need: there are places in the world where none of our modern means of transportation can work, and one is compelled to borrow their services.

**The seal on the whole inventory.** After enumerating these blessings comes **inna Rabbakum la-Ra'ufun Rahim** — "Truly, your Lord is full of kindness, Most Merciful." Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: your Lord is the One who has subjugated the cattle to you. The gentleness is the conclusion drawn from the inventory. An animal many times your strength stands still while you load it, and Ibn Kathir names the reason — it was subdued for you. He cites the ayah in which Allah says that of what His Hands have created He created the cattle for people, "so that they may own them, and We subdued them so that they may ride some and they may eat some" (36:71–72).

He also cites the traveller's remembrance Allah teaches in 43:12–14: that when you settle onto the back of your mount you should remember the favour of your Lord and say, *"Glory be to the One Who subjected this to us, and we could never have it (by our efforts). And verily, to Our Lord we indeed are to return!"*

**A second list, deliberately different.** Ayah 8 opens a second category. Ibn Kathir: this refers to another category of animals that Allah has created as a blessing for His servants — horses, mules and donkeys — "all of which He made for riding and adornment," and this, he says, is the main purpose for which these animals were created. Ma'arif explains why they are listed separately from the *an'am*: since mention had been made of camels and oxen, it was appropriate to mention quadrupeds created exclusively for draft and riding, from whose milk or meat one does not benefit, because in religious law they are the cause of moral diseases and are therefore prohibited. **Zinah**, adornment, Ma'arif glosses as that same favourable quality of life which the pleasing possession of these animals gives their owners. The difference between the two lists is exact: with the *an'am*, eating was explicitly named; here only riding and adornment are.

**From the Sunnah**, Ibn Kathir cites three narrations at this point:

- It was reported in the Two Sahihs that Jabir bin 'Abdullah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade us to eat the meat of domestic donkeys, but he allowed us to eat the meat of horses."
- Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud reported, with two chains of narration each of which meet the conditions of Muslim, that Jabir said: "On the day of Khaybar we slaughtered horses, mules and donkeys. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade us from eating the mules and donkeys, but he did not forbid us from eating the horses."
- According to Sahih Muslim, Asma' bint Abi Bakr (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "At the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ we slaughtered a horse and ate it when we were in Al-Madinah."

**The ruling that follows from the silence.** Ma'arif builds a legal point on that difference: with the *an'am* the eating of their meat was declared among their benefits, whereas with horses, mules and donkeys the benefits named are riding and looking good, and eating is not mentioned — which provides the proof that the meat of horse, mule and donkey is not halal. As for mule and donkey, the majority of the jurists agree on its being haram, and Ma'arif notes that a hadith on the subject states its unlawfulness clearly. Horse meat is different: there are two conflicting narrations of hadith, one putting it as halal and the other as haram, and consequently the sayings of the jurists of the Muslim community became divided, some declaring it halal and others haram. It was because of these conflicting arguments, Ma'arif says, that Imam Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him) did not call horse meat *haram* as he did the meat of donkey or mule, but called it *makruh* — reprehensible. Ma'arif attributes the discussion to *Ahkam al-Qur'an* of al-Jassas.

**"And He creates what you do not know."** Ma'arif builds a striking point on a grammatical detail. Earlier in the passage the verb is past tense — **khalaqa**, "He created." But at the close of ayah 8 the tense turns future: **yakhluqu** — "He creates, or will create — what you do not know." Ma'arif reads this change as clearly indicating means of transport and other things that had not yet come into existence: railroads, automobiles, aeroplanes, and everything else that will be invented and used in the future. The creation of all these things is really nothing but the act of the Absolute Creator, since no science, classical or modern, can create iron or copper or lighter metals, nor wood, nor air, nor water — science does no more than learn the art of using what has been created by Divine power. Ma'arif adds why such things were not named outright: mentioning words for railroads, automobiles and aeroplanes would have brought no benefit and would only have left people bewildered, since conceiving of such things then was not easy and no words for them were in use. And it records that Mufti Muhammad Shafi's father, Maulana Muhammad Yasin, said that their teacher Maulana Muhammad Ya'qub Nanautawi, the great teacher of teachers, used to say: "The rail has been mentioned in the Holy Qur'an," and would quote this very ayah as proof.

**Adornment yes, arrogance no.** Ma'arif draws a second ruling from ayat 6 and 8 read together: beauty and embellishment are allowed, while pride and arrogance are haram — and it locates the line precisely. The outcome of beauty and embellishment is that it makes a person happy with himself, or shows the blessing of Allah openly; when that happens, he does not nurse the idea in his heart that he deserves the blessing, nor does he take others to be low and contemptible, but keeps foremost in mind that all the good things of life given to him are the gift and blessing of Allah. Pride and arrogance are the opposite: a person takes himself to deserve the blessing while taking others to be low. The difference is not in the possession; it is inside the owner.

## From the roads you travel to the road that reaches Allah — ayah 9

Ibn Kathir explains the pivot: when Allah had mentioned the animals used for physical journeys, He also referred to the moral and religious routes people may follow — and Ibn Kathir notes that this is a recurring Qur'anic move, from physical or tangible things to beneficial spiritual and religious matters, as when Allah says "take a provision for the journey, but the best provision is taqwa" (2:197), and when, after mentioning the clothing granted to the children of Adam, He says "the raiment of righteousness, that is better" (7:26).

**Wa 'ala Allahi qasd al-sabil** — "And it is up to Allah to show the right way." Ibn Kathir sets this beside "verily, this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow the other paths, for they will separate you away from His path" (6:153) and "This is the way which will lead straight to Me" (15:41). He reports Mujahid as saying, "The true way is up to Allah," and reports al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: "It is up to Allah to clarify, to explain the guidance and misguidance" — also reported by 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, and the opinion of Qatadah and ad-Dahhak. Ma'arif states it as a standing promise: Allah has taken it upon Himself to make clear and explicit the straight path which takes its follower to Him.

**Wa minha ja'ir** — "But there are ways that stray." Ibn Kathir explains: they deviate from the truth. Ibn 'Abbas and others said, "These are the different ways" — the various opinions and whims. Ibn Kathir also records that Ibn Mas'ud recited the phrase as *wa minkum ja'ir*, "But among you are those who stray." Both readings land in the same place: the crooked road has travellers, and they are people like you.

**"And had He willed, He would have guided you all."** Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah telling us that all of that happens by His will and decree, citing "If your Lord had willed, then all who are in the earth would have believed" (10:99), and 11:118–119, which ends with the fulfilled word of the Lord that Hell will be filled with jinn and men together. Ma'arif approaches the same clause from the side of wisdom: had Allah so willed, He would have made everyone compulsorily be on the right path, and it was within His power to do so — but wisdom and expedient considerations required that there be no compulsion. Let the two paths stand before everyone, and let whoever elects to take whichever path be free to take it. The Straight Path takes people to Allah and to Jannah; the other, crooked ways take people to Jahannam.

Ma'arif also notes the *placement* of this ayah. It has been introduced parenthetically, in the middle of a description of blessings that resumes afterwards, and its purpose is warning: despite having clear signs and open proofs, people do not benefit by them, but "go on straying endlessly."

## Living it

- **Take the argument personally.** Ayah 4 is a mirror. Strength and speech are exactly the gifts that tempt a person to turn critic of the One who gave them — that is Ma'arif's reading of the verse. The cure Ibn Kathir names is remembering what you were made to be: a servant, not an opponent.
- **Let ordinary comforts become evidence.** Ayat 5–8 count wool, milk, meat, a good-looking herd and a means of travel as proofs of Allah's Oneness. Your coat, your fridge and your car sit in exactly that list. Ibn Kathir's citation of 43:12–14 gives the practical response: when you settle into your seat, remember the favour of your Lord and glorify the One who subjected it to you — including the ending, *"and verily, to Our Lord we indeed are to return."*
- **Enjoy beauty without letting it swell you.** Ma'arif's test is usable today. Displaying a blessing is fine so long as the heart does not claim to have deserved it and does not look down on anyone.
- **Do not blame the map.** Ayah 9 removes the excuse. Allah has taken it upon Himself that the straight path be made clear and explicit; if a person ends up on a crooked road, it is not because the straight one was hidden.

passages.title: Rain, sea, mountains and stars serve you
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is doing.** Having just spoken of the cattle He created for man, Allah now widens the frame to the whole working world: the rain and what grows from it, night and day, sun, moon and stars, the coloured variety of the earth, the sea with its fish and pearls and ships, and the mountains, rivers, roads and landmarks that make travel possible. Ayat 17 and 18 then land the argument the whole list was built for — the One who creates cannot be put on a level with things that create nothing, and His favours are beyond counting.

Two threads hold the unit together. The first is the verb **سخّر (sakhkhara)** — "He subjected it," put it at your service — used of the sky in ayah 12 and the sea in ayah 14. The second is a set of closing refrains: *a sign for people who ponder* (11), *signs for people who understand* (12), *a sign for people who take heed* (13).

## The three refrains: three different demands on the mind

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to why the closing formula changes each time. After the crops, olives, palms, grapes and fruits of ayah 11 comes **يَتَفَكَّرُونَ (yatafakkarūn)** — *those who ponder* — because, as that commentary explains, the link between pastures, crops, trees and their flowers and fruits and the creativity and wisdom of Allah needs some reflection to see. Put a grain or a date-stone into the ground and water it: that act alone cannot automatically cause it to grow into a huge tree with flowers of many colours opening all over it. No tiller, no farmer, no landowner made that happen. Their role, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it bluntly, is nil. But because a man *does* sow and water and appears to be doing something, it takes thought to see past his hand to the real Cause.

After the night and day, sun, moon and stars in ayah 12 comes **يَعْقِلُونَ (yaʿqilūn)** — *those who use reason*. Here, the same commentary notes, no great amount of thinking is required: that these things are subservient to the command of Allah is an open fact. Anyone with some reason in him would understand — because with vegetation and trees there was at least the appearance of some human input, whereas in this case there is none at all.

After the varied produce of the earth in ayah 13 comes **يَذَّكَّرُونَ (yadhdhakkarūn)** — *those who take heed, who let themselves be reminded*. Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase as those who remember the blessings of Allah and give thanks to Him for them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the condition: no deep thinking is needed here either, because the proof has been furnished openly — but one must look at it carefully and learn his lesson. Someone with no sense or concern, who simply pays no attention, could hardly hope to benefit from it. So the passage asks, in turn, for thought, for reason, and for an attentive heart — and the third is the one a person can most easily refuse.

## One water, many flavours (ayat 10–11)

Ayah 10 opens with rain "from the sky," and Ibn Kathir notes the order: Allah has just mentioned the blessing of cattle and other animals He granted mankind, and now mentions the rain that has been fulfilling the needs and bringing joy to people and their cattle alike.

**لَّكُم مِّنْهُ شَرَابٌ — "from it you drink."** Ibn Kathir's comment is easily missed: He made it *fresh and pure* so that they can drink it — not salty and undrinkable. That the water falling on you is sweet is itself a decision, not a default.

**شَجَرٌ فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ.** The word *shajar* is mostly applied to a tree standing on a trunk. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it is sometimes also used in an absolute sense for everything that grows on land, including grass on stems or tendrils — and that is the sense meant here, because the pasturing of cattle is mentioned immediately afterwards, and that is mostly a matter of grass. The verb **تُسِيمُونَ (tusīmūn)** derives from *isāmah*, which means to leave cattle to graze freely in a pasture. It is a picture, not an abstraction: animals let out to feed themselves on what the rain raised. Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd all said this refers to grazing animals, including camels.

Ayah 11 then names the produce — crops, olives, date palms, grapes, "and every kind of fruit." Ibn Kathir fixes on the marvel in it: **with this one kind of water**, He makes the earth sprout plants with different tastes, colours, scents and shapes. One input, endless outputs. He reads the sign as a proof that there is no god besides Allah, quoting the challenge of Sūrat al-Naml: *"…and sends water down for you from the sky, from which We cause wonderful gardens full of beauty and delight to grow? You are not able to cause the growth of their trees. Is there any ilah (god) with Allah?"* (27:60).

## "Subjected for you" — and what that does not mean (ayat 12–13)

Ayah 12 moves to the sky: night and day, sun and moon subjected, and the stars "subjected by His command." Ibn Kathir describes it as a single ordered system — night and day following one another, the sun and moon revolving, the stars both fixed and moving through the skies, offering light by which people may find their way in the darkness. Each of these heavenly bodies travels in its own orbit, which Allah has ordained for it, without deviating in any way. All of them are under His subjugation, His control and His decree.

He supports this with the ayah from al-Aʿrāf: *"Indeed, your Lord is Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth in Six Days, and then He rose (Istawa) over the Throne. He brings the night as a cover over the day, seeking it rapidly, and (He created) the sun, the moon, the stars (all) subjected to His command. Surely, His is the creation and commandment. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of all that exists!"* (7:54). Ibn Kathir's own comment on the refrain — *signs for people who understand* — is that these are indications of His immense power and might, for those who think about Allah and understand His signs.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a correction here. "He subjugated for you the day and the night" means Allah made them subservient *to His command* in order that they may serve man — the night brings him comfort, the day smooths out the avenues of his work. It never means that day and night start alternating under human command. The subjection is Allah's, the benefit is yours, and the two are not the same thing.

Ayah 13 turns from sky to ground: *"and whatever He has created for you on the earth, of varying colours."* Ibn Kathir spreads this out — when Allah points out the features of the skies, He also points out the wondrous things He has created on earth: the variety of its animals, minerals, plants and inanimate features, all having different colours and shapes, benefits and qualities.

## The sea, and everything it carries (ayah 14)

Ayah 14 is a small catalogue of its own, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts three benefits in it.

**First, food.** "That you may eat from it fresh tender meat" — *laḥman ṭariyyan*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees a hint in Allah calling the fish *fresh meat*: it is free of any condition of slaughtering that is necessary with other animals. Ibn Kathir states it directly: Allah put fish and whales in the seas and made their flesh permissible to eat, whether they are caught alive or dead, at all times, including when people are in a state of *iḥrām* — the state pilgrims enter.

**Second, adornment.** *"And that you bring out from it ornaments you wear."* **حِلْيَة (ḥilyah)** literally means *zīnah* — that which beautifies, embellishes, adorns. Ibn Kathir says Allah created pearls and precious jewels in the oceans and made it easy for His servants to recover from the ocean floor ornaments they can wear; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies them as the pearls and precious coral stones divers bring up, worn by women as necklaces or earrings. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then pauses on a grammatical detail: though these ornaments are worn by women, the Qurʼān uses the masculine form — *talbasūnahā*, "you wear it." His reading is that the wearing of ornaments by women is in reality in the interest of men; that a woman looking good is, in his words, "in reality, the right of man," and that a husband "can even compel his wife to wear dress and ornaments which look good on her." He adds that men too can use precious stones on their rings. That is this commentator's inference from the grammar, not the plain wording of the ayah.

**Third, travel and trade.** *"And you see the ships ploughing through it."* **الفُلْك (al-fulk)** means boat or ship; **مَوَاخِر (mawākhir)** is the plural of *mākhirah*, from *makhr*, to cleave or plough through the water — vessels traversing the sea, cutting through the waves. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the sense of the ayah: Allah has made the sea one of the means of reaching distant countries, so that human beings may travel by it and bring in or send out their commercial goods. That is why the ayah says *"that you may seek of His bounty"* — the bounty is your *rizq*, your sustenance — because trading through the sea routes is most economical and beneficial.

Ibn Kathir attaches a piece of human history to this. It is Allah who taught mankind to make ships, which is the inheritance of their forefather Nūḥ, peace be upon him. He was the first to travel by ship; he was taught how to make them; then people took this knowledge from him and passed it down from generation to generation through the centuries, so that they could travel from country to country, bringing goods from here to there and from there to here.

The ayah ends: *"and that you may perhaps be grateful."* Food, beauty and wealth are all named, and gratitude — for His bounty and blessings — is named as their purpose.

## Mountains that keep the ground still (ayah 15)

**رَوَاسِيَ (rawāsiya)** is the plural of *rāsiyah*, which denotes a huge mountain. **أَن تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ** — *lest it shake with you* — uses **مَيْد (mayd)**, meaning to shake, swing or sway from side to side through loss of balance. Ibn Kathir says plainly that Allah placed in the earth mountains standing firm, which make it stable and keep it from shaking in such a manner that the creatures dwelling on it would not be able to live, and he recalls *"and the mountains He has fixed firmly"* (79:32).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works the image out further: Allah has not made the sphere of the earth from components that are uniformly solid and balanced, so it is heavier on one side and lighter on another, and on either view of the earth — taken as stationary, as commonly held by early thinkers, or as orbitally moving, as determined by some early and most modern scientists — that imbalance would have produced exactly this turbulence. To stop it and to provide a balance for the terrestrial composition, Allah placed on the earth the weight of the mountains so that it would not shake. He is careful about how far to take this: the earth's orbital movement is something the Qurʼān neither affirms nor rejects, and he closes with *Allah knows best*. The ayah is teaching you Whose hand steadies the ground, not settling a question of astronomy.

**"And rivers and roads, that you may be guided."** Ibn Kathir's treatment of rivers is one of the warmest passages in his commentary. Allah has made rivers which flow from one place to another, bringing provision for His servants: they arise in one place and bring provision to people living in another, flowing through lands and fields and wildernesses, through mountains and hills, until they reach the land whose people they are meant to benefit — meandering left and right, north and south, east and west, rivers great and small, flowing sometimes and ceasing sometimes, flowing rapidly or moving slowly, as decreed by Allah. In the middle of that description he breaks off into testimony: *there is no god besides Him and no Lord except Him.*

The roads are of a piece with this. Allah also made roads or routes along which people travel from one land or city to another, and He even made gaps in the mountains so that there would be routes between them: *"And We placed broad highways for them to pass through"* (21:31).

## Landmarks and stars (ayah 16)

**عَلَامَات (ʿalāmāt)** are the markers by which a lost traveller reorients — Ibn Kathir names signs like great mountains and small hills and so on, things that land and sea travellers use to find their way if they get lost; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists mountains, rivers, trees, homes and things like that, set up to help people find their way on the earth. Because trade-oriented travel was mentioned just above, it was considered appropriate to mention alongside it the conveniences Allah has provided in the heavens and the earth to help travellers cover distances and reach their destinations.

Then: **وَبِالنَّجْمِ هُمْ يَهْتَدُونَ** — *"and by the stars they are guided."* Ibn Kathir specifies: in the darkness of the night; this was the opinion of Ibn ʿAbbas. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads something into the way this is phrased — the modality of the address seems to hint that the initial purpose of the creation of the stars is something else, and that along with it, their additional benefit is that they help a traveller chart his course. A star is not a signpost by nature; Allah made it serve as one for you.

## The question the whole list was building to (ayah 17)

**أَفَمَن يَخْلُقُ كَمَن لَّا يَخْلُقُ** — *"Is then He Who creates the same as one who does not create? Will you not then reflect?"*

Ibn Kathir puts it as Allah telling us of His greatness, and that worship should be directed to Him alone and not to any of the idols, which do not create but are rather themselves created. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the argument the way the sequence intends: when it stands proved that Allah alone made the heavens and the earth, made the mountains and rivers, vegetation and animals, trees and plants with their fruits and flowers — how can that most sacred Being, the Creator of all these things, become, for no reason, like idols and icons which cannot create anything? Why would you not understand something so elementary?

That is the whole logic of ayat 10–17 in one line: *tawḥīd* — that Allah is One, and that there is none worthy of worship except Him — is not merely asserted here, it is *demonstrated*, from rain, grass, orbits, fish, pearls, ships, mountains, rivers and stars.

## Favours past counting — and why the ayah ends in forgiveness (ayah 18)

**وَإِن تَعُدُّوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ لَا تُحْصُوهَا** — *"And if you would try to count the favours of Allah, you would never be able to count them. Truly, Allah is Forgiving, Most Merciful."*

The ending is unexpected. A list of blessings should close with a call to gratitude; it closes instead with forgiveness. Ibn Kathir explains why: if Allah were to ask you to thank Him for all of His blessings, you would not be able to do so, and if He were to command you to do so, you would be incapable of it. If He punishes you, He is never unjust in His punishment — but He is Forgiving and Most Merciful; He forgives much and rewards for little. Ibn Jarir's wording is quoted: it means that Allah is Forgiving when you fail to thank Him properly, if you repent and turn to Him in obedience and strive to do that which pleases Him; and He is Merciful to you and does not punish you if you turn to Him and repent.

So the divine names at the end are not decoration. They answer the panic a sincere person feels on realising that the debt named in this passage cannot be paid. It cannot. You are not asked to pay it — you are asked to turn toward the One you owe.

## Living it

- **Let ordinary things testify.** The passage builds its case entirely out of what you already see every day: sweet water, grass, an orchard, a sunset, a fish, a mountain, a night sky. The problem was never a shortage of evidence; it was inattention. Ayah 13, on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, asks only that you look carefully and learn your lesson.
- **Match the faculty to the sign.** Some blessings need pondering (ayah 11), some need only plain reason (ayah 12), some need only that you stop paying no attention (ayah 13). Ask which of the three you are neglecting.
- **Take the gifts as gifts.** Rain made fresh and pure so you can drink it, fish made lawful without slaughter, a sea that carries your trade, mountains that keep the ground from shaking, stars that show the way — read each as an act of a Giver, not a fact of nature.
- **Thank, then seek forgiveness for the thanks.** Ayah 18 gives the believer's posture exactly: try to count, fail, and take shelter in *al-Ghafūr al-Raḥīm* — the Forgiving, the Most Merciful.

passages.title: Lifeless idols against the Ever-Living Lord
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Having spent the preceding ayat listing Allah's blessings in detail — the heavens and the earth, the mountains and rivers, the vegetation and animals, the trees and plants with their fruits and flowers — the Qur'an now presses the conclusion those blessings were always pointing to: Allah alone made all of this, so Allah alone is worthy of worship. Ayat 19–23 make that point by setting two realities side by side. On one side stand the objects people call upon besides Allah: created rather than creating, dead rather than alive, with no knowledge even of when the Hour will come. On the other stands Allah, whose knowledge reaches what is hidden inside people's hearts.

**What holds the passage together.** Ayah 19 and ayah 23 say almost the same sentence — Allah knows what is concealed and what is revealed — and everything in between sits inside that frame. The idols are exposed as knowing nothing at all (ayah 21); the One who alone is worthy of worship is the One from whom nothing at all is hidden (ayat 19 and 23). Notice too the small shift in pronoun. In ayah 19 the address is direct — *mā tusirrūna wa mā tuʿlinūn*, "what **you** conceal and what **you** reveal." In ayah 23, after the denial and pride described in ayah 22, the same knowledge is stated about them — *mā yusirrūna wa mā yuʿlinūn*, "what **they** conceal and what **they** reveal." The one truth is put first to the listener, and then said of those who turned away from it.

## The argument this passage completes

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the context plainly. The verses immediately before this described Allah's many blessings in detail, proved that He alone is their Creator, and established that He is unique in this. What follows here is an admonition against people's failure to recognize the fact standing behind that whole catalogue: *Tawḥīd*, the Oneness of Allah, besides whom there is none worthy of worship. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the argument as a question: when it stands proved that Allah alone made the heavens and the earth, the mountains and rivers, the vegetation and animals, the trees and plants with their fruits and flowers, how can that most sacred Being, the Creator of all these things, become — for no reason at all — like idols and icons which cannot create anything? Why would you not understand something so elementary?

That last line is the tone of the passage. It is not an intricate proof. It is an appeal to something elementary, put to adults who had made themselves incapable of grasping it.

## Ayah 19: the One who knows the inside

Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and weighty: Allah tells us that He knows what is hidden in people's hearts as well as what is apparent, and He will reward or punish everyone for their deeds on the Day of Resurrection — if their deeds are good they will be rewarded, and if their deeds are evil, they will be punished.

Two things stand out there. The first is the reach of this knowledge: not merely what is apparent, but what is hidden in hearts. The second is what that knowledge is *for*. Ibn Kathir does not leave it as bare information; he ties it straight to the Day of Resurrection and to reward and punishment. What is concealed — the intention, the private contempt, the arrogance nobody sees — is already on the record, and it will be answered for.

It is worth noticing where this sentence sits: *before* the discussion of the idols, not after. The tragedy that follows is that people give their hopes to something that cannot even perceive them, while the One who perceives everything about them is the very One they turn away from. That is exactly the contrast Ibn Kathir will draw out at the end of ayah 21.

## Ayat 20–21: an inventory of what the idols cannot do

**They create nothing; they are themselves created.** Ayah 20 says that those they invoke besides Allah "cannot create anything — they are themselves created." Ibn Kathir explains that the idols which people call on instead of Allah cannot create anything, they are themselves created, and he brings the words of Al-Khalil (Ibrahim) to his people: "Do you worship that which you (yourselves) carve? While Allah has created you and what you make!" (37:95–96). The absurdity is stacked two deep. The idol is a made thing. And the hands that made it are themselves a made thing. Worship travels backwards down a chain of manufacture instead of upwards to the One who created both the carver and the carving.

**They are dead, not alive.** Ayah 21 opens with *amwātun ghayru aḥyāʾ* — "dead, not alive." Ibn Kathir explains: they are inanimate and lifeless; they do not hear, see, or think. Feel the wording. It would have been enough to say "dead." The Qur'an adds "not alive," shutting the door on any lingering sense that some spark, some presence, some residue of power might still be in the stone. Ibn Kathir's three verbs close it completely: no hearing to receive the prayer, no sight to see the worshipper before it, no thought to weigh the request.

**They do not even know when the Hour will come.** The ayah closes: *wa mā yashʿurūna ayyāna yubʿathūn*. Ibn Kathir renders this "and they know not when they will be resurrected," and glosses it: they do not know when the Hour will come. The translation carried with our text turns the phrase toward those who worship them instead — "not even knowing when their followers…" Either way, Ibn Kathir states the force of it in a single question: they do not know when the Hour will come, so how can anyone hope for any benefit or reward from these idols? They should hope for it from the One who knows all things and is the Creator of all things.

That is the passage's argument in one sentence, and it comes from Ibn Kathir himself. Worship is hope directed somewhere. Direct it at what knows nothing and creates nothing, and you have simply thrown it away.

## Ayah 22: "Your Deity is One Deity" — and the reaction to it

Ibn Kathir heads this section "None is to be worshipped except Allah," and his gloss on *ilāhukum ilāhun wāḥid* is worth reading slowly: Allah tells us that there is none to be worshipped besides Him, the One, the Unique, the Lone, the Self-Sufficient. So the sentence is not merely an arithmetical claim that there happens to be one deity somewhere; as Ibn Kathir reads it, it is the claim that there is none to be worshipped besides Allah at all. This is the point the whole catalogue of blessings was building toward: the Creator of the gift is the One deserving of the worship.

Then the ayah turns to how this lands on hearts that have already rejected the Hereafter: "their hearts are in denial, and they are proud." Ibn Kathir says the hearts of the disbelievers deny this and are astonished by it, and he illustrates with two other passages. First their astonishment: "Has he made the gods (all) into one?! Verily, this is a curious thing!" (38:5) — to them, oneness was not a relief but an oddity. Second their visceral reaction: "And when Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter are filled with disgust, and when those besides Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice!" (39:45).

That is a striking diagnostic, and notice how the ayah and the verse Ibn Kathir cites both tie the same two things together: disbelief in the Hereafter, and revulsion at the mention of Allah alone. When there is no reckoning to answer to, the mention of one absolute Lord is not comforting news; it is an intrusion. Notice also where these texts locate the problem — in the *heart*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān has already said the evidence is elementary. What blocks it, then, is not a missing argument.

**Pride: the real obstacle.** On *wa hum mustakbirūn*, "and they are proud," Ibn Kathir says: they are too proud to worship Allah, and their hearts reject the idea of singling Him out. It is not pride held above other people here; it is pride held above the act of worship itself. And Ibn Kathir cites what Allah says about that: "Verily! Those who scorn My worship, they will surely enter Hell in humiliation!" (40:60). The one who scorned to lower himself is brought low. The posture he chose becomes the sentence he receives.

## Ayah 23: the frame closes

The ayah opens with *lā jarama*, which Ibn Kathir explains simply as meaning "truly": truly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. And Ibn Kathir tells us what that knowledge means for them here: He will requite them for that in full.

This is why the frame matters. Idolatry can be public and visible — a carved shape, a rite performed in the open — but the pride Ibn Kathir has just described lives in the heart, where nobody can see it, and a person can carry it while looking perfectly ordinary to everyone around him. Ayah 23 removes that hiding place. The concealed and the revealed stand equally known, and both are requited in full.

The passage ends: "Truly, He does not like the proud." Ibn Kathir quotes these closing words and adds nothing to them, and there is a fittingness in that. Allah has told us plainly what He does not love. That alone is enough to act on.

## Living it

**Ask where your hope actually goes.** Ibn Kathir's question is the practical heart of the passage: how can anyone hope for benefit or reward from what does not hear, see, or think, and does not know when the Hour will come? Few of us carve statues. But the same question can be turned on anything we quietly treat as the real source of our security or our rescue. The test the passage gives is simple — does it create anything? Does it know anything? Hope, Ibn Kathir says, belongs with the One who knows all things and is the Creator of all things.

**Watch the heart's reaction, not just the tongue's words.** Ayah 22 tests people by what happens inside them when Allah alone is mentioned — disgust in one heart, and rejoicing at the mention of others besides Him. That reaction is more honest about a person than any statement of belief.

**Take pride seriously as a barrier to worship.** The passage does not present pride as a minor flaw of manner. Ibn Kathir presents it as the very thing that stops a person from worshipping Allah and from singling Him out, and he attaches to it Hell in humiliation (40:60) and, in ayah 23, Allah's own words that He does not like the proud. Worship is precisely the act the proud refuse — which makes every act of it a refusal of that pride.

**Live as though the hidden is seen, because it is.** The passage opens and closes on the same truth. What you conceal is not concealed. That should sober anyone carrying a private arrogance, and it should be a deep comfort to anyone whose sincerity, struggle, and unseen good is known to no one else at all.

passages.title: The deniers' verdict: tales of the ancients
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** Ayat 24–29 follow a single dismissive answer all the way to its end in the Fire. When the polytheists are asked what their Lord has sent down, they wave the question away: "Tales of the men of old" (24). Everything that follows is the price of that dismissal — the load they will carry for themselves and for those they misled (25), the precedent of earlier plotters whose own building came down on their heads (26), their exposure on the Day of Resurrection (27), and finally the moment of death, when they try to take it all back and are told that Allah already knows what they did (28–29). One answer, traced to its end.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The sūrah has been describing Allah's blessings and proving that He alone is unique in the creation of the universe, and it then made a pointed reference to how the polytheists chose to stick to their own ways of error. Now the text moves a step further: they were "not content with their own straying" and tried that others should also go astray like them — and this passage states the punishment they would get for doing that.

Notice also how the passage is placed. Maʿārif points out that the same question — *"What has your Lord revealed?"* — is put again five ayat later, in ayah 30, this time to believers who fear Allah; there we get their answer and the promise of reward for it. So ayah 24 is one half of a matched pair. Two groups, one question, two answers, two destinations. Reading 24–29 without knowing that 30 is coming is like hearing only the first of two witnesses.

**Who was asking?** The Qur'an does not explicitly say. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that commentators have expressed different views: some say the question was asked by disbelievers, others that it was asked by Muslims, still others take one of the two questions (24 and 30) to have been asked by the polytheists and the other by Muslims. But the Holy Qur'an has kept it ambiguous, and Maʿārif draws the lesson from that silence: there is no need to ask where the question came from — "What has to be seen is the answer and, more importantly, its ultimate consequence," which the Qur'an has itself chosen to describe. The passage is not interested in the interviewer. It is interested in what you say when the question lands on you.

## "Tales of the men of old" — a slogan, not a conclusion

Ibn Kathir's first observation about their reply is about its tone: they said this *"not wanting to answer."* It is a shrug engineered to close a subject rather than face it. The content of the charge, Ibn Kathir explains, is that nothing is revealed to him — what he is reciting to us is just tales of the men of old, taken from the previous Books. Ibn Kathir places it beside the fuller version of the same accusation elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"And they say: 'Tales of the ancients, which he has written down, and they are dictated to him morning and afternoon'"* (25:5).

But this was never a settled intellectual position, and Ibn Kathir shows why. Of that accusation he says plainly: they tell lies against the Messenger ﷺ and say things contradicting one another, but all of it is false. Watch what else they used to say about the same man — that he was a sorcerer, a poet, a soothsayer, or a madman. Ibn Kathir quotes: *"Look at the parables they make of you, so they have gone astray, and they are not able to find the right way"* (17:48), and adds the principle underneath it — **once they have gone beyond the bounds of the truth, whatever they say will be in error.** Leave the truth and you do not arrive somewhere else stable; you spend the rest of your life generating explanations that contradict each other.

Then Ibn Kathir tells us how the slogan was actually produced. They settled on an idea proposed by their leader, an individual known as Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah Al-Makhzumi, and the Qur'an itself films him working it out: *"He thought, and plotted. So let him be cursed, how he plotted! And once more let him be cursed, how he plotted! Then he thought. Then he frowned and he looked in a bad tempered way; then he turned back, and was proud. Then he said: 'This is nothing but the magic of old'"* (74:18–24) — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, something that had been transmitted and passed down. And then the line that gives the whole thing away: *"So they dispersed having agreed on this opinion."*

So the verdict in ayah 24 is not one man's honest reaction to hearing the Qur'an. It is a talking point — thought over, frowned over, and agreed upon before they dispersed. Hold that thought, because it is exactly why the next ayah charges them not merely with their own unbelief but with the unbelief of others.

## The double load (25)

The words are heavy on purpose. *Awzār* — burdens, loads. And the two measurements around them are precisely calibrated: their own burdens **in full** (*kāmilah*), and **some of** (*min*) the burdens of those they misled. Ibn Kathir: "they will carry the burden of their own sins and some of the burden of those who followed them and agreed with them," so they are "held guilty not only for going astray themselves, but also for tempting others and having them follow them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words: the total curse of their sins has to fall on them anyway on the Day of Judgment, and on top of that, part of the curse of the evil consequences of their role in misguiding others will also fall on them.

Ibn Kathir reads the opening *li-* of *li-yaḥmilū* as pointing to the decreed outcome: "We decreed that they would say that, so they will carry the burden…" The mockery and the load are not two separate events with a gap between them; the sentence runs straight from the mouth to the shoulders.

**And nothing is deducted from the follower.** This is the safeguard that stops the ayah from being turned into an excuse. Mujahid states it flatly: "They will bear the burden of their own sins, and they will bear the sins of those who obeyed them, but that will not lessen the punishment of those who obeyed them at all." So "I was only following what everyone was saying" buys nothing. The leader's extra load is added to his own account; it is not moved off yours. Ibn 'Abbas, in the report of al-'Awfi, reads our ayah together with *"They shall bear their own loads, and other loads besides their own; and they shall be questioned about their false allegations on the Day of Resurrection"* (29:13).

Ibn Kathir then cites a hadith for the law that stands behind all of this — quoting it here without naming a collection — and the law runs in both directions:

> "Whoever invites people to guidance, he will receive a reward like that of those who follow him, without diminishing their reward in the least. And whoever invites people to misguidance, he will bear a burden of sin like that of those who follow him, without diminishing their burden in the least."

Read that twice, because the first half is as true as the second. The same machinery that makes a repeated sneer catastrophic makes a repeated word of truth an investment that keeps paying after you are in the ground. Whatever you put into circulation keeps earning — for you or against you — long after you have forgotten saying it. Ayah 25 closes by naming what such a person is hauling: *evil indeed is that which they shall bear.*

## They are not the first (26)

Ayah 26 answers a question the deniers never asked: has this been tried before? *"Those before them indeed plotted…"* — *makr*, scheming, the quiet arranging of an outcome.

Who is meant? Al-'Awfi reported that Ibn 'Abbas said this refers to Namrud (Nimrod), who built the tower; others said it refers to Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar). But Ibn Kathir judges: **the correct view is that this is said by way of example**, to refute what was done by those who disbelieved in Allah and associated others in worship with Him. It is not the file of one named man; it is a verdict on a whole way of behaving. Ibn Kathir brings Nuh's words about his own people as the same phenomenon in an older age: *"And they have hatched a mighty scheme"* (71:22) — meaning, they used all sorts of ploys to misguide their people, and tempted them to join them in their shirk by every possible means. And he brings the scene where the followers round on the leaders on the Day of Resurrection: *"Nay, but it was your plotting by night and day, when you ordered us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him!"* (34:33). That is ayah 25's shared burden shown from the other side — the followers still ruined, and pointing.

Then the image. They built something. Allah came at their building **from the foundations** — Ibn Kathir: "He uprooted it and brought their efforts to naught." The roof fell down upon them **from above them**, and the torment overtook them **from directions they did not perceive.** Every clause is a reversal of what a plot is for. A plot exists to control what happens and to see it coming; here the blow lands from the one place that was never watched. A structure exists to shelter you; here the ceiling is the thing that falls. And the strike is not at the decoration but at the footings, so that everything above comes down at once.

Ibn Kathir sets two other verses alongside it: *"Every time they kindled the fire of war, Allah extinguished it"* (5:64), and *"But Allah's (torment) reached them from a place where they were not expecting it, and He cast terror into their hearts so that they destroyed their own dwellings with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So then take admonition, O you with eyes (to see)"* (59:2). Note where that last one ends — not with a report but with an instruction to the reader who still has eyes.

## The Day the secrets are read out (27)

The ruin of the building was in this world. Ayah 27 says *"Then, on the Day of Resurrection, He will disgrace them"* — and Ibn Kathir defines the disgrace precisely: Allah "will expose their scandalous deeds and what they used to hide in their hearts, and He will bring it out in the open." He cites *"The Day when all the secrets will be (exposed and) examined"* (86:9).

The punishment is fitted to the crime. Scheming lives on concealment; so the sentence is publication. Ibn Kathir supports this with a hadith found in the Two Sahihs, reported by Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that on the Day of Resurrection a banner will be set up for every deceitful person, its size in accordance with the amount of his deceit, and it will be said: "This is the one who deceived so-and-so, the son of so-and-so." Thus, as Ibn Kathir puts it, what they used to plot in secret will be made public, and Allah will humiliate them before all of His creation.

Then Allah Himself puts the question — Ibn Kathir says it is asked "in rebuke and reprimand" — *"Where are My (so-called) partners, those over which you caused so much discord?"* Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase: you fought and made enemies for their sake, so where are they now to help and save you? He adds *"Can they help you or (even) help themselves?"* (26:93) and *"Then will (man) have no power, nor any helper"* (86:10). When evidence and proof is established against them, and the Word of Allah is justified against them, and they are unable to give any excuse, realising that escape is impossible — then the closing verdict is spoken by *those who have been given the knowledge*, whom Ibn Kathir describes as the leaders in this world and the Hereafter, who know about the truth in both: *"Indeed it is a Day of disgrace and misery for the disbelievers."* Ibn Kathir explains: today those who disbelieved in Allah and worshipped others who have no power either to benefit or to harm them are now surrounded by disgrace and punishment. The final word on that Day belongs to those given knowledge.

## The surrender that comes too late (28–29)

Now the passage pulls back from the Last Day to the moment each of them actually meets it: death. Ibn Kathir titles this section *the condition of the disbeliever during and after death*. Allah informs us of the state of the idolaters "who are doing wrong to themselves when death approaches and the angels come to seize their evil souls." Note where the wrong lands: the ayah does not describe them as wronging the Prophet ﷺ — *ẓālimī anfusihim*, they are wronging **themselves**.

And then, at the very last moment, the collapse: *fa-alqaw al-salam* — they submit. Ibn Kathir explains it as a performance: "they will make it appear as if they used to listen and obey," saying *"We did not do any evil."* The same people who had agreed together on a verdict about the Qur'an now deny they ever did anything wrong. Ibn Kathir shows it is a reflex that survives death itself: *"By Allah, our Lord, we were not idolators"* (6:23), and *"On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all together; then they will swear to Him as they swear to you"* (58:18). They will swear to Allah with the same instinct they used when swearing to people — as though the technique that worked in the marketplace could work at the Throne.

The reply is a single word: *balā* — "Yes (you did)." It is the word that overturns a denial, and Ibn Kathir presents it as Allah rejecting what they say. What follows is not an argument, because there is nothing to argue: *"Truly, Allah is Most Knowing of what you did."* The case does not need proving; it needs only reading. (The rendering here puts the reply on the angels' lips; Ibn Kathir presents it as Allah's own rejection of their claim.)

Then ayah 29: *"So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein — and indeed, what an evil abode there is for the arrogant."* The passage ends by naming the disease, and the name is not ignorance or intellectual difficulty. It is *al-mutakabbirīn*, the arrogant: Ibn Kathir says this is a miserable position in the abode of humiliation "for those who were too arrogant to pay attention to the signs of Allah and follow His Messengers." Trace it back through the passage and it is one thread — al-Walid "turned back, and was proud"; and they said *tales of the men of old* rather than face the question they had been asked. Arrogance, not evidence, produced the verdict in ayah 24.

Ibn Kathir also notes the timing, which is sobering: they will enter Hell from the day they die with their souls, and their bodies will feel the heat and hot winds of their graves; then when the Day of Resurrection comes, their souls will be reunited with their bodies, to abide forever in the Fire — *"It will not be complete enough to kill them nor shall its torment be lightened for them"* (35:36), just as Fir'awn's people are exposed to the Fire *"morning and afternoon"* before the Hour is established (40:46). There is no interval of nothingness between the closing of the eyes and the sentence.

## Living it

**Answer the question.** The whole passage hangs on a reply to *"What has your Lord revealed?"* Maʿārif tells us the Qur'an kept the questioner ambiguous precisely so we would attend to the answer and its ultimate consequence. When the Book comes up — from a colleague, a child, a stranger, your own heart at 3am — the shrug is itself a position, and it is the one being judged here.

**Weigh what you pass on.** Ayah 25 is not aimed at private doubt but at circulated doubt. The line you forward, the joke you repeat, the take you post: by the hadith Ibn Kathir quotes above, that is a channel that keeps running after you have moved on — carrying reward or carrying load, without subtracting anything from anyone else's account.

**"Everyone was saying it" is not a defence.** Mujahid's note is deliberate: the leader's extra burden does not come off the follower's back.

**Do not scheme against a truth you have not faced.** Ayah 26 records people before them who plotted; Allah struck at the foundation of their building, the roof fell on them from above, and the torment overtook them from directions they did not perceive. The verse Ibn Kathir quotes alongside it closes with the only sane response: *take admonition, O you with eyes.*

passages.title: Those mindful of Allah: their answer and reward
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** In ayah 30 a question is put to the people of taqwa — the very same question that had been put to the deniers at ayah 24: *"What is it that your Lord has revealed?"* Their one-word answer opens out into everything that follows: good in this world, a better home in the next, Gardens of Eternity in ayah 31, and finally, in ayah 32, the angels themselves greeting the believer at the moment of death with *"Peace be upon you."*

What holds the three ayat together is that they trace a single unbroken arc — from a word spoken about revelation in this life, to the welcome spoken at the door of Paradise.

## The same question, two answers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. After the sūrah had laid out Allah's blessings and established that He alone creates, it turned to the polytheists who chose to stay in their error — and not only that, but who wanted others to go astray with them. That is where the first version of this question appears, at ayah 24, addressed to them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls their reply "haughty and ignorant."

Ibn Kathir states it plainly: asked *"What is it that your Lord has revealed?"*, they answer reluctantly, "He did not reveal anything, these are just the fables of old."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what that answer really is: a flat refusal to admit that any word from Allah had genuinely come down. They dismissed the Qur'an as nothing but tales of people from early ages — and by spreading that lie they pulled others down with them. The consequence, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is twofold: the whole weight of their own sins falls on them on the Day of Judgment, and on top of that a share of the evil consequence of the role they played in misguiding others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the account by noting what was then said — that the burden of sins these people are piling up on their shoulders is a terribly evil burden.

Then, a short distance later, the same question is put again — this time to those who fear Allah. Ibn Kathir frames our passage in exactly these terms: here we are told about **the blessed, as opposed to the doomed.** Same words, opposite hearts, opposite destinies. That contrast is the frame you should read ayat 30–32 inside.

## Who is asking?

Notice that the Qur'an never explicitly says who put the question. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that this silence produced genuine difference of opinion among the commentators: some said the question was asked by the disbelievers, others that it was asked by the Muslims, and still others took one of the two questions to have come from the polytheists and the other from the Muslims.

Rather than settle it, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ambiguity as deliberate. The Qur'an has kept it ambiguous, it says, to indicate that there is no need to ask where the question came from. What has to be seen is **the answer — and, more importantly, its ultimate consequence**, which is precisely what the Qur'an itself chose to describe.

That is a quietly liberating way to read the passage. The question is not a historical curiosity to be pinned to a particular interrogator. It is a question that finds every person: *what do you say has come down from your Lord?* And the passage answers not by identifying the asker, but by following each answer to where it ends.

## "Good." — the answer of the mindful

Their reply is a single word: **khayran** — "that which is good."

Ibn Kathir fills in the sentence that word is standing in for: *He revealed something good.* And he explains what makes it good — it is **mercy and blessings for those who followed it and believed in it.**

Sit with the difference. The deniers gave a verdict on the Qur'an from the outside, as spectators: old fables, nothing new. Those with taqwa answer from the inside, as people who have actually received something. They are not producing a theological argument; they are reporting an experience of Allah's speech. It came down, and it was good — good in itself, and good for whoever takes it up.

There is also a lesson in who gets to answer this way. Ibn Kathir describes the ones who say it as **"those who had Taqwa (piety and righteousness)"** — the answer follows the state of the heart. The tongue is only reporting what the life already knows.

## The "good" turns out to be a promise

The second half of ayah 30 does something easy to miss. Having recorded their answer — "that which is good" — the passage does not move on. It shows you what that good actually consists of. Ibn Kathir marks the transition: *"Then we are told about Allah's promise to His servants which He revealed to His Messengers."*

So the promise that follows is not a new subject. It is the content of the answer. When they said "good," this is the good:

**"For those who do good in this world, there is good."** Ibn Kathir reads this to mean that whoever does good in this world, Allah rewards him for his good deeds **in this world and in the next**, and he brings alongside it a verse from later in this same sūrah:

> *"Whoever works righteousness — whether male or female — while being a true believer, verily to him We will give a good life, and We shall certainly reward them in proportion to the best of what they used to do."* (16:97)

Two things in that cross-reference are worth pausing on. First, the reward is not held back entirely for later: Ibn Kathir is explicit that it comes **in this world and in the next**, and the ayah he cites speaks of a good life given here. Second, the measure of reward is "the best of what they used to do." The reckoning is generous; it is calibrated to a person's best, not their average.

**"And the home of the Hereafter will be better."** Ibn Kathir explains this simply: better than the life of this world, and the reward there more complete than the reward here.
