Instead, as Maʿārif describes it, "a general decrease sets in": wealth, health, fitness, means of sustenance, comfort and peace all go on shrinking, until the day comes when the people so punished disappear from the face of the earth for good. This is the sense behind the translation "destroy them gradually."

Both senses are traced back to early authorities. The fear-sense reaches us through Ibn Kathir, who reports it from Ibn ʿAbbās (by way of Al-ʿAwfī) and from Mujāhid, Ad-Daḥḥāk and Qatādah; the *tanaqquṣ*-sense reaches us through Maʿārif, which reports it from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and other Imams of tafsir. It is less a conflict than a word with two live senses, each describing a real way that Allah's grip closes.

**How ʿUmar settled it.** Maʿārif preserves a report from **Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab**, whom Maʿārif calls "the noble tābiʿī" — a *tābiʿī* being someone of the generation that came after the Prophet's ﷺ Companions. Sayyidnā **ʿUmar** himself hesitated over the meaning of this word. He addressed the Companions from the minbar and asked them what they understood *takhawwuf* to mean. The gathering fell silent. Then a man from the tribe of **Hudhayl** spoke up: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is a particular idiom of our tribe. We use this word in the sense of *tanaqquṣ* — to decrease gradually." ʿUmar pressed him: do the Arabs use it in that sense in their poetry? The man said they do, and recited a couplet of **Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī**, a poet of his own tribe, in which the word carried exactly that meaning. ʿUmar then turned to the people and said: **"O people, learn about the poetry of Jāhiliyyah, because there lies the key to the explanation of your Book and the sense of your speech."**

Notice what the scene teaches before any conclusion is drawn from it. The Commander of the Faithful did not bluff; he asked. And the answer came from an ordinary tribesman who happened to know his own dialect.

**Two things Maʿārif draws out of this report:**

- **Casual Arabic is not enough to understand the Qur'an.** Being able to speak and write Arabic does not by itself qualify a person to understand revelation. What is needed is a level of competence and awareness that reaches back to the classical usage of the Arabs of the Jāhiliyyah — because the Qur'an was revealed in *that* language and *that* idiom. Maʿārif goes so far as to call learning Arabic literature at that level incumbent on Muslims.
- **Reading pre-Islamic poetry is permissible**, even though such poetry is inevitably full of pagan themes, customs, sayings and doings that run counter to Islam. Because the need — understanding the Qur'an — is so weighty, reading and teaching that poetry was declared permissible.

## Why a passage of threats ends in mercy

After four ways of being seized, ayah 47 lands on: **فَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمْ لَرَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ** — "Indeed your Lord is full of kindness, Most Merciful." Why here?

**Ibn Kathir's answer:** precisely *because* He does not hasten to punish. The delay itself is the kindness. He cites what is reported in the Two Sahihs: *"No one is more patient in the case of hearing offensive speech than Allah, for they attribute to Him a son, while He alone is giving them provision and good health."* Read that against ayat 45–47: the same people plotting against Him are eating His provision and enjoying the health He gives them, and He does not strike.

But respite is not acquittal. Ibn Kathir immediately cites, also from the Two Sahihs: *"Allah will let the wrongdoer continue until, when He begins to punish him, He will never let him go."* The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then recited: "Such is the punishment of your Lord when He seizes the (population of) towns while they are doing wrong. Indeed, His punishment is painful, (and) severe" (11:102). Ibn Kathir adds: "And many a township did I give respite while it was given to wrongdoing. Then I punished it. And to Me is the (final) return (of all)" (22:48).

**Maʿārif's reading of the wording is finer still.** First, Allah says *your **Rabb*** — your Lord. The choice of that name, Maʿārif observes, hints that all these punishments which overtake people in this world are there **to warn them**, as part of the dictates of divine mercy. Second, *Raʾūf* is preceded by the emphatic **lām of taʾkīd** ("لَرَءُوفٌ") — stressing that Allah is *Very* Kind, *Very* Merciful. The hint, Maʿārif says, is that the warnings sent during the life of this world are in reality called for by His intrinsic kindness and mercy: they exist so that heedless men and women would learn from the warning and correct their deeds. Maʿārif titles this section pointedly — **even the punishment of this world is mercy in disguise**.

## Living it

**Do not read delay as permission.** The whole passage is aimed at a particular feeling — the settled sense of being safe. Nothing has happened, therefore nothing will. Ibn Kathir's framing removes the ground from under that feeling: the silence is Allah's patience, not His approval.

**Watch what your wrongdoing recruits.** Ibn Kathir specifies people who do evil *and call others to do likewise*. Influence multiplies a sin. Whatever you make normal for others, you carry.

**Take a decline seriously.** On the *tanaqquṣ* reading of ayah 47, a slow shrinking of health, provision, ease and peace can itself be the seizure. Maʿārif's own conclusion tells you what such a warning is *for*: not despair, but that a person learn from the warning and correct their deeds. A losing season is an invitation to return before the door narrows further.

**Learn the language properly.** ʿUmar's instruction from the minbar is a live one. Depth in Arabic — not conversational fluency, but the classical usage the Qur'an was revealed in — is a key to the Book.

**Hold the two ends together.** Ayat 45–47 do exactly that: four hammer blows of possibility, and then the reminder that your Lord is Raʾūf, Raḥīm. Fear without that ending becomes despair; the ending without that fear becomes carelessness. The passage gives you both in a single breath.

passages.title: All creation bows in submission to Allah
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** Allah answers denial not with an argument but with something anyone can see: the shadow at your feet, shifting from right to left, morning and evening, prostrating to its Lord all day long. Ayat 48–50 run in one sweep from the lowest rung of creation to the highest — from the shadows of mute objects, through the moving creatures of the earth, up to the angels — and Ibn Kathir's heading over the whole stretch is simply *Everything prostrates to Allah*.

## Where this falls in the sūrah

Ibn Kathir's summary of what Allah is doing here is worth keeping in view from the start. Allah "informs us about His might, majesty and pride, meaning that all things submit themselves to Him and every created being — animate and inanimate, as well as the responsible — humans and Jinns, and the angels — all humble themselves before Him."

Just before this, the sūrah mentioned various punishments that could seize disbelievers within this world, and it closed that warning with the words **fa-inna rabbakum la-Raʼūfun Raḥīm** — "So, indeed your Lord is Very Kind Very Merciful." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out how carefully that closing line is built. First, by using the word **Rabb** (Lord), "the hint given is that all these punishments which overtake human beings in this world are there to warn them as part of the dictates of Divine mercy." Then comes **Raʼūf** (Kind), headed by the intensifying particle *lām* — the *lām of taʼkīd*, an emphatic particle attached to a word to press its meaning home. The stress on Allah being Very Kind and Very Merciful carries the hint that the warnings sent during the life of this world "were, in reality, called for by His intrinsic Kindness and Mercy so that heedless men and women would learn from the warning and correct their deeds."

That is the door into ayah 48. Having been reminded that His warnings are mercy, they are now asked, with great gentleness, simply to *look*.

## Ayah 48: "Have they not observed things that Allah has created?"

The question is not whether they have worked through a difficult idea. It is whether they have *observed*. And the evidence chosen is utterly ordinary — **mā khalaqa Allāhu min shayʼ**, anything at all that Allah has created. Pick any object. Watch its shadow.

The ayah continues: "(how) their shadows shift from right to left, prostrating to Allah while they are humble." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah "tells us that everything that has a shadow leaning to the right and the left, i.e., in the morning and the evening, is by its shadow, prostrating to Allah." The shadow does not stay put. It leans one way early and the other way late, and that daily leaning is itself named as prostration.

**Wa hum dākhirūn — "while they are humble."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is plain: it "means, they are in a state of humility." Notice what creation is *not* described as doing. It is not negotiating, not deliberating, not weighing whether to comply. It is simply humbled, and it stays humbled.

## The early authorities on the shadow

The commentary preserves several early readings of what prostration means for things that have no minds:

- **Mujahid** said: "When the sun passes its zenith, everything prostrates to Allah, may He be glorified." Ibn Kathir notes that Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and others said the same. At the hour the sun tips past its highest point and every standing thing begins to throw its shade again, all of creation is described as going down.
- **Mujahid** also said, more sharply: "The prostration of every thing is its shadow" — and he mentioned the mountains, saying that their prostrations are their shadows. The granite peak that will never bend has, all along, been laying something down before Allah.
- **Abu Ghalib Ash-Shaybani** said: "The waves of the sea are its prayers." The restless heaving of the ocean, which looks like the least orderly thing in nature, is read as worship in progress.

Ibn Kathir then makes the observation that ties this together: "It is as if reason is attributed to these inanimate objects when they are described as prostrating." The Qurʼān speaks of stones and mountains and waves the way one would speak of worshippers, because in the matter that counts most — submission to Allah — that is exactly how they behave.

## Ayah 49: everything, with nothing left over

**Wa lillāhi yasjudu mā fī as-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍi min dābbah** — "And to Allah prostrate all that are in the heavens and all that are in the earth, of the moving creatures."

Ibn Kathir sets alongside it another ayah where Allah says the same thing in wider terms: "And to Allah (alone) all who are in the heavens and the earth fall in prostration, willingly or unwillingly, and so do their shadows in the mornings and in the afternoons." (13:15)

That second verse adds the phrase that carries the whole passage: **ṭawʻan wa karhan**, willingly or unwillingly. Submission is not the optional part. What is optional is only the spirit in which it is given. And note that the verse ends where ayah 48 began — with shadows, in the mornings and in the afternoons. Bodies and the shade those bodies throw are both counted in.

**Dābbah**, rendered "moving creature," sweeps in the animal life of the earth alongside the human being. Ibn Kathir's summary of who is included leaves no one standing outside it: every created being, "animate and inanimate, as well as the responsible — humans and Jinns, and the angels."

## The angels, named on their own

Everything in the heavens is already covered by the opening of ayah 49 — and then the angels are named anyway, with a description of their own: **wa al-malāʼikatu wa hum lā yastakbirūn**, "and the angels, and they are not proud." Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line: "they prostrate to Allah and are not too proud to worship Him."

Set that against how the passage began. Ibn Kathir said these ayat are Allah informing us of "His might, majesty and pride." That is where might and majesty belong. The angels — the highest order of created beings in the picture, and the ones with the most to be impressed by in themselves — are described precisely by what they do *not* claim. They are not too proud to worship. Greatness in a creature turns out to be no exemption at all; it is simply one more thing that bows.

## Ayah 50: fear from above, and obedience without gaps

**Yakhāfūna rabbahum min fawqihim** — "They fear their Lord above them." Ibn Kathir: this means "they prostrate out of fear of their Lord, may He be glorified." The ayah affirms that their Lord is above them, and the commentary stays with what the words say: the fear is real, and what it produces is a prostration.

That is worth pausing over. The angels' worship is not easy familiarity. They live in the presence of a Lord whose majesty they perceive far better than we do, and it moves them. And their fear does not send them running — it puts them on the ground. Right fear of Allah drives a servant toward Him, not away.

**Wa yafʻalūna mā yuʼmarūn** — "and they do what they are commanded." Ibn Kathir's gloss covers both halves of obedience: "they continually obey Allah, doing what He tells them to do and avoiding that which He forbids." *Continually* is the key word. No gap, no slack season, no command deferred until later. This is what makes the angels a standard and not merely a wonder — the substance of what they do is available to us in kind, if not in degree: do what you are told, leave what you are forbidden, and do not stop.

## The mark at the end of ayah 50

In the muṣḥaf, ayah 50 closes with the small symbol ۩ — the sign of a prostration in recitation. So the passage does not end with an argument. It ends by asking your body for the very thing it has just described the whole universe doing. You have been shown mountains prostrating by their shadows, seas praying by their waves, angels bowing without pride. Now the reciter is invited to go down too.

## Living it

**Look up from the argument.** The passage answers denial with observation, not debate: *have they not observed?* When faith feels abstract, the Qurʼān's own method here is to send you outside — to the shifting shade, the animal doing exactly what it was made for, the tide. Ibn Kathir's heading says it in four words: *Everything prostrates to Allah*. You are surrounded, at every moment, by creation already worshipping.

**Notice that you are already submitting.** Since all that is in the heavens and the earth falls in prostration "willingly or unwillingly," the real question the passage puts is not *whether* you will submit but in what spirit. Your own prostration is not an alien posture imposed on you; it is a human being finally getting into step with everything else that exists.

**Pride is the one thing that breaks the pattern.** The angels' description is negative before it is positive — first *they are not proud*, then *they do what they are commanded*. Obedience follows the removal of self-importance. Wherever obedience is failing in a life, that is the first place to look.

**Let midday remind you.** Mujahid, Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak all tied this prostration to the sun passing its zenith: when it tips past its highest point, everything prostrates to Allah. Let the moment the shadows begin to lean be a call — everything around you has just bowed.

**And remember what opened the door here.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point about the previous ayah — that even the warnings and punishments of this world flow from Allah being *Raʼūf* and *Raḥīm*, so that heedless men and women "would learn from the warning and correct their deeds" — is what makes this passage an invitation rather than a threat. Allah did not have to show anyone the evidence. He showed it out of kindness, so that we would look, and join the prostration while there is still time to join it willingly.

passages.title: One Lord alone, yet ingratitude after relief
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These five ayat take the single greatest truth — that Allah alone is worthy of worship — and then bring it down from the heavens to the reader's own life: to the blessings already in his hands, and to the cry that leaves his mouth the moment disaster strikes. The unity of the passage is that movement. Ayah 51 gives the command; ayah 52 grounds it in Allah's total ownership; ayah 53 brings it down to your own blessings and your own panic; ayah 54 exposes what many people do the instant the danger passes; ayah 55 names that behaviour for what it is — ingratitude — and closes with a warning dressed as an invitation.

Ibn Kathir sums up the opening of the passage in one sentence: Allah is telling us that there is no god but He, that no one else should be worshipped except Him, alone, without partners, "for He is the Sovereign, Creator, and Lord of all things." Everything that follows in these ayat is an unpacking of that "for".

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the note struck just before this passage. Having mentioned various punishments that could seize disbelievers within this world, the passage before ours ends: **fa-inna rabbakum la-raʼūfun raḥīm** — "So, indeed your Lord is Very Kind, Very Merciful."

That ending is doing careful work. First, Allah is named there as **Rabb** — "your Lord". The hint given by that name, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is that all these punishments which overtake human beings in this world are there to warn them, as part of the dictates of Divine mercy. Then comes **Raʼūf** — Kind — headed by the intensifying particle *lām* (the *lām of taʼkīd*, the prefix that adds emphasis to the word that follows), placing stress on the fact that Allah is Very Kind and Very Merciful. The hint, again, is that the warnings sent during the life of this world are in reality called for by His intrinsic Kindness and Mercy, so that heedless men and women would learn from the warning and correct their deeds.

Hold that in mind, because our passage ends with a threat — and the threat is issued by the same Lord who has just been described as Very Kind and Very Merciful.

## "Do not take two gods" (ayah 51)

Ibn Kathir renders the ayah: **"Do not worship two gods. Indeed, He (Allah) is only One. Then fear Me Alone."** Three movements in one breath — a prohibition, a statement of fact, and a command that follows from the fact.

His heading over the section says it plainly: *Allah Alone is Deserving of Worship*. Allah tells us that there is no god but He, and that no one else should be worshipped except Him, alone, without partners — and Ibn Kathir gives the reason in the same sentence: **"for He is the Sovereign, Creator, and Lord of all things."** That is the logic of the whole passage in miniature. The claim to be worshipped alone rests on being the sole Owner, the sole Maker, the sole Master. If that is who He is, a second is not merely forbidden; there is no room for one.

Notice too where the command lands: **"Then fear Me Alone."** Not only worship — *fear*. The passage will return to this in the very next ayah with the question, "Will you then fear any other than Allah?"

And note who is speaking. Ayah 51 opens "**And Allah has said** …" — the ruling on tawhid is not being reported by a preacher or argued by a philosopher. It is Allah's own speech about Himself.

## Everything is His — and religion is His *wāṣiban* (ayah 52)

Ayah 52 supplies the grounds. **"To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth"** — which is why Ibn Kathir calls Him "the Sovereign, Creator, and Lord of all things." Ownership on that scale leaves nothing over that a second god could claim.

Then a word that the early authorities discussed carefully: **wa lahu-d-dīnu wāṣiban** — "and to Him belongs *al-dīn* (religion, obedience), *wāṣiban*." Ibn Kathir records three explanations:

- **"Forever."** This is what Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Maymun bin Mahran, As-Suddi, Qatadah and others said it means. Allah's right to religion and obedience does not lapse with time.
- **"Obligatory."** It was also reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said this. On this reading, *wāṣiban* says that this devotion is *due* — a debt owed, not an optional gift the servant may or may not present.
- **"Purely for Him."** This is Mujahid's explanation — meaning, as Ibn Kathir puts it, that worship is due to Him Alone, from whoever is in the heavens and on earth.

These explanations enrich rather than contradict one another: obedience owed to Allah is permanent, it is binding, and it belongs to Him purely.

**Two ways to read the question that follows.** The ayah then asks: **"Will you then fear any other than Allah?"** Ibn Kathir reports that the scholars took this in two different ways, and it is worth knowing both:

- On the opinion of **Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrimah**, the ayah is *merely stating the case* — describing reality as it already is. Ibn Kathir cites alongside it: **"Do they seek other than the religion of Allah, while to Him submitted all creatures in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly. And to Him shall they all be returned"** (3:83). Willingly or unwillingly, every creature is inside His dominion.
- On the opinion of **Mujahid**, it is by way of *instruction* — i.e., it is saying: you had better fear associating partners in worship with Me, and be sincere in your obedience to Me. Ibn Kathir places alongside this reading Allah's words, **"Surely, the pure religion (sincere devotion) is for Allah only"** (39:3).

One reading opens your eyes; the other takes you by the collar. Both land in the same place.

## Every blessing has one address (ayah 53)

Having established His ownership, Allah now turns from the cosmos to your own hands: **"Whatever blessings you have are from Allah."**

Ibn Kathir's comment is that Allah is telling us here that He is the One Who has the power to benefit and to harm, and that the provisions, blessings, good health and help His servants enjoy are from His bounty and graciousness towards them. Note the range: not just the dramatic rescues, but *provision* (the daily income), *good health* (the thing nobody notices until it fails), and *help* (every hand that ever arrived at the right moment). Every one of them is traced back to a single source.

**"Then whenever hardship touches you, to Him you cry aloud for help."** The cry here is not a composed request but a raised one — Ibn Kathir's rendering keeps the word *aloud*. And his explanation of *why* people do this is the pivot of the whole passage: it is **"because you know that none has the power to remove that harm except for Him, so when you are harmed, you turn to ask Him for help and beg Him for aid."**

That is the argument. Not "you *should* know" — *you already know*. Ibn Kathir brings the sea as the illustration: **"And when harm touches you at sea, those that you call upon vanish, except for Him. But when He brings you safe to land, you turn away. And man is ever ungrateful"** (17:67). On a boat that is going down, the ones called upon simply vanish — all but Him.

## The turn (ayah 54)

**"Then, when He has removed the harm from you, behold! some of you associate others in worship with their Lord."**

The word "behold" in Ibn Kathir's rendering catches the suddenness: the reversal arrives the moment the pressure lifts. Laid out plainly, the sequence is deliberately embarrassing — He gives you every blessing; harm comes; you cry to Him alone because you know there is no one else who can lift it; He removes it; and then partners are assigned to Him.

Two details repay attention. First, the ayah says **"a group of you" / "some of you"** — *farīqun minkum* — not all. The Qur'an is precise; it does not sweep everyone into the charge. But that precision also removes the comfort of hiding in the crowd, because the reader is left asking which group he is in. Second, the partners are assigned **"to their Lord" — *bi-rabbihim***. He is still *their Lord* at the very moment they do it — the same title, *Rabb*, that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān showed carries the note of care even when what follows is a warning.

## "So they are ungrateful for what We have given them" (ayah 55)

Ibn Kathir notes that the *lām* at the head of this ayah — the prefix on *li-yakfurū*, rendered "So" in his text — was discussed. It was said that it **indicates sequence**: it marks what came next, the outcome that followed. It was also said that it **serves an explanatory function**, the sense being: 'We decreed that they would conceal the truth and deny the blessings that Allah has bestowed upon them. He is the One Who bestows blessings and the One Who removes distress.'

That last line is worth pausing over, because it fixes the offence in place. The One who bestows the blessing and the One who removes the distress are not two parties: they are the same One — and He is the One being denied.

**"So enjoy yourselves — but you will soon come to know."** Ibn Kathir introduces this as a threat: Allah threatens them, saying *fa-tamattaʿū*, meaning, **do what you like and enjoy what you have for a little while**. That last phrase is the whole point; the enjoyment is real but rationed. And *fa-sawfa taʿlamūn* — "but you will soon come to know" — means, Ibn Kathir says, **the consequences of that**. The ayah does not spell the consequences out. It leaves them just over the horizon, which is more unsettling than any description would be.

## Living it

**Do the accounting honestly.** Ayah 53 says every blessing you have is from Allah. That is not only about rescues; Ibn Kathir lists provisions, blessings, good health and help. Sit with your own list — the income, the body that still works, the person who showed up when you needed one — and follow each line back to its source.

**Watch the moment *after* relief.** The passage does not fault the cry of ayah 53; that cry is the natural response of someone who knows none but He can lift the harm. The failure in ayah 54 happens *afterwards*, in the ordinary hours once the danger passes. Diagnosis: notice how you speak about a crisis that resolved. Was it Allah who removed it — or the doctor, the contact, the lucky timing, your own cleverness? To cry out to Him in the storm and then turn away on dry land is exactly the pattern of 17:67, which Ibn Kathir places beside this ayah.

**Aim the fear correctly.** On Mujahid's reading of ayah 52, "Will you then fear any other than Allah?" is instruction: fear associating partners in worship with Him, and be sincere in your obedience to Him. And on Mujahid's explanation of *wāṣiban*, worship is due to Him Alone — sincerity is not an extra polish on worship; it is what worship is.

**Hear the warning as kindness.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point about the preceding ayat sits naturally beside the threat that closes ours. A warning that reaches you while you can still act on it is what a Lord who is Raʼūf and Raḥīm does for the heedless — so that they would learn from the warning and correct their deeds. "You will soon come to know" is spoken *before* the knowing, and that timing is itself a mercy.

passages.title: A share for the idols, daughters for Allah
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat lay out what Ibn Kathir calls "some of the heinous deeds" of the idolaters of Arabia — and they are placed side by side so that we can see they are really one deed. They took what Allah had provided for them and carved out a share of it for their idols (ayah 56); they assigned daughters to Allah (ayah 57); and they could not themselves bear to be given a daughter (ayat 58–59). The same crooked scale is at work throughout. Ibn Kathir puts his finger on it twice: of the offerings, "they gave preference to their gods over Him"; of the children, "they choose the males for themselves, rejecting the daughters that they assign to Allah."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the two traits censured in the second half of the passage. First, "they would take the birth of a baby girl to be so bad that they would go about hiding from people to avoid being disgraced before them." Then, "on top of it, they had turned so irrational that the child they did not like to have as their own, that they would be audacious enough to attribute to Allah Almighty by declaring that the angels were His daughters!"

And the passage names the fault in four words at the end: *alā sāʼa mā yaḥkumūn*, "Certainly, evil is their decision."

## Ayah 56: a share cut out of Allah's own gift

Ibn Kathir opens by telling us what kind of people are being described: those "who used to perform baseless worship of other gods besides Him, such as idols and statues, with no grounds for doing so." They would take the provision Allah had given them and give their idols a share of it.

Notice how the ayah declines to dignify those gods with a name. Ibn Kathir renders the phrase **li-mā lā yaʿlamūn** as "to what they have no knowledge of," and supplies the identification in a bracket: "(false deities)." These are the same gods he has just described — worshipped with no grounds at all. And the thing being handed over is **mimmā razaqnāhum** — "of that which *We* have provided them with." The gift is being redistributed in front of the Giver.

Ibn Kathir brings a verse from Sūrat al-Anʿām to show how the division actually worked in practice:

> "They say: 'This is for Allah,' according to their claim, 'and this is for our partners.' But the share of their 'partners' is not directed to Allah, while the share of Allah is directed to their 'partners'! How evil is that with which they judge." (6:136)

The accounting was rigged. If something meant for the idols strayed into Allah's portion it was pulled back; if something in Allah's portion strayed toward the idols it was left there. "That is they assigned a share for their idols as well as Allah," says Ibn Kathir, "but they gave preference to their gods over Him."

Keep an eye on the closing words of that verse — "How evil is that with which they judge." It is the very sentence our passage will land on in ayah 59. The same verdict covers the offering and the offspring, because it is the same crime of judgement.

## The oath at the end of ayah 56

Then the tone changes. **Ta-llāhi la-tusʼalunna ʿammā kuntum taftarūn** — "By Allah, you shall certainly be questioned about (all) that you used to fabricate."

Ibn Kathir's comment is worth sitting with: "Allah swore by His Almighty Self to question them about these lies and fabrications. He will most certainly call them to account for it and give them the unrelenting punishment in the fire of Hell."

So this is not a warning issued in passing. Ibn Kathir reads it as an oath — Allah swearing by His own Almighty Self — and the certainty carries straight into the words: you shall *certainly* be questioned. It is a sworn appointment.

And note what they will be questioned about: not merely the portion they misallocated, but **mā kuntum taftarūn** — what they *used to fabricate*. The share given to the idols was the visible symptom; the fabrication behind it is what the questioning is for.

## Ayah 57: daughters for Allah

From the misallocated provision, the ayah moves straight to the misallocated child — and Ibn Kathir shows that this is where the fabrication becomes grotesque.

"Then Allah tells us how they used to regard the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, as being female, and that they considered them to be Allah's daughters, and they worshipped them with Him. In all of the above, they made very serious errors."

Ibn Kathir lays those errors out, and they come in layers, each worse than the last.

**First**, "they attributed offspring to Him when He has no offspring." This is the root error, and it is a matter of creed before it is a matter of taste. That is why the ayah interrupts itself the moment the claim is uttered: **subḥānahu** — "Glorified (and Exalted) is He." Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: "meaning, above their claims and fabrications." The word does not argue; it recoils. It puts distance between Allah and the sentence just spoken.

**Second**, having invented offspring for Him, "then they assigned Him the kind of offspring they regarded as inferior, namely daughters, which they did not even want for themselves." Ibn Kathir cites Sūrat al-Najm on this: "Are the males for you and the females for Him? That is indeed an unfair division!" (53:21–22) — and Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt: "But no! It is from their falsehood that they say: 'Allah has begotten.' They are certainly liars! Has He (then) chosen daughters rather than sons? What is the matter with you? How do you decide?" (37:151–154)

**Third**, they took the angels — "who are servants of the Most Merciful" — regarded them as female, "and they worshipped them with Him."

Then the ayah's last words land like a blade: **wa lahum mā yashtahūn** — "And for themselves, what they desire." Ibn Kathir: "meaning they choose the males for themselves, rejecting the daughters that they assign to Allah. Exalted be Allah far above what they say!" They kept what they wanted. What was left over went upward.

## Ayah 58: the face that darkens

Now the Qur'an stops arguing and simply shows us a man.

**Wa idhā bushshira aḥaduhum bil-unthā** — rendered here as "Whenever one of them is given the good news of a baby girl." A child has been born; the announcement is framed as good news. But look at what it does to him:

**ẓalla wajhuhu muswaddan** — "his face becomes dark." Ibn Kathir: "meaning with distress and grief." The colour drains and the features close.

**wa huwa kaẓīm** — "and he is filled with inner grief." Ibn Kathir explains: "meaning he is silent because of the intensity of the grief he feels." He does not shout. He says nothing at all — which is far more chilling than shouting. And nobody around him has done anything but bring him news of a birth.

## Ayah 59: hiding, and the two burials

**Yatawārā min al-qawm** — "He hides himself from the people." Ibn Kathir: "meaning he does not want anyone to see him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the social mechanism: they took the birth of a baby girl "to be so bad that they would go about hiding from people to avoid being disgraced before them." His grief is not even private sorrow. It is bound up with disgrace in front of an audience.

**min sūʼi mā bushshira bihi** — "because of the evil of that whereof he has been informed." The Qur'an lets two words collide within a single line: the same verb of announcement, *bushshira*, that opened ayah 58, and now *sūʼ*, evil. Nothing about the child has changed between the two ayat. Only the scale he is weighing her on.

Then the ayah gives us his deliberation, and it is a horror to read as a question with two options:

**a-yumsikuhu ʿalā hūnin am yadussuhu fī l-turāb** — "Shall he keep her with dishonor or bury her in the earth?"

Ibn Kathir unpacks the first option, and this is the part most readers skim past: to keep her *ʿalā hūn* means "should he keep her, humiliating her, **not letting her inherit from him and not taking care of her, preferring his male children over her**?" So option one is not mercy. It is a slower version of the same contempt — the girl lives, but she is cut out of the inheritance, denied proper care, ranked below her brothers in her own home.

And the second: "**or bury her in the earth?**" — Ibn Kathir: "meaning bury her alive, as they used to do during the days of ignorance."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the whole miserable calculation as the man himself experienced it: should he swallow his pride, "embrace the disgrace of becoming the father of a baby girl and resign to the disaster with patience, or just ditch it alive into the dust and get rid of it?" That is the moral universe the Qur'an is dismantling — one in which a newborn daughter is a "disaster" to be either endured or disposed of.

And then Ibn Kathir asks the question the whole passage has been building toward: **"How could they dislike something so intensely, yet attribute it to Allah?"**

That is the hinge. Ayah 57 and ayah 59 are the same accusation from two directions. A man who would bury a daughter in the sand to avoid the neighbours' faces will, in the same breath, tell you that Allah has daughters.

## "Certainly, evil is their decision"

**Alā sāʼa mā yaḥkumūn.** Ibn Kathir: "meaning how evil are the words they say, the way they want to share things out and the things they attribute to Him."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precise reading here, noting that this has been pointed out in Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ with reference to Ibn ʿAṭiyyah: this closing sentence "actually incorporates these very two traits" the passage has censured —

1. "that their decision to take girls to be a punishment and a disgrace is by itself an evil decision"; and
2. "that the thing they would consider a matter of disgrace for their own selves, they would be too ready to attribute to Allah Taʿālā."

So the verdict is not only about theology and not only about baby girls. It is one verdict on one faculty: *ḥukm*, judgement — the deciding, the apportioning, the working out of what a thing is worth. Their scales are broken, so everything they weigh comes out wrong: what a gift is worth, what a daughter is worth, what their Lord is worth.

## Living it

The passage is uncomfortably practical, and it is worth being honest about how it reaches us.

**Ibn Kathir's description of "keeping her with dishonor" is a checklist, not a relic.** Not letting her inherit. Not taking care of her. Preferring the male children over her. Wherever a daughter is treated as a lesser claim on a father's money, time, education, or delight, the passage is speaking — the sand has simply been replaced with something more presentable.

**The word of announcement is a standard to be measured against.** The ayah is rendered "Whenever one of them is given the good news of a baby girl" — and then it shows us the man whose face darkens at exactly that news. What the heart does at such an announcement is a test of whose scale it is using.

**And the deepest lesson is about Allah, not about ourselves.** These men held a low opinion of daughters and then handed daughters to Allah. That is Ibn Kathir's astonished question — how could they dislike something so intensely, and still attribute it to Him? Whatever a person truly thinks of Allah eventually shows up in what he considers good enough to offer Him.

The believer's response is the word the ayah itself supplies at the very moment the false claim is made: **subḥānahu**. Glorified and Exalted is He — as Ibn Kathir says, "above their claims and fabrications," and "Exalted be Allah far above what they say." Whatever is deficient, whatever we would not want for ourselves, whatever is unworthy — Allah is far above it. And so what we bring Him should be the first and best of what He gave us, not the leftovers.

passages.title: The highest description is Allah's; punishment deferred, not cancelled
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These three ayat close a long exposure of pagan belief and then turn it on its head. Ayah 60 delivers the verdict on people who speak badly about Allah; ayah 61 answers the question that verdict raises — if their crime is this ugly, why is the world still standing?; ayah 62 returns to the fabrication, adds the lie the fabricators tell themselves about their own future, and names where it ends. What holds them together is a single thread: **what a person says about Allah, and the deadline attached to saying it.**

## The indictment these ayat are answering

To feel ayah 60 you have to hear what comes just before it, which Ibn Kathir lays out in full. The idolaters took the provision Allah Himself had given them and set aside a share of it for idols — and, as the Qur'an says elsewhere in an ayah Ibn Kathir quotes here, whatever was allotted to the "partners" never found its way to Allah, while whatever was allotted to Allah did find its way to the partners (6:136). They gave their gods preference over the One who fed them.

Then they went further. They called the angels — servants of the Most Merciful — female, made them Allah's daughters, and worshipped them alongside Him. Ibn Kathir counts the errors stacked inside that one belief: they attributed offspring to Allah when He has no offspring; then they assigned Him the kind of offspring **they themselves regarded as inferior**; the very kind they did not even want for themselves. As the Qur'an puts it in an ayah he cites, "Are the males for you and the females for Him? That is indeed an unfair division!" (53:21–22).

And ayah 59 shows what that "inferior" meant in practice. When a man was told a daughter had been born, his face became dark — Ibn Kathir glosses this as distress and grief — and he was *kaẓīm*, which Ibn Kathir explains as **silent because of the intensity of the grief he feels**. He hid himself from the people, not wanting anyone to see him. Then came his two options: keep her *ʿalā hūn*, with dishonour — Ibn Kathir spells this out as humiliating her, not letting her inherit from him, not taking care of her, preferring his male children over her — or "bury her in the earth," which Ibn Kathir says means bury her alive, as they used to do during the days of ignorance.

Ibn Kathir then asks the question the whole passage turns on: **how could they dislike something so intensely, yet attribute it to Allah?**

## Ayah 60: the two descriptions

> *"For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is an evil description, and for Allah is the highest description. And He is the All-Mighty, the All-Wise."*

Ibn Kathir's reading is precise on both halves. *Mathal al-sawʾ* — the evil description — means that **only imperfection is to be attributed to them**. And *wa lillāhi al-mathal al-aʿlā*, "and for Allah is the highest description," means **He is absolutely perfect in all ways, and this absolute perfection is His alone**.

Notice how exactly this answers the crime. They were people who *divided* — this portion for Allah, this portion for our partners; sons for us, daughters for Him. Ayah 60 does the dividing properly and finally: every defect belongs on their side of the line, every perfection on His, and the perfection is not shared. The same men who could not bear one flaw in their own household attached flaw after flaw to their Lord.

There is a second sting the sources point to. Ibn Kathir sets this passage beside 43:17, where the man is informed of the news of "that which he sets forth as a parable to the Most Gracious" — and *his own* face becomes dark. The thing he calls fit for Allah is the thing he cannot stand to receive. His face is the evidence against his creed.

And notice whom the ayah names: "those who **do not believe in the Hereafter**." The Qur'an ties this evil description to the denial of the Day of Resurrection — and it is on the Day of Resurrection, Ibn Kathir says at the close of ayah 62, that the Fire is theirs.

## "And He is the All-Mighty, the All-Wise"

The ayah closes with two of Allah's names, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Tafsīr Rūḥ al-Bayān, draws a fine point out of the second. Treating the birth of a baby girl as a nuisance and a disgrace, and hiding from people because of it, **amounts to challenging Divine wisdom** — because the creation of male and female among the created is the very requisite of that wisdom. The man skulking away from his neighbours is not merely being cruel to an infant. He is passing a verdict on how Allah arranged the world. That is why an ayah about false descriptions of Allah closes by naming Him the Wise.

## What this asks of a Muslim about daughters

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this as a ruling, not a sentiment. Clear indications are visible in these ayat that **taking the birth of a girl in the family to be a disaster or disgrace is not permissible under Islam** — this is done by disbelievers.

It then goes further than mere tolerance. Quoting *Shrʿah*, Tafsīr Rūḥ al-Bayān says a Muslim **should be happier at the birth of a girl** in the family, so that it becomes a refutation of the act of the people of Jāhiliyyah — the pagan period before Islam, the "days of ignorance" in which, as Ibn Kathir noted above, infant daughters were buried alive. A narration is cited to that effect: *Blessed is the woman who gives birth to a girl in her first pregnancy.* (The commentary introduces this simply as a hadith, without naming a collection, so take it as the teaching that commentary transmits — I cannot trace it to a named book for you.) Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a supporting hint from the wording of the Qur'an itself: in 42:49, "He bestows on whomsoever He wills females and bestows on whomsoever He wills males," the word *ināth* (females) has been made to precede the word for males — which the commentary reads as an indication that the birth of a girl from the first pregnancy is better.

A second narration is transmitted there too, again without a named collection: *Whoever finds any of such girls entrusted to his care, and he treats them fairly and favourably, then, these girls will stand as a curtain between him and Hell.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up: taking the birth of a girl to be bad is a detestable custom of the pagan period; Muslims must abstain from it, and should in fact be pleased and satisfied with the promise of Allah against it.

## Ayah 61: deferred, not cancelled

> *"And if Allah were to punish mankind for their wrongdoing, He would not leave on it a single moving creature — but He defers them to an appointed term; and when their term comes, they can neither delay nor advance it an hour."*

After a catalogue of blasphemy that ugly, the natural question is why the sky has not fallen in. Ayah 61 answers it, and the answer is not what the guilty assume.

Ibn Kathir reads this as a statement about **Allah's patience with His creatures even though they do wrong**. If He were to punish them for what they have done, there would be no living creature left on the face of the earth — meaning, he explains, that He would have destroyed **every animal on earth after destroying the sons of Adam**. The Lord — magnificent is His glory — is forbearing; He covers people's faults; He waits until the appointed time and does not rush to punish them. If He did, there would be no one left.

That detail about the animals is startling enough that Ibn Kathir supports it with a report. Ibn Jarīr reported that Abū Salamah said: Abū Hurayrah heard a man saying, "The wrongdoer harms no one but himself." He turned to him and said: **"That is not true, by Allah! Even the buzzard dies in its nest because of the sins of the wrongdoer."** Sin is never a private transaction. Its damage runs outward through a world that never signed up for it — which is why the ayah can say that immediate punishment would leave not one moving creature on the earth.

Two things follow from the ayah, and they cut in opposite directions.

**The mercy in it.** Every additional day the world is given is not an oversight; it is forbearance, and the covering of faults. Every reader breathing today is living inside that reprieve.

**The trap in it.** The ayah calls what is being deferred *ẓulm* — their wrongdoing — not a misunderstanding. Nothing has been struck from the record. There is only an appointed term, already fixed. And when that term arrives, "they can neither delay nor advance it an hour." The very silence the wrongdoer reads as acquittal is a countdown he cannot move by a single moment in either direction. He cannot postpone it when he finally wants more time, and he cannot bring it forward when he grows tired of waiting.

## Ayah 62: the lie the tongue tells

> *"They assign to Allah that which they dislike, and their tongues assert the lie that the better things will be theirs. No doubt the Fire is for them, and they will be forsaken."*

The ayah returns to the theology of ayah 60 and then adds something new.

**"They assign to Allah that which they dislike."** Ibn Kathir reads this on two levels: daughters, first — the thing they could not bear to receive — and partners, second, who are **merely His servants**; and yet, as he points out, not one of these men would like to have someone sharing in his wealth. They demanded for themselves an exclusivity they refused to grant their Creator.

**"And their tongues assert the lie that the better things will be theirs."** Ibn Kathir explains this as a denunciation of their claims that better things will be theirs **in this world, and in the Hereafter**, and he lines up ayat that record the actual sentences such people speak:

- Given goodness after harm has touched him, a man is sure to say, "Ills have departed from me" — surely he is cheerful and boastful (11:9–10).
- Another says, "This is due to me; I do not think that the Hour will occur. But if I am brought back to my Lord, then, with Him, there will surely be the best for me" (41:50).
- Another disbelieved in Allah's ayat and said, "I shall certainly be given wealth and children" (19:77).
- And the man of the garden goes into it while wronging himself: "I do not think that this will ever perish... and if indeed I am brought back to my Lord, then surely, I shall find better than this when I return to Him" (18:35–36).

Notice what those quoted ayat have in common: ease arrives, and the man reads it as a verdict in his favour — and in the same breath he says, "I do not think that the Hour will occur." His tongue then dresses that assumption up as certainty. The ayah names it: *al-kadhib*, a lie.

Ibn Kathir's summary of them all is the heart of the ayah: **these people combined bad deeds with the false hopes of being rewarded with good for those bad deeds, which is impossible.**

**"No doubt."** The Arabic is *lā jarama*, which Ibn Kathir renders as: truly, it is **inevitable** that —

**"for them is the Fire"** — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, on the Day of Resurrection.

**"And they will be forsaken"** — *mufraṭūn*, a word the early scholars read in two ways, and the source gives both rather than choosing between them. Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Qatādah and others said it means **they will be forgotten and neglected there**, which Ibn Kathir links to "So today We forget them just as they forgot meeting on this day of theirs" (7:51). It was also reported from Qatādah that *mufraṭūn* means **they are hastened into the Fire**. Ibn Kathir sees no contradiction between the two: they will be hastened into it on the Day of Resurrection, then forgotten there — left to dwell there for eternity.

That is the passage's final answer to ayah 61. The men who noticed that nothing was happening to them receive, in the end, exactly what they seemed to want: to be left alone.

## Living it

**Watch what you say about Allah.** These ayat treat speech about Allah as the most serious speech there is — an evil description or the highest one. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: absolute perfection is His alone. Every deficiency you are tempted to attribute to Him belongs nowhere near Him.

**Do not read delay as approval.** Ayah 61 does not say the wrongdoing was overlooked or forgotten; it says the punishment is deferred to an appointed term — one you cannot move forward or back by an hour.

**Hope has to be tethered to deeds.** The lie in ayah 62 is not hoping for good from Allah — it is expecting good *while stacking up the opposite*. Ibn Kathir calls that combination impossible.

**Receive daughters as a gift, and let it show.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes joy at a daughter's birth a live refutation of the practice of Jāhiliyyah, and the narration it transmits says of the man who finds such girls entrusted to his care and treats them fairly and favourably, that these girls will stand as a curtain between him and Hell.

passages.title: Revelation sent to settle their disputes
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Allah opens with an oath — "By Allah!" — that messengers were sent to communities long before Muhammad ﷺ, and that Shaytan made those communities' own deeds seem fair to them (ayah 63). Then, in ayah 64, Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ the reason the Book was sent down to him: to clearly explain to people the very matters they differ over, and to be guidance and mercy for a people who believe.

**What holds the two ayat together.** They are two halves of one movement. Ayah 63 names the disease — a people whose own deeds have been made to look attractive to them by Shaytan — and ayah 64 names the cure — a Book sent down so that the Prophet ﷺ may make things clear. Shaytan's work is to make wrong look fair; revelation's work is clarification. The passage is that contest, in two verses.

## The oath at the opening

Ayah 63 begins **تَٱللَّهِ** — "By Allah!" An oath, before the sentence has even reached its subject. And the sentence that follows is itself emphatic: *"By Allah! We have surely sent messengers to communities before"*; in Ibn Kathir's rendering, *"By Allah, We indeed sent (Messengers) to the nations before you."*

That weight is not decoration. The point being underlined is one the Prophet ﷺ needed to feel in his chest, not merely know in his mind: **you are not the first, and this is not a failure.**

## "We sent to communities before you"

The word is **أُمَم** (*umam*) — rendered here as "communities," and by Ibn Kathir as "the nations before you," "the nations of the past." Messenger after messenger, community after community.

Ibn Kathir reads this ayah as consolation. Allah, he says, sent Messengers to the nations of the past **and they were rejected** — so, in Ibn Kathir's wording of the meaning: *you, O Muhammad, have an example in your brothers among the Messengers, so do not be distressed by your people's rejection.*

Notice how gently that is put. The Prophet ﷺ is not told his grief is wrong; he is told he is in company. The men he is placed beside are called his **brothers** — the same road, the same reception. When the people of Makkah turned away, they were not doing something new to the world; they were repeating something as old as prophethood itself.

## The reason people rejected the Messengers

Then the ayah gives the cause, and it is not the one people usually reach for. Ibn Kathir states it plainly: as for the idolators' rejection of the Messengers, **the reason for this is that the Shaytan made their deeds attractive to them.**

That is the force of **زَيَّنَ** (*zayyana*) — the ayah's own word, which Ibn Kathir renders as Shaytan having "made their deeds seeming fair to them," "made their deeds attractive to them." The obstacle described here is not a missing proof. It is that their own conduct had been made to look good to them. A man who has been shown that his practice is wrong but *finds it attractive* will not be moved by one more argument. And that is exactly why the ayah pivots to a Book whose stated work, in the next verse, is to explain clearly.

## "So today he is their helper"

**فَهُوَ وَلِيُّهُمُ ٱلْيَوْمَ** — "So today he is their helper."

The line lands like a closing door. Ibn Kathir explains: they will be suffering punishment while Shaytan is their only helper, **and he cannot save them**, so they have no one to answer their calls for help, and theirs is a painful punishment.

Look at the bargain that has been struck. The one who spent a lifetime making their deeds look attractive is, on the day it matters, the only helper they have left — and he is powerless. There is no third party left to appeal to. That, and not merely the punishment itself, is the desolation the ayah leaves you with: calls for help going out into a silence, because the only "helper" who remains was never a helper at all. The ayah closes: **and theirs will be a painful torment.**

## Why the Qur'an was revealed (ayah 64)

**وَمَآ أَنزَلۡنَا عَلَيۡكَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ إِلَّا لِتُبَيِّنَ لَهُمُ ٱلَّذِي…** — "And We have not revealed the Book to you, except that you may clearly explain to them those things in which they differ, and (as) a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe."

Ibn Kathir heads this section simply: **"The Reason why the Qur'an was revealed."** Not one reason among several — the reason, as the verse itself states it. Allah says to His Messenger ﷺ that He has revealed the Book to him **to explain the truth to mankind in matters which they dispute over** — so the Qur'an is **a decisive arbitrator for every issue that they argue about.**

An arbitrator is not one voice among the disputants. It is the voice that ends the dispute. That reframes what a believer is doing when he opens the Book in the middle of a disagreement: he is not gathering material for his side, he is going to the judge.

And note who does the explaining. The Book is revealed to the Prophet ﷺ **"to explain the truth to mankind"** — **لِتُبَيِّنَ**, "that *you* may clearly explain." Revelation and the one who conveys it come together; the text is not handed to the world unaccompanied.

## Guidance for hearts, mercy for those who hold on

The ayah then adds two words, and Ibn Kathir gives each a precise scope:

- **وَهُدًى** — *and (as) a guidance.* Ibn Kathir: **"meaning, for their hearts."** Not primarily for the intellect or the tongue — for the heart, which is where the trouble of the previous ayah lay. The cure is aimed exactly where the disease was.
- **وَرَحْمَةً** — *and a mercy.* Ibn Kathir adds a qualification that is easy to skim past: **"for the one who adheres to it."** The mercy is real, but it is not absorbed by proximity. A Book recited but not followed is not what is being described. Adherence is the channel through which the mercy actually reaches a person.
- **لِّقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ** — *for a people who believe.* That is where the verse comes to rest.

On that closing phrase, Ibn Kathir's comment reaches forward into the next ayah (65), which lies just outside our two verses but is where he lands the thought: **just as Allah causes the Qur'an to bring life to hearts that were dead from disbelief, so He brings the earth to life after it has died, by sending down water from the sky.** Both are sent *down*. Both arrive on ground that has nothing to offer. Neither the earth nor the heart revives itself.

## A note from the surrounding passage

The bundle's Ma'arif ul Qur'an material here is commentary on the earlier part of the sūrah rather than on ayat 63–64 — it hangs on the closing words of ayah 60, **وَهُوَ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلْحَكِيمُ**, "And He is the Mighty, the Wise." It is worth a brief mention, since it shows the same two forces at work: a custom that felt settled and respectable, and revelation arriving to correct it.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes (citing Ruh al-Bayan) that in that phrase there is **a hint that taking the birth of a baby girl to be a nuisance and disgrace, and hiding from people because of it, amount to challenging Divine wisdom** — since the creation of male and female is the very requisite of that wisdom. It then states the ruling: **taking the birth of a girl in the family to be a disaster or disgrace is not permissible under Islam.** That is what the disbelievers did. Quoting a work it names *Shr'ah*, Tafsir Ruh al-Bayan also says that a Muslim **should be happier at the birth of a girl**, so that this becomes a refutation of the practice of the people of Jahiliyyah.

In that same passage two sayings of the Prophet ﷺ are related. Ma'arif ul Qur'an introduces the first only with "Says a Hadith" — no collection is named, so it is conveyed here exactly as it is given and attributed to no collection: *Blessed is the woman who gives birth to a girl in her first pregnancy.* The second it introduces as "In another Hadith," marking it (Ruh al-Bayan): *Whoever finds any of such girls entrusted to his care, and he treats them fairly and favourably, then, these girls will stand as a curtain between him and Hell.*

Its summary: taking the birth of a girl to be bad is a detestable custom of the pagan period; Muslims must abstain from it, and should instead be pleased and satisfied with the promise of Allah against it. *And Allah knows best.*

## Living it

- **If you are rejected while calling to good, read ayah 63 again.** The Messengers before were rejected; the Prophet ﷺ himself was told not to be distressed by his people's rejection. Rejection is not by itself evidence that you are wrong.
- **Audit what looks attractive to you.** Shaytan's method as described here is not disproving the truth to you; it is making your own deeds seem fair. The habit you defend most warmly deserves the most honest look.
- **Take real disputes to the Book as an arbitrator, not as ammunition.** Ibn Kathir calls the Qur'an a decisive arbitrator for every issue people argue about — which only helps someone willing to lose the argument to it.
- **Cross from reciting to adhering.** The guidance is for the hearts; the mercy, in Ibn Kathir's wording, is *for the one who adheres to it.*

passages.title: Rain, milk, fruit and the honey bee
passages.tafsir:
Four signs, all of them ordinary: water falling on dead ground, milk drawn out of a living body, fruit that human hands turn into either nourishment or ruin, and honey manufactured by an insect. What binds ayat 65–69 into one unit is that each closes by summoning a different faculty in whoever receives it — a people who **listen** (65), a people who **reason** (67), a people who **reflect** (69). The passage climbs from hearing, to understanding, to sustained thought.

## Rain, and the hearts it stands for (65)

Ibn Kathir ties the falling water to the revelation Allah had just been speaking of: **"Just as Allah causes the Qur'an to bring life to hearts that were dead from disbelief, so He brings the earth to life after it has died, by sending down water from the sky."**

The faculty this first sign addresses — "a sign for people who **listen**" — Ibn Kathir explains as "those who understand the words and their meanings," not those who merely register sound.

## Milk: a lesson written into the body (66)

Ayah 66 does not call this a "sign" but an **ʿibrah**, a lesson. Ibn Kathir glosses it as "a sign and an evidence of the wisdom, power, mercy and kindness of the Creator," and identifies *al-anʿām* (the cattle) as camels, cows and sheep.

**A grammatical curiosity.** The ayah says *nusqīkum mimmā fī buṭūnihi* — "in **its** belly," a masculine singular pronoun, though *al-anʿām* is a plural treated as feminine; 23:21 uses the feminine *buṭūnihā* for the same statement. Ibn Kathir says the singular refers to one of the cattle, or it could refer to the whole species — "Either way is plausible." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Qurṭubī, explains that 23:21 follows the *meaning* of the plural while here the pronoun follows the *word* itself as a collective; "examples of this usage abound in Arabic."

**"From between excretions and blood, pure milk."** Ibn Kathir describes the milk as "free of blood, and… pure in its whiteness, taste and sweetness": it lies between excrement and blood in the animal's belly, yet once the food is fully digested each goes its own way — blood to the veins, milk to the udder, urine to the bladder, waste to its exit — and "none of them gets mixed with another after separating, and none of them is affected by the other." Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, described the same process: the fodder settles, the stomach heats it, the waste settles below with milk above it and blood above that, and the liver then separates the three and directs each to where it belongs.

Sit with the geography of that: the milk in the glass has passed within a hair's breadth of filth and of blood, and arrives white. That is the *ʿibrah*. Two words complete it — **khāliṣ**, pure, and **sāʾigh**, "palatable to the drinkers," which Ibn Kathir explains as meaning there is "nothing to cause one to choke on it." And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the verb *nusqīkum*, "**We** give you to drink": the milk arrives as a finished product, "pure and pleasant, food and drink in one," since "no subsequent human effort or artifice is needed here."

**Two practical points from ayah 66.** Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (cited via al-Qurṭubī) held that eating good food is not against *zuhd* — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines as not inclining towards worldly enjoyments for the sake of spiritual purity — especially when it is acquired by lawful means and no extravagance is made in it. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, again citing al-Qurṭubī, reports that the Prophet ﷺ said that when you eat something you say, "O Allah, bless it for us and have us eat better than it," but when you drink milk you say, "O Allah, bless it for us and give us more of it" — *more*, not *better*, because in human cuisine there is no nutrient better than milk, which is why it is the very first food given to every man and animal.

## Fruit: the gift that hands over a choice (67)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets ayah 67 against ayah 66. Milk involves no human intervention. Fruit does: from the date palm and the grapevine, *you* make things. And because human ingenuity and artifice now intervene, the same blessing forks into the two outcomes the ayah names — **sakar**, intoxicant, and **rizq ḥasan**, goodly provision. "Now the option is theirs. Let them make what they would: Make what intoxicates and knocks their reason out, or make food out of them and get strength and energy!"

Ibn ʿAbbās, quoted by Ibn Kathir: "Strong drink is the product of these two fruits that is forbidden, and the good provision is what is permitted of them." Ibn Kathir explains this as referring to the fruits when they are dried, like dates and raisins, "or products derived from them such as molasses, vinegar and wine (of grapes, dates) which are permissible to drink before they become strong (becomes alcoholic), as was stated in the Sunnah."

**Where the scholars differed.** According to the majority of commentators, *sakar* means what intoxicates (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Jaṣṣāṣ); some ʿulamāʾ have also taken it to mean vinegar, or non-intoxicating *nabīdh* (al-Jaṣṣāṣ, al-Qurṭubī).

**Was this ayah permitting wine?** Ibn Kathir notes that the wording "indicates that it was permissible to drink it before it was forbidden," and that intoxicating drink derived from dates has the same status as that derived from grapes — as do strong drinks from wheat, barley, corn and honey, "as is explained in detail in the Sunnah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the chronology plainly: **these ayat are Makkī by consensus; the unlawfulness of liquor came after that, in Madinah**, and at the time of this ayah's revelation Muslims used to drink openly. Yet the hint was already embedded — by setting *rizq ḥasan* opposite *sakar*, the ayah quietly tells you *sakar* is **not** a good provision. So it cannot be used to prove the lawfulness of what intoxicates: the purpose here is to state the nature of Allah's blessings and the different forms they take when used, and someone using a thing wrongfully does not stop it being the blessing it is.

**Why "for people who reason"?** Ibn Kathir: "It is appropriate to mention reason here, because it is the noblest feature of man. Hence Allah forbade this Ummah from drinking intoxicants, in order to protect their ability to reason." The ayah that mentions what destroys the intellect is the ayah that calls the intellect to witness.

## The bee: a command given to an insect (68–69)

**"And your Lord *inspired* the bee."** The verb is *awḥā*, the same root as *waḥy*, revelation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful: it is not used here in its technical sense of revelation, but in its literal sense — a speaker communicating something particular to the addressee, secretly, in a way others cannot perceive. Ibn Kathir says simply: "What is meant by inspiration here is guidance."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that for the rest of creation the Qur'an says "He gave everything its form, then provided it with guidance" (Ṭā Hā 20:50) — a universal law. For this tiny creature it was specially said "**your Lord** inspired," indicating "that it has a prominent status among other life forms by virtue of its intelligence, sense and functional insight" — a standing the same commentary illustrates (from al-Jawāhir) with the colony's system of governance: one ruling bee, and a strict division of labour among guards, those who protect the eggs, those who nurture the young, architects and engineers, and those who collect wax — all obeying in order.

**The three instructions.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayat 68–69 as a sequence of three commands.

**One — build.** "Take habitations in the mountains and in the trees and in what they erect." The word is *buyūt*, "houses" — generally used for where human beings live. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds two hints in that: since bees have to prepare honey, they should first make a safe home; and their homes will not be like the homes of common animals. The cells are hexagonal, so exact that "measuring them with a pair of compasses and rulers will hardly spell out a difference" — never a square or pentagon, since some of their corners would turn out functionally useless. Ibn Kathir says the same: "a solid structure, with its hexagonal shapes and interlocking forms there is no looseness in its combs." The *sites* are specified too: altitude helps provide fresh, clean and almost-filtered air flow for the production of honey, and protects the hive from breakage or damage.

**Two — eat.** "Then eat of all the fruits." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *kull*, "all," does not mean the fruits and flowers of the whole world but those within easy reach that serve the desired purpose — the same idiom as the queen of Sabaʾ being "given of everything" (27:23), which means what befitted her station as ruler.

**Three — travel.** *Fasluki subula rabbiki dhululan.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: a creature that forages miles from home ought to find the return difficult; instead its flight routes are made easy, the airspace subjugated for this humble bee, since winding pathways on land would carry the likelihood of going astray. Ibn Kathir records a genuine difference over *dhululan*: Qatādah and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam read it as "in an obedient way," understanding it as a description of the route of migration — Ibn Zayd comparing 36:72 and noting that people move the bees' home from one land to another and the bees follow them. Ibn Kathir judges more likely the reading that describes the routes themselves — "follow these routes as they are easy for you," as stated by Mujāhid — while Ibn Jarīr said that **both** opinions are correct.

Ibn Kathir's portrait of the returning bee: "Then each bee comes back to its hive without swerving to the right or left, it comes straight back to its home where its offspring and honey are. It makes wax from its wings, and regurgitates honey from its mouth, and lays eggs from its rear, then the next morning it goes out to the fields again."

## Honey: "in it there is a cure for people"

"There comes forth from their bellies a drink of varying colours." Ibn Kathir: white, yellow, red, or of other good colours, "depending on the different things that the bees eat." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes the variation to difference of climate and to what the bees suck from, and notes that milk from milch animals does not turn red or yellow under different climates and foods, while honey does take different colours. And the deepest wonder in that commentary: this tasty and blissful drink comes out of the belly of a tiny animal which is itself armed with poison. **"The emergence of antidote from poison is really a unique exhibit of the most perfect power of Allah."**

**How much healing?** Ibn Kathir cites some of those who spoke about the study of Prophetic medicine: had the wording been "in it is *the* cure for people," it would be the remedy for all diseases; but it says "in it is **a** cure," meaning it is the right treatment for every "cold" disease, because honey is "hot," and a disease should be treated with its opposite. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān arrives at the same place through grammar: *shifāʾ* appears here as an indefinite noun (*nakirah*), so that it is a cure for every disease "is not apparent on this basis" — yet its *tanwīn*, which carries the sense of greatness, does prove that the healing in honey is of a great and distinct nature.

**From the Sunnah.** Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded in their Ṣaḥīḥs — from Qatādah, from Abū al-Mutawakkil ʿAlī ibn Dāwūd al-Nājī, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī — that a man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "My brother is suffering from diarrhoea." He ﷺ said, "Give him honey to drink." The man went and gave him honey, then came back and said, "O Messenger of Allah! I gave him honey to drink, and he only got worse." The Prophet ﷺ said, "Go and give him honey to drink." So he went and gave him honey, then came back and said, "O Messenger of Allah! It only made him worse." The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Allah speaks the truth and your brother's stomach is lying. Go and give him honey to drink."* So he went and gave him honey, and he recovered.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, recounting the same incident, draws out the sense: there was nothing wrong with the suggested remedy — it was the patient's particular temperamental condition that had delayed its actual effect.

Ibn Kathir also reports from the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to like sweet things and honey — the wording being al-Bukhārī's; and al-Bukhārī also recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās that he ﷺ said: "Healing is to be found in three things: the cut made by the cupper, or drinking honey, or in branding with fire (cauterizing), but I have forbidden my Ummah to use branding."

**Conviction is part of the cure.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from al-Qurṭubī that Ibn ʿUmar, if an abscess appeared on his body, would treat it by applying honey to it; asked why, he replied that Allah had said of it in the Qur'an, "in it there is a cure for people." The commentary connects this to the Ḥadīth Qudsī *"I am with the belief of My servant in Me"* — a Ḥadīth Qudsī being what was communicated to the Prophet ﷺ by his Lord, its meanings from Allah, while its words are the Messenger's ﷺ own.

**Seeking treatment is permitted — and sometimes required.** From "in it there is a cure for people," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān infers that treating diseases with medicine is permissible, since Allah mentions it as a reward and blessing. Some Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ, "Should we use medicine?" He said: "Why not? Do take advantage of treatment, because for every disease Allah has created, He has also created a matching medicine. But there is no cure for one disease." They asked which; he said: "Extreme old age." (Abū Dāwūd, Tirmidhī, as cited from al-Qurṭubī.) Khuzaymah asked the Prophet ﷺ whether blowing on the sick and treating ourselves with medicines could change the destiny determined by Allah, and was told: "These too are nothing but the very forms of Divinely-appointed destiny" — taking the means is not opposing *qadar*, it is part of it. There is consensus of all ʿulamāʾ on the justification of seeking treatment and using medicine; where some pious Muslims of the past declined it for themselves — as the ailing Ibn Masʿūd did when ʿUthmān offered to call a physician — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that as a transitory state of the soul, not a ruling: ʿUthmān's very offer is proof that treatment is permitted, "rather, there are situations when doing so becomes mandatory as well."

**The bee's own honour.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites, from Nawādir al-Uṣūl with reference to al-Qurṭubī, a hadith it renders: "All bees will go to Hell (like other hurting creatures). They will be made a punishment for the people of Hell, except the honey bee." And it notes another hadith, referred to Abū Dāwūd, in which he ﷺ prohibited killing it.

## "For a people who reflect"

Ibn Kathir explains what the reflection is *about*: that Allah inspires this weak little creature to travel through the vast fields and feed from every kind of fruit, then gather it for wax and honey, "which are some of the best things"; those who think about the might and power of the bee's Creator, who causes all of this to happen, learn from it "that He is the Initiator, the All-Powerful, the All-Wise, the All-Knowing, the Most Generous, the Most Merciful."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns this into a direct summons. By causing rains to come down He gives new life to dead lands; winding through the impurities of feces and blood He makes pipelines of pure and pleasant milk flow for you; on date palms and grapevines He grows sweet fruits; and through a tiny living creature with a poisonous bite He provides an excellent combination of food, drink, taste, flavour and cure. **Would you still keep calling on gods and goddesses of your own making?** Would your reason still keep looking for escape from truth by suggesting that this whole phenomenon is some charismatic working of blind, deaf and inert matter? These marvels, it says, are "the loudest of heralds announcing that our Creator is One, unique and wise."

The same commentary draws one further note from the bee's obedience: beside human beings, there is consciousness and intelligence in other living creatures too — "There is nothing which does not recite His praises" (17:44) — but the degrees of intelligence differ. Human intelligence is the most complete, which is why humans are the ones obligated with the precepts and injunctions of the Sharīʿah, and why one who does not remain rational due to insanity is not so obligated. The bee obeys an instruction it never had to be argued into; the human being, given more, is asked to listen, to reason, and to reflect.

## Living it

- **Do not despise lawful good things** — good food acquired by lawful means, without extravagance, is no lapse in piety — and put a word of remembrance on what you eat and drink.
- **Guard your reason,** and **seek treatment when ill,** knowing that taking the means is itself one of the forms of Allah's decree, not a challenge to it.
- **Let the ordinary become evidence.** Rain, milk, a date, a spoon of honey — these are not background noise but signs, waiting for someone who will listen, reason, and reflect.

passages.title: Lifespan, provision and family — yet they deny the favour
passages.tafsir:
Three sentences, each beginning the same way in the Arabic — *wa'Llāhu*, "And Allah…" — take the argument of the sūrah out of the wider world and set it down inside the reader's own body and household. The first is your lifespan: He made you out of nothing, He takes you back, and some of you He keeps until knowing itself drains away. The second is your income: He did not make people equal in provision, and the very inequality you live with becomes an argument against the idolatry you defend. The third is your family and your food: a spouse of your own kind, children and grandchildren from her, and good things to eat. And twice, after the gifts have been counted, the passage closes on the same wound — that the favour of Allah is denied.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the link backwards. The preceding ayat had pointed to water, vegetation, cattle and the honey bee, reminding human beings of Allah's perfect power of creation and of His blessings on those He created. Now, it says, human beings "have been invited to ponder over the very state they are in."

## The first gift: existence, and the clock that runs on it

Ibn Kathir reads the opening as a statement about who is actually running things: "Allah tells us that He is controlling the affairs of His servants.
