He is the One Who created them out of nothing, then He will cause them to die." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in the plainest terms: "Human beings were nothing. Allah Taʿālā blessed them with existence. Then, by sending death when He willed, He terminated that blessing."

Between those poles the ayah sets a third possibility. Some, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, are "much before their death, carried to such a stage of extreme old age that their senses do not work, they lose the strength of their hands and feet. They understand nothing, nor can they remember what they do." Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "sent back to senility"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "carried back to the worst part of the age." Both are speaking of **arḏal al-ʿumur** — a phrase Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines as "the extreme old age when all physical and mental faculties become weak and confused."

## Carried back to where you began

The wording carries a hint, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches it: *back* implies you have been there before. "Man has seen a time of weakness earlier too. This was the early stage of childhood marked by its lack of understanding and physical strength, and dependence on others in eating, drinking, getting up and sitting down. Then came youth, the time to prosper and move ahead. Then, gradually, man is carried to a stage of the same age of helplessness as it was in early childhood." Life, on this reading, is an arc that returns to its own starting point.

Ibn Kathir quotes elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"Allah is He Who created you in a state of weakness, then gave you strength after weakness, then after strength gave you weakness"* (30:54).

**"So that they know nothing after having known."** Ibn Kathir glosses it: "after he knew things, he will reach a stage where he knows nothing because of weakness of mind due to old age and senility." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds it slowly: "What he knows now, he may not know moments later. All information he has, he may forget and become like a child born yesterday who has no knowledge or awareness or understanding or intelligence." This, it notes in passing, is the phenomenon of old age that in our own time has given birth to the study of gerontology.

**How old is "the worst part of the age"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is candid that "the definition… remains undetermined," and lists what was said: some put it at eighty, some at ninety, and a statement reported from Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) puts it at seventy-five — for which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names its source as the Ṣaḥīḥayn, "the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections," as quoted by Mazharī. But the commentary judges the weightier definition to be the one that measures faculties rather than birthdays: the age at which the senses no longer stay active, "as a result of which a person forgets everything he knows" — the very thing the Qur'an alludes to when it says *"that he knows nothing after having knowledge."*

Ibn Kathir quotes Zuhayr bin Abī Sulmā's famous Muʿallaqah: "I became exhausted from the responsibilities of life. Whoever lives for eighty years, no wonder he is tired. I saw death hitting people like a crazed camel, and whoever it hit dies, but whoever is not hit lives until he grows old."

## Seeking refuge from the far end of life

Because this stage is real, the Prophet ﷺ asked to be spared it. Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhārī, commenting on this very ayah, reported a narration from Anas bin Mālik that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray:

> "I seek refuge with You from miserliness, laziness, old age, senility, the punishment of the grave, the Fitnah of the Dajjāl and the trials of life and death."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that he ﷺ always prayed to be protected "from the evil of age," and in another narration, "from that I be carried to the worst part of the age." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives these without naming a collection.)

**A word of hope.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from Ḥaḍrat ʿIkrimah (may Allah be pleased with him): "This state will not prevail upon the reciter of the Qur'an." Take it as an encouragement to keep the Qur'an on your tongue for as long as your tongue obeys you.

**"Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful."** The ayah closes on two of Allah's names — *ʿAlīm* and *Qadīr* — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows they are not ornament. From knowledge, "He knows everyone's age." From power, "He does what He wills. If He wills, He can have a strong young man be overtaken by the signs of the worst part of old age, and should He so will, even a hundred-year-old aged man could remain a strong young man." Youth is not an achievement and age is not an accident; both are held by "that sole Being in whose divinity there is no partner or associate."

## The second gift: provision, and the case hidden in your own pay

Allah "has favoured some of you over others in provision." Ibn Kathir's rendering: "those who are so honoured will by no means hand over their wealth and properties to those whom their right hands possess, so that they may be equal with them in that." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same fact plainly: "he who was given preference in provision and made rich and need-free would never accept to distribute his wealth among his slaves and servants in a way that they too become his equals in wealth."

**Then why do you do to Allah what you would not accept for yourself?** Ibn Kathir explains that the idolaters claimed Allah has partners while admitting, in the same breath, that these partners are His servants — in their Talbiyah for Ḥajj, "they used to say, 'Here I am, there are no partners for You except Your own partner, You own him and everything he owns.'" So Allah confronts them with their own words: "You would not accept for your servant to have an equal share in your wealth, so how is it that Allah would accept His servant to be His equal in divinity and glory?"

Ibn Kathir sets alongside it the parable of 30:28 — *"He sets forth a parable for you from yourselves: Do you have partners among those whom your right hands possess to share as equals in the wealth We have granted you, those whom you fear as you fear each other?"* And al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that Allah is saying: "If they did not want their servant to have a share with them in their wealth and wives, how can My servant have a share with Me in My power?" In another report Ibn ʿAbbās compresses it to a single line: **"How can they accept for Me that which they do not accept for themselves?"**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān walks the same reasoning. The idolaters themselves accept that the idols and other created things they worship are "after all, created and owned by Allah Taʿālā." A created, owned thing cannot become the equal of its Creator and Master. And to worship it anyway is not merely a failure of logic but a rejection of the Giver: "if they had admitted that all these blessings have been given by Allah Taʿālā without the intervention of any self-carved idol, icon, human being and Jinn, then how could they have equated these things with Allah Taʿālā?"

**"Do they then deny the favour of Allah?"** Ibn Kathir makes the denial concrete: "they assign to Allah a share of the tilth and cattle which He has created. They denied His blessings and associated others in worship with Him."

## Why the shares were never made equal

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the inequality of ayah 71 as deliberate: Allah "has not, in His infinite wisdom, and in view of His consideration for human good, made all human beings equals in terms of rizq or provision."

It sketches the resulting society in three tiers: the rich man who "owns a lot of things, keeps a staff of all sorts of servers, spends as he wishes, and his servers too benefit through him"; the one made to work for others and to receive his living from them; and one in between, "neither so rich as to spend on others, nor so poor and needy as to be dependent upon others even in the necessities of life."

The wisdom, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues it: Allah created human beings "with varying degrees of temperaments as conditioned by intelligence, strength and functional ability," classified low, high and average — "a fact which cannot be rejected by any reasonable person." Differences in what they earn follow from that, "so that every single person is rewarded in terms of individual capability." Impose flat equality by force and "it will take only a few days when disruption and disorder become openly visible through the entire spectrum of human dealings," because "if the capable and the incapable were made equal, it will discourage the capable."

**But difference is not licence.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic that alongside this natural variation Allah "has also established a strong system of economic equilibrium which aims that no particular group or party or a few individuals take over the treasures of wealth and centers of economic activity" — citing *"so that wealth does not come to be revolving among the rich from among you"* (59:7). Interest and gambling are declared unlawful, which "demolished the foundations of illegitimate capitalism." The poor and needy are given a *right* in the wealth of every Muslim — *"in their wealth, there is a known right for the asking and the deprived"* (70:24) — so that supporting them "is not supposed to be some favour done to them. In fact, it is the fulfilment of a duty." The estate of a deceased person is distributed among the individual heirs, "eliminating the concentration of wealth." And natural streams, the high seas and the self-growing produce of mountain forests are "the common capital of the entire creation of Allah," which no individual or group may take into private ownership.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then measures the two great modern systems against this. Capitalism, in which some individuals or groups "virtually take over the nerve centers of wealth through the medium of interest and gambling." And communism, which raised the slogan of removing the gap between rich and poor and delivered instead the erasure of the person, so that "the worth of a human person is no more than a part of its machines." Even the champions of equality could not hold the line — Nikita Khrushchev, before the Supreme Soviet on 5 May 1960: "We are against the movement to eliminate difference in wages" — and it cites Lyon Sidov's remark that "perhaps, there is no developed capitalist country where the disparity in the wages of workers is as high as in Soviet Russia." The Qur'an, it concludes, "has provided a system in between the two extremes."

**Living it.** Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī reported that ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī: "Be content with your provision in this world, for the Most Merciful has honoured some of His servants over others in terms of provision **as a test of both**. The one who has been given plenty is being tested to see if he will give thanks to Allah and fulfil the duties which are his by virtue of his wealth…" Ibn Kathir notes that this was reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim. Whichever side of the disparity you stand on, you are the one under examination.

## The third gift: a spouse of your own kind, and children after children

**"Allah has made for you spouses from among yourselves"** — from your own selves, your own kind.

Ibn Kathir draws out why the phrase matters: "If He had given them mates of another kind, there would be no harmony, love and mercy between them. But out of His mercy He has made the Children of Adam male and female, and has made the females wives or mates for the males." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees in the same-kind pairing a purpose — that spouses "remain mutually familiar" and that the distinction and nobility of the human species stays stable across generations — and then a second implication that lands squarely in married life: because spouses belong to each other's kind, "their needs and feelings are common to both, therefore, mutual consideration is but necessary for them."

**"And from your spouses, sons and grandsons."** Ibn Kathir reports that *ḥafadah* here means one's children's children — the opinion of Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd; Shuʿbah narrated from Abū Bishr from Saʿīd bin Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās, "children and grandchildren, who are one's children and one's children's children." He records other views too — that it means servants and helpers, or sons-in-law and in-laws — and offers his own reconciliation: since the word refers back to the wives, it must cover "children, children's children, and sons-in-law, because they are the husbands of one's daughter or the children of one's wife."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān keeps the root sense in view: the real meaning of *ḥafadah* is one who helps and serves, and that this word should be used for children "suggests that children should always be at the service of their father and mother" — a point it attributes to Qurṭubī. The word for your children is the word for those who serve.

**Why mention grandchildren at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees a hint in it: naming the second generation shows that "the real purpose behind creating spouses is the procreation and survival of human race so that they have children, then, their children have their children."

**Why are the children traced to the mothers?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the wording as deliberate: "the role of the mother in the birth and the creational formation of the child is more pronounced than that of the father. The father contributes only a lifeless drop." The place where that drop passes through stage after stage, from transformation into human form and shape to becoming alive — "where all these inimitable achievements of nature take place" — is the womb of the mother. "Therefore, in the Hadith, the right of the mother has been made to precede the right of the father."

**"And provided you with good things."** Ibn Kathir: this means "your food and drink." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the logic of the sequence: "once a human child is born, food is needed for its personal survival. That too was provided by Allah Taʿālā."

## The same accusation, twice

Twice the passage stops and asks what people have done with all of it. First: **"Do they then deny the favour of Allah?"** Then, after the household: **"Do they then believe in falsehood, and in the favour of Allah they disbelieve?"**

Ibn Kathir defines both halves of that second question. *Al-bāṭil*, falsehood, means "idols and rivals to Allah." And to disbelieve in the favour means "concealing the blessings that Allah has given them and attributing them to others." That is the precise force of the Arabic *kufr* here — not a philosophical denial that anything exists, but a covering-over of something plainly in front of you, and a redirection of thanks to the wrong address.

Ibn Kathir closes with a hadith he describes as authentic, in which Allah addresses His servant on the Day of Resurrection, reminding him of His blessings: *"Did I not give you a wife? Did I not honour you? Did I not subject horses and camels to your use, and cause you to occupy a position of leadership and honour?"* (He does not name a collection at this point.) The questions on that Day are the contents of this passage read back to you, item by item.

## What the passage asks of you

Read together, the three ayat are a single audit of a life: every item has one Owner, and the passage's whole complaint is that people accept the gifts and misfile the credit.

Three things follow. **Recognise the Giver by name**, since Ibn Kathir's entire reading of the middle ayah is that the fault is not in receiving but in attributing. **Be under no illusion about your own strength**, since the same power that gave a young man his faculties can withdraw them, and the Prophet ﷺ himself sought refuge from that end. And **treat your provision as an examination paper**, in the terms of ʿUmar's letter — the one given plenty tested in gratitude and in the duties his wealth imposes, and the whole community answerable for a system in which wealth is not left "revolving among the rich."

passages.title: Idols that provide nothing, and the two parables
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** After a run of Allah's gifts — spouses, children and grandchildren, provision from good things — these four ayat turn to the people who receive all of that from Allah and then worship something else. Ayah 73 exposes what the false gods can actually provide: nothing. Ayah 74 forbids the mental habit that lies behind idolatry in the first place — reasoning about Allah by analogy with created things. Then ayat 75 and 76 answer with two parables that Allah Himself sets forth, each showing that even *within* creation two beings of the same kind can fail to be equal — so how could anything created ever be set beside the Creator?

That is the thread: **provision → the ban on false comparisons → two comparisons made rightly, by Allah Himself.**

## Ayah 73: they worship what cannot provide for them

Just before this passage, Allah lists intimate mercies. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what is packed into them: Allah created spouses *from among yourselves* — from the same genus — so that husband and wife remain mutually familiar, and so that the distinction and nobility inherent in the human species stays stable through the generations. Because they belong to each other's genus, their needs and feelings are common to both, which is exactly why mutual consideration between them is necessary. The mention of *grandsons* alongside sons points to the deeper purpose: not one household but the survival of the human race, children and then their children. Then "and gave you provision from good things" — what guarantees each person's own survival once born. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, quoting Qurṭubī, that the real meaning of **ḥafadah** (rendered "grandsons") is *one who helps and serves*, and its use for children suggests that children should always be at the service of their father and mother.

So the reader arrives at ayah 73 warm with a sense of having been given everything. And the ayah lands like cold water: *and they worship, besides Allah, those who do not have power to grant them any provision from the heavens or the earth.*

Ibn Kathīr frames the whole section as a denunciation. Allah tells us about the *mushrikīn* — those who set up partners with Him — who worship others besides Him even though He alone is the bountiful Provider, the Creator and Sustainer, without partners or associates; and still they worship idols and make rivals for Him.

What does it mean that these objects of worship cannot grant provision "from the heavens or the earth"? Ibn Kathīr unpacks it concretely: **nobody can cause rain to fall, or make plants and trees grow.** Rain from the sky, growth from the soil — the two halves of the world's food supply, and neither is in any idol's grip.

Then Ibn Kathīr adds the most humbling detail of all: **they cannot do these things for themselves, even if they wanted to.** A being that cannot provide for itself is being asked to provide for its worshippers. The absurdity is not argued; it is simply displayed.

## Ayah 74: "So do not coin similarities for Allah"

**فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا لِلَّهِ الْأَمْثَالَ** — rendered in our sources as *So do not give examples on behalf of Allah*, *do not set up equals to Allah*, *do not coin similarities for Allah*.

Ibn Kathīr gives the meaning plainly: **do not set up rivals to Him, or describe anything as being like Him.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this sentence as clarifying something essential about the reality of things as they relate to Allah — and warns that where it is ignored, it becomes the breeding ground of all sorts of rejectionist doubts and scruples. Here is the mechanism it describes. People generally take Allah on the analogy of their own humankind: they look to the highest-placed among themselves, a king and ruler, and declare him similar to Allah. Then, relying on that wrong assumption, they start seeing the divine system on the analogy of a human monarchy. They take a cue from the fact that no king can run the administration of a whole kingdom by himself; he delegates to subordinate ministers and officials who act on his behalf. So, they propose, there must likewise be other objects of worship under Allah's authority who help Him carry out His tasks. *This*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is the general theory of all idol-worshippers and polytheists.

And this sentence of the Qurʼān cuts off the very root of those doubts: to take examples of what has been *created* and apply them to Allah, the Creator, is unreasonable in itself. He is far above similarities and analogies and conjectures and guesses.

Two things are worth holding onto here.

**First, this is not a ban on parables as such** — the very next ayah begins, "Allah sets forth a parable," and so does the one after it. Allah may set forth a likeness; the creature may not coin one *for Him*. The direction of the comparison is everything.

**Second, notice how wide Ibn Kathīr's wording makes the prohibition.** It is not only *do not set up rivals to Him* but also *do not describe anything as being like Him*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the same boundary from the other side: He is far above similarities, analogies, conjectures and guesses.

The closing words, **"Truly, Allah knows and you know not,"** mean, as Ibn Kathīr explains: **He knows and bears witness that there is no god but Him, but you are ignorant and associate others in worship with Him.** The comparison-makers are not merely mistaken; they are reasoning from ignorance about the only One who fully knows.

## Ayah 75: the first parable — the owned slave and the man who spends

Having forbidden false comparisons, Allah now supplies true ones.

The first: a servant under the possession of another, who **has no power of any sort** — set against a man on whom Allah has bestowed good provisions from Himself, **and he spends from that secretly and openly.** Can they be equal?

Notice how the second man is described: not by what he holds back but by what he spends — and in both registers, the hidden and the open.

**The commentators read this parable in two ways, and Ibn Kathīr reports both.**

Al-ʿAwfī reported that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: "This is the example which Allah gives of the disbeliever and the believer." This was also the view of **Qatādah** and **Ibn Jarīr**. On this reading, the servant who has no power over anything is like the disbeliever, and the one who is given good provisions and spends of them secretly and openly is like the believer.

Ibn Abī Najīḥ reported that **Mujāhid** understood it differently: it is an example given of the idol and the True Deity — can the two be the same?

Ibn Kathīr sets the two readings side by side without dismissing either. Either way, he adds, once the difference between them is this clear and this obvious, **no one can be unaware of it except the one who is foolish.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the argument's real force, which runs from the lesser to the greater. The two figures in this parable — the owner and the owned — are **of the same genus and the same kind**. Yet even here, within one shared nature, equality is impossible. When these two cannot be equal to each other, how then could you equate someone or something created by Allah with Him?

Then come the ayah's own words: **"All the praises and thanks are to Allah. Nay! But most of them know not."** That last clause echoes ayah 74's "you know not." Across this passage, idolatry keeps being diagnosed as a failure of knowledge.

## Ayah 76: the second parable — the burden who brings back no good

The second parable is sharper. One man is **dumb** — unable to speak — with **no power over anything**, and he is **a burden on his master**: whichever way his master directs him, he **brings no good.**

**Mujāhid** said this parable too refers to idols on one side and, on the other, the True Deity, may He be exalted. And Ibn Kathīr spells out how the description fits an idol point by point: the idol **is dumb and cannot speak or say anything, good or otherwise. It cannot do anything at all — no words, no action. It is dependent, and is a burden on its master.**

Sit with that last phrase. The thing being worshipped is not the one carrying; it is the one being carried. Ibn Kathīr glosses **"whichever way he directs him"** as *wherever he sends him*, and **"he brings no good"** as *he does not succeed in what he wants.* Every errand comes back empty.

Al-ʿAwfī likewise reported that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: "This is also an example of the disbeliever and the believer", as in the previous ayah — so both parables carry both readings.

Against this figure stands **"one who commands justice and is himself on the straight path."** Ibn Kathīr: *commands justice* means fairness — **one whose words are true and whose deeds are righteous.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān separates the two halves of that description beautifully:

- **He bids justice and teaches what is good** — this is a model of his **intellectual** perfection.
- **He himself takes the path of moderation and right guidance** — this is the model of his **practical** perfection.

Set against the power of this intellectually and practically perfect man is the other man, who **cannot do anything for himself, nor anything right for others.** And once again Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the same point, now even more emphatically: these two men, despite being of one genus, one species and one brotherhood, cannot be equal to each other. So how can some created being or thing become equal to **the Creator and Master of the universe, who is Absolute in Wisdom, Absolute in Power, and All-Knowing and All-Aware?**

## The two parables do not repeat each other

The contrasts are drawn along different lines. In the first, the difference between the two figures is what they possess and what they do with it — one has no power of any sort, the other has been given good provisions and spends of them secretly and openly. In the second, the difference is speech and benefit — one cannot say anything, good or otherwise, and returns from every errand empty-handed; the other commands justice in words that are true, and walks the straight path himself. And in both, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the two being compared share one genus — and still they are not equal.

## Living it

**Trace every provision back to the One who gives it.** Ibn Kathīr's gloss on ayah 73 is worth keeping in view: no one can cause rain to fall or make plants and trees grow. Allah alone is the bountiful Provider, the Creator and Sustainer, without partners or associates — so thanks belong with Him.

**Refuse the king-and-ministers picture.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identified this as the general theory behind idolatry: assuming Allah must operate like a scaled-up human ruler who needs deputies to help Him carry out His tasks. Whenever your reasoning about Allah begins "well, a person in that position would…", ayah 74 is speaking to you. He is far above similarities, analogies, conjectures and guesses.

**Be the second man in each parable.** Spend from what you have been given — **secretly and openly**, both. Command what is just. And keep to the path of moderation and right guidance yourself, so that the teaching and the walking are one thing. Ibn Kathīr's description of that man is a standard worth holding oneself to: **true in word, righteous in deed.**

**Ask which figure you resemble in ayah 76.** The man in the parable is described as dependent, a burden on his master, sent out and bringing back no good. It is a description one can quietly measure oneself against.

And when the contrast finally becomes clear, ayah 75 has already given you the words for it: **الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ** — *all the praises and thanks are to Allah.*

passages.title: Knower of the unseen: senses, birds, homes and shade
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat answer one question. The question, left hanging by the parables just before this passage, is whether anything created can be set beside its Creator. The answer arrives in two movements: first, that the unseen of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, who is able to do all things (ayah 77); then, that every faculty in your body and every comfort in your life came from Him and is held up by Him (ayat 78–81). The thread stitching them together is the drumbeat of "and Allah…" — Allah brought you out, Allah made your homes, Allah made shade for you — until the passage closes with the purpose behind the whole list: "that you may submit yourselves to His will."

## The bridge from what came before

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the parable immediately preceding: one man who "bids justice and teaches what is good" — his intellectual perfection — and who himself "takes the path of moderation and right guidance" — his practical perfection; set against a man who "cannot do anything for himself nor can he do anything right for others." Two men of one species, and even they are not equal. Maʿārif draws the conclusion that is the doorway into our passage: "So, how can some created being or thing become equal to the Creator and Master of the universe who is Absolute in Wisdom, Absolute in Power, and All-Knowing and All-Aware?"

Ayah 77 takes up exactly those two attributes and states them outright.

## Ayah 77: knowledge no one shares, power nothing resists

Ibn Kathir titles his comment here "The Unseen belongs to Allah and only He has Knowledge of the Hour," and reads the ayah as Allah "telling us of the perfection of His knowledge and ability to do all things, by telling us that He alone knows the Unseen of the heavens and the earth."

Then he adds: "No one knows anything about such things except for what Allah informs about as He wills." It is not won by cleverness or effort. It is given, in the measure He chooses to give.

Then power. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah's complete power, "which no one can oppose or resist, means that when He wants a thing, He only has to say to it 'Be!' and it is." He sets our ayah beside two others: "And Our commandment is but one as the twinkling of an eye" (54:50), which he glosses as "whatever He wills happens in blinking"; and "The processes of creating you all and resurrecting you all are but like that of a single person" (31:28). Raising every human being who ever lived costs Him no more than raising one.

Ibn Kathir treats them as one statement: "And the matter of the Hour is not but as a twinkling of the eye, or even nearer. Truly, Allah is Able to do all things."

## Ayah 78: you arrived knowing nothing

From the vastness of the unseen the passage turns, startlingly, to the delivery room. "And Allah has brought you out from the wombs of your mothers while you knew nothing. And He gave you hearing, sight, and hearts, that you might give thanks."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what that phrase settles: "knowledge is not an ingrained personal excellence of man. When born, man has no knowledge or skill." Whatever a person later comes to know, he did not bring it with him. Instead, Maʿārif says, "in proportion to growing human needs, man is made to absorb some knowledge, bit by bit, directly from Allah Taʿālā in which no role is played by the parents or teachers."

And yet the newborn is not left helpless. Maʿārif describes the first curriculum: "First of all, man was taught to cry. This one qualification alone provides all he needs at that time. Hungry or thirsty, he cries. Feels hot or cold, he cries." And who taught him? Maʿārif asks pointedly: if the child were not "inducted into this act of crying as part of his or her early education from a side no less than that of Allah Himself, who else could have trained the child" to cry precisely when there is a need? Alongside it, Maʿārif notes, "Nature has poured a special kind of love in the hearts of the father and the mother for the needs of the infant," so that when they hear the child they are "all too eager to find out what is bothering the baby." And Allah taught the infant by inspiration to use gums and lips to draw milk — a skill, Maʿārif says, that "no teacher anywhere could dare make this newborn learn."

**Why hearing, then sight, then hearts.** The order of *as-samʿ, al-abṣār, al-afʼidah* is not decorative. Maʿārif suggests hearing is mentioned first "perhaps for the reason that the very first knowledge, and the most of it, comes through nothing but ears. In the beginning, eyes are closed, but ears hear." And it holds for a whole lifetime: "the amount of information one acquires in a whole life time is mostly what has been heard with ears. Information collected visually is much less than that."

Third comes *afʼidah*, which Maʿārif identifies as the plural of *fuʼād*, the heart — and the ayah places it third, Maʿārif says, because "after these two, comes information which one deduces by deliberating into things heard and seen." Ibn Kathir glosses "hearts" here as "meaning reason," and describes the apparatus working together: hearing "to recognize voices," sight "to see visible things," and reason by which "a person can distinguish between what is harmful and what is beneficial." He also notes that these do not arrive fully formed: "These abilities and senses develop gradually in man. The more he grows, the more his hearing, vision and reason increase, until they reach their peak."

**Where does understanding sit?** Here the commentators record a genuine difference. Ibn Kathir says the seat of reason is the heart "according to the correct view, although it was also said that its seat is the brain." Maʿārif frames the same question with the science of its day: "Scientists identify the human brain as the center of understanding and reason. But, the statement of the Qurʼan tells us that though the brain plays a role in this process of reasoning, yet the real center of knowledge and reason is the heart."

**Why speech is missing from the list.** Maʿārif raises the question and gives two answers. First, "speech plays no role in the acquisition of knowledge. It is, rather, a source of the expression of knowledge" — and this ayah is about the instruments by which a person who knew nothing comes to know. Second, on the authority of Imam Al-Qurtubi, the word *samʿ* already "is inclusive of *nuṭq* (speech) as a corollary, as experience bears out that a person who hears speaks as well," while one who cannot hear does not learn to speak. Maʿārif closes that reasoning with *wallāhu aʿlam*, "and Allah knows best," and explains the phrase: it belongs "where definite knowledge about a subject in flux is not available or accessible or reliable," and serves a believer as "a safety device against the possibility of having made any false statements, which may be a sin."

**What the senses are for.** The ayah ends *laʿallakum tashkurūn*, "that you might give thanks." Ibn Kathir is blunt about the design intent: "Allah has created these faculties in man to enable him to worship his Lord, so he uses all these organs, abilities and strengths to obey his Master." On his reading, the thanks the ayah asks for shows itself in the *use* of the gift.

## The hadith Ibn Kathir cites here

To show what such a life looks like, Ibn Kathir brings the hadith reported by Al-Bukhari in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah says:

"Whoever takes My friend as an enemy, has declared war on Me. My servant does not draw near to Me with anything better than his doing that which I have enjoined upon him, and My servant keeps drawing near to Me by doing Nawafil (supererogatory) deeds until I love him. And when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his vision with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes and his foot with which he walks. Were he to ask Me for anything, I would give it to him, if he were to call on Me, I would respond, if he were to seek Me for refuge I would surely grant him it. I do not hesitate to do anything as I hesitate to take the soul of My believing servant, because he hates death and I hate to upset him, but it is inevitable."

What Allah says of Himself in these closing words we affirm as it came, in the way of the Salaf: without likening Him to anything in His creation, and without emptying the words of the meaning He intended by them.

Ibn Kathir supplies the meaning of the hadith immediately, and it is the safeguard against reading into it what is not there: "when a person is sincere in his obedience towards Allah, all his deeds are done for the sake of Allah, so he only hears for the sake of Allah, he only sees for the sake of Allah — meaning he only listens to or looks at what has been allowed by Allah. He does not strike or walk except in obedience to Allah, seeking Allah's help in all of these things." Ibn Kathir adds that some versions of the hadith, which he notes are "narrated outside the Sahih," carry the extra line after "his foot with which he walks": "So through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he strikes and through Me he walks."

The faculties Allah gave are the very faculties turned back to His obedience. Note too the hadith's order: nothing draws a servant nearer than what Allah has enjoined, and the voluntary extras carry him on until Allah loves him.

## Ayah 79: the birds

"Have they not seen the birds glide in the open sky? None holds them up but Allah." Ibn Kathir describes them as held "in the sky, between heaven and earth, and how He has caused them to fly with their wings in the sky." What holds them there? "They are held up only by Him, it is He Who gave them the strength to do that, subjecting the air to carry them and support them." Both halves of the miracle are His: the wing that beats and the air that answers it. He cites the parallel in Surat Al-Mulk: "Do they not see the birds above them, spreading their wings out and folding them in? None holds them up except the Most Gracious. Verily, He is the All-Seer of everything" (67:19).

Notice the contrast with ayah 77: there, an unseen no one can inspect; here, something visible above every head. And note how the ayah closes — "in this are clear signs for people who believe." The birds fly the same way over everyone; the clause names who reads that flight as a sign.

## Ayah 80: the house as a place of peace

*Bayt*, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, means "a house where night could be spent," and it quotes Imam Al-Qurtubi's working definition: "Whatever is above your head and provides shade for you is roof or sky, and whatever holds you atop is earth, and whatever screens you out from all four sides are walls, and when (all these components are) put together properly, that is a house."

But the ayah does not call it shelter. It calls it *sakan* — a place of rest and peace. Maʿārif treats that single word as the Qurʼan making "the logic and wisdom of making houses fully evident, that is, its real purpose is to have comfort of the body and peace of the heart." The reasoning is simple: "the avenues of human work lie outside houses," and such work "owes its existence to human movement and struggle"; the home is where you go "when tired after moving around and doing things, and rest and enjoy peace."

Maʿārif then presses this into an uncomfortably relevant critique: "The world of today is at the height of its building craze. Limitless expenditure is incurred on their superficial finishing. But, there are very few homes among them which would provide peace of mind and heart." Worse, "the artificially imposed additions in them become the very agents which destroy comfort and peace," and even without such extravagance, "the kind of people one confronts in the house is a misfortune which sucks that peace away." Compare an elegant house with a modest hut, it says, and "the dweller of the hut who is blessed with comfort and peace for his body and heart is certainly living in a better place."

Maʿārif links this to marriage, whose real purpose "was also determined to be peace," in the Qurʼan's words *litaskunū ilayhā*, "so that you may enjoy peace with her" (30:21) — the same root as *sakan*. Home and marriage are measured by one standard, and "a married life which fails to achieve this purpose remains deprived of the real benefit destined for it."

**The travelling house.** The ayah then names the other kind of home: dwellings from the hides of cattle. Ibn Kathir notes they are "light and easy to carry on journeys and can be erected wherever they stop, whether they are traveling or are settled" — hence "which you find so light when you travel and when you camp." Then the furnishings: "out of their wool, fur and hair" refers, he says, to sheep, camels and goats respectively. On *athāth*, Ibn Kathir reports it was said to mean wealth, or articles of convenience, or clothing, and concludes: "The correct view is more general in meaning than this; it means that you make carpets, clothing and other things from their wool, hair etc., which you use as wealth and for trade." Ibn ʿAbbas said *al-athāth* means "articles of convenience and comfort," a view also held by Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, ʿAtiyah Al-ʿAwfi, ʿAtaʼ Al-Khurasani, Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah.

And the ayah ends *ilā ḥīn* — "for a while." Ibn Kathir: "until the appointed time." Every comfort just listed has an appointed end. The gifts are real; permanent they are not.

**A ruling drawn from the ayah.** Maʿārif takes the mention of hides, wool, fur and hair as proof "that it is Halal to use everything out of the hide, wool and hair of animals." As Maʿārif reads it, the ayah carries no restriction "that the animal be properly slaughtered or be a dead animal," nor "any restriction as to their meat being Halal or Haram": hides may be used "by tanning them," while "as for hair and wool, the death of the animal leaves just no effect on them." Maʿārif identifies this as "the Madhab (creed) of the great Imam, Abu Hanifah," and notes the exception: "the hide of swine and all parts thereof are unclean and unfit for use under all conditions."

## Ayah 81: shade, refuges, clothing, armour

The list continues outward from the home. **Shade** — Qatadah said this "means trees." **Refuges in the mountains** — *aknān*, which Ibn Kathir explains as "fortresses and strongholds," the shelter you did not have to build. **Garments to protect you from the heat** — Ibn Kathir: "clothing of cotton, linen and wool."

Then the same word, *sarābīl*, is used a second time in the same ayah for something very different: garments "to protect you from your violence," which Ibn Kathir explains as "shields made of layers of sheet iron, coats of mail and so on." One kind of clothing shields you from the weather; the other shields you from each other. That the list of Allah's favours has to include armour is a quiet, sobering comment on the creature receiving the favours.

**Why only heat is mentioned.** A shirt protects from cold as well, so why name heat alone? Maʿārif reports the answer of Imam Al-Qurtubi and other commentators: the Qurʼan "has been revealed in the Arabic language, its first addressees are Arabs, therefore, it speaks by taking Arab habits and needs into account. Arabia is a hot country where the very thought of snow and winter chill is far-fetched, therefore, the statement was left with the mention of protection from heat as being sufficient." Maulana Ashraf Ali Thanavi, in Bayan al-Qurʼan, adds a second answer from within the surah itself: earlier, at 16:5, the Qurʼan had already said of the cattle, "and for you, there is provision against cold in them" — so the warmth had been covered, and only the heat needed mention here.

## Where the passage lands

"Thus does He perfect His favor for you, that you may submit yourselves to His will." Ibn Kathir reads the perfecting of favour practically: "thus He gives you what you need to go about your business, so that this will help you to worship and obey Him." The senses, the sustaining air, the house, the tent, the shade, the mountain refuge, the shirt, the coat of mail — the whole inventory exists to make possible a life in which worship can happen. And *laʿallakum tuslimūn* is interpreted, Ibn Kathir says, "by the majority to mean submitting to Allah or becoming Muslim."

The three purpose-clauses across the passage give the argument in miniature: *that you might give thanks* (78), *signs for people who believe* (79), *that you may submit yourselves to His will* (81). Gratitude, faith, surrender — three names for the one correct response to a life you did not build.

**Living it.** Take one thing today — the hearing you were given before your eyes opened, the roof over the bed you woke in, the coat you put on — and follow it back past the shop and the builder to the One who made it and holds it there, as the bird is held in the open sky. Then use it for what it was given for. On Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 78, that use is exactly what *shukr*, thankfulness, looks like.

passages.title: The Prophet's duty is only to convey
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close a long catalogue of Allah's gifts — homes, leather tents, wool and fur and hair, shade, shelter in the mountains, clothing, armour — with a sudden turn. Ayah 82 tells the Prophet ﷺ what he is, and is not, answerable for when people turn away from all of that. Ayah 83 says something about the people who turn away: they are not ignorant of the Giver. What holds the two ayat together is a line drawn between two things that are easily confused — delivering the message, which is the messenger's duty, and accepting it, which never was.

## The blessings that come just before

Ayah 82 opens with "Then, if they turn away," so we need to know what they are turning away from. Ibn Kathir walks through the ayat just before it. Allah has given people homes to dwell in and protect themselves with, "in which they find all kinds of benefits," and He has also given them homes made from the hides of cattle — leather — "which are light and easy to carry on journeys and can be erected wherever they stop, whether they are traveling or are settled." The wool, fur and hair mentioned in ayah 80 refer, Ibn Kathir notes, to sheep, camels and goats respectively.

On the word *athāth*, rendered "furnishings," Ibn Kathir reports Ibn 'Abbas as saying that it means "articles of convenience and comfort" — the view also of Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, 'Atiyah Al-'Awfi, 'Ata' Al-Khurasani, Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah. It has also been explained as what you take from these animals, that is, wealth, or as clothing. Ibn Kathir's own conclusion is that "the correct view is more general in meaning than this": that from their wool and hair you make carpets, clothing and other things, which you use as wealth and for trade. And the closing phrase *ilā ḥīn*, "for a while," he explains as "until the appointed time" — every one of these comforts has an end stamped on it.

Then ayah 81. Shade, which Qatadah explained as "trees." *Aknān* in the mountains, meaning "fortresses and strongholds." Garments to protect from the heat, meaning clothing of cotton, linen and wool. And coats of mail to protect you from your own violence — "such as shields made of layers of sheet iron, coats of mail and so on." Then the summary: *"Thus does He perfect His favor for you, that you may submit yourselves to His will."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss on that summary is the hinge of the whole passage. Allah "gives you what you need to go about your business, so that this will help you to worship and obey Him." And on *la'allakum tuslimūn*, "that you may submit yourselves to His will," he notes that this "is interpreted by the majority to mean submitting to Allah or becoming Muslim."

So on this reading the blessings are not an end in themselves. They are what you need in order to get on with a life of worship and obedience, and they carry an implied claim on whoever enjoys them. Ayat 82 and 83 deal with the person who takes the gift and rejects the claim.

## A note on how the message was pitched

Maarif ul Quran pauses on a small detail in ayah 81 — the phrase *sarābīl taqīkum al-ḥarr*, "shirts which protect you from heat." Why heat only, when a shirt protects a person "from heat and cold both"?

Maarif reports the answer given by Imam Al-Qurtubi and other commentators: the Qur'an "has been revealed in the Arabic language, its first addressees are Arabs, therefore, it speaks by taking Arab habits and needs into account." Arabia is a hot country "where the very thought of snow and winter chill is far-fetched," so mentioning protection from heat was sufficient. Maulana Ashraf Ali Thanavi, in Bayan al-Qur'an, offers a further explanation: earlier in this same sūrah the Qur'an had already said, *"and for you, there is provision against cold in them"* (16:5), so with protection from cold already mentioned, only heat needed mentioning here.

It is worth holding that alongside ayah 82. On the commentators' explanation, the message these people turned from was pitched in their own language and framed with their own habits and needs in view, nothing repeated that had already been said. Whatever the cause of their turning away, this passage does not present it as a failure of clarity.

## Ayah 82: the boundary of the Prophet's ﷺ duty

*"Then, if they turn away…"* Ibn Kathir renders the sense of this clause with striking directness: **"meaning, after this declaration and reminder, do not worry about them."** The consolation is aimed squarely at the Prophet ﷺ. The declaration has been made and the reminder given; if people walk away from it, the weight of that walking is not his to carry.

*"…your duty (O Muhammad) is only to convey (the Message) in a clear way."* Two features of that sentence are worth sitting with, and both are right there in the wording.

The first is the word **only**. Both renderings of the ayah in front of us place it in the sentence: the duty is *only* to convey. That word does not enlarge the Prophet's ﷺ task; it bounds it. What lies outside the boundary — their hearts, their choices, the final outcome — is not on his account. Ibn Kathir adds, of the Prophet ﷺ, "and you have delivered the Message to them": the duty the ayah names is one he affirms was carried out.

The second is **"in a clear way."** The duty is not merely to say the words but to convey clearly. That is a mercy and a standard at once. It lifts from the Prophet ﷺ — and from anyone who inherits his work of calling — the crushing responsibility for another person's guidance. But it also sets a real bar. A muddled, half-explained, hostile or careless delivery has not yet met the condition the ayah names.

## Ayah 83: they know — and still they deny

*"They recognize the grace of Allah, yet they deny it (by worshipping others besides Allah) and most of them are disbelievers."*

Ibn Kathir spells out what that means: **"they know that Allah is the One Who grants these blessings to them, and that He is Bountiful towards them, but they still deny this by worshipping others besides Him and thinking that their help and provisions come from others besides Him."**

Notice how he puts it. The denial does not sit in place of the knowledge; it sits alongside it. They *know* — and they *still* deny. The recognition is not erased by the refusal; it is present the whole time.

And Ibn Kathir names two forms this denial takes, which are worth separating.

The first is **denial in worship**: knowing where the gift came from, and directing devotion elsewhere.

The second is quieter and lives inside the chest: **"thinking that their help and provisions come from others besides Him."** That one does not announce itself. A person can state the truth accurately and still, in the way he actually thinks about his rent, his job, his contacts and his health, be crediting a source other than the Giver.

So what ayah 83 describes, on Ibn Kathir's reading, is not a failure of information. This is worth setting beside ayah 82: no further clarity of delivery can undo a refusal that co-exists with knowledge rather than arising from ignorance.

The passage then closes with the verdict — *"and most of them are disbelievers."* Ibn Kathir lets the phrase stand without further comment, and it is better not to press it further than he does. Its plain force is in the word *most*: this is not presented as a rare exception among them.

## Living it

**If you carry the message to anyone**, ayah 82 is both your job description and your relief. Convey, and convey clearly. Then let go. Ibn Kathir's phrase is the one to keep: *do not worry about them.* Anxiety over a relative's or a friend's response, guilt over their refusal, the temptation to force or engineer a result — the ayah quietly removes all of that from your side of the ledger. What remains on your side is real work: was the conveying actually clear? Was it honest and understandable to *this* listener? The commentators' note on ayah 81 — that the Qur'an speaks "by taking Arab habits and needs into account," addressing its first hearers in terms fitted to their own lives — is a good instinct to imitate.

**And read ayah 83 against yourself first.** It is not written only about other people. Ask where the reflex of the heart goes when relief arrives: to the person who helped, to your own competence, to luck — or to Allah, who "is the One Who grants these blessings" and "is Bountiful towards" you? Knowing the Giver and still crediting the help and the provision elsewhere is precisely what Ibn Kathir describes here.

**Finally, hold on to what the blessings were for.** Ibn Kathir says Allah gives you what you need to go about your business "so that this will help you to worship and obey Him," and that *la'allakum tuslimūn* is understood by the majority to mean submitting to Allah, becoming Muslim. The house, the clothes, the shade, the safety, the trade — on this reading all of it is equipment for a life handed back to Allah. And it is all *ilā ḥīn*, until the appointed time. The gifts run out. What they were meant to produce in you does not.

passages.title: Witnesses on the Day the idols disown
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These six ayat set us down on the Day of Resurrection and let us watch a scene of testimony. Allah raises a witness over every nation, those who disbelieved are refused permission to excuse themselves, the gods they served turn on them and call them liars, everything surrenders — and finally the Prophet ﷺ is brought as a witness over this Ummah (the community that follows him), with the Book he was given mentioned in the very next breath.

**What holds them together.** The passage opens and closes with almost the same words. Ayah 84: *"And on the Day when We resurrect a witness from each nation…"* Ayah 89: *"And on the Day when We resurrect a witness from each nation from among themselves, and We bring you as a witness against these."* Everything in between — the excuse that is refused (84), the torment that is not lightened (85), the gods' denial (86), the universal surrender (87), the added punishment (88) — belongs inside that Day. The closing mention then turns towards us: our Prophet ﷺ, and the Book he was charged with conveying.

## The witness is their own Prophet (ayah 84)

Ibn Kathir tells us that Allah is describing the predicament of the idolaters on the Day when they will be resurrected in the realm of the Hereafter: **He will raise a witness from every nation — that is, their Prophet — to testify about their response to the Message he conveyed from Allah.**

Notice how precise the wording is. Ayah 89 adds *min anfusihim*, which Ibn Kathir's rendering gives as "from among themselves." The witness raised over a people is their own Prophet, one from among them — the very man who carried the Message to them is the one who reports on how they received it.

**"Then those who disbelieved will not be given leave."** Ibn Kathir glosses this: *they will not be allowed to offer any excuse.* He supports it with Allah's words about the same Day: *"That will be a Day when they do not speak. And they will not be permitted to present any excuse"* (77:35–36).

This is worth sitting with. In this world we always have an explanation ready, and there is always someone to hear it. On that Day, as the ayah Ibn Kathir cites puts it, they do not speak, and the permission to present an excuse is not given.

**"Nor will they be allowed to seek Allah's pleasure."** Ibn Kathir renders this as: *nor will they be allowed to return to the world to repent and ask for Allah's forgiveness.* Two things are withheld in a single ayah: the chance to explain yourself, and the chance to go back and put it right. Both of those are in your hands today. That is the whole force of the ayah.

## The torment that is not lightened and not delayed (ayah 85)

Two mercies that soften every worldly hardship are named and removed.

**"It will not be lightened for them."** Ibn Kathir: *it will not be reduced for them even for a moment.* No relief inside the punishment.

**"Nor will they be given respite."** Ibn Kathir: *it will not be delayed for them; rather they will be taken quickly from the place of gathering, with no calling to account.* No delay before the punishment either — no waiting period they can shelter inside. His phrase is stark and it is best left exactly as he wrote it: *with no calling to account.*

Ibn Kathir then relates what he describes as reported in the Hadith — he does not name a collection at this point, so neither will we. It describes the bringing forth of Hell: it is pulled by seventy thousand ropes, each rope held by seventy thousand angels; a neck stretches forth from Hell towards the people and expels a gust of hot air, and no one is left but falls to his knees. Then it says, "I have been entrusted to deal with every stubborn, arrogant one who joined another god with Allah," and it goes on to mention other types of people; then it comes down upon them and picks them up from where they are standing **as a bird picks up a seed.**

That last image is the one that lodges. Not a battle, not a struggle — the effortless motion of a bird taking a grain off the ground.

Ibn Kathir then lines up the Qur'an's own descriptions: the Fire seen *"from a far place"* with its *"raging and roaring,"* the guilty *"thrown into a narrow part of it, chained together,"* crying for destruction — and told to cry not once but repeatedly (25:12–14); *"the guilty shall see the Fire and apprehend that they are about to fall into it. And they will find no way to avoid it"* (18:53); and the warning that it will come upon them *"all of a sudden and will perplex them,"* with no power to avert it and no respite (21:39–40).

## The gods turn on their worshippers (ayah 86)

Ibn Kathir heads this section: *the gods of the idolaters will disown them at the time when they need them most.*

Read the scene slowly. *"And when those who associated partners with Allah see their partners"* — Ibn Kathir specifies: those whom they used to worship in this world.

Then they speak: *"Our Lord! These are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You."* Notice the words they still use. Standing before their Lord, on that Day, they are still saying "our partners."

**And the answer comes back.** *"But they will throw their statement back at them: 'You are indeed liars!'"* Ibn Kathir gives the sense: *those gods will say to them, "You are lying. We never commanded you to worship us."*

Ibn Kathir gathers the parallels, and together they make one unmistakable Qur'anic theme:

- *"And who is more astray than one who calls upon others besides Allah — such as will not answer him till the Day of Resurrection, and who are even unaware of their invocations to them? And when the people are gathered, they will become their enemies and will deny their worship"* (46:5–6). Note the two stages the ayah itself sets out: in this life the false deities are **unaware** of the calls; when the people are gathered, they become **enemies**.
- *"And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they might give them honour, power and glory. Nay, but they will deny their worship, and become their adversaries"* (19:81–82). They were taken up for honour and glory; the ayah's answer is a flat *"Nay."*
- The words of Al-Khalīl, Ibrāhīm عليه السلام: *"but on the Day of Resurrection, you will disown each other"* (29:25).
- And the summons: *"Call upon your partners"* (28:64).

Ibn Kathir adds that there are many other similar ayat.

## Everything surrenders (ayah 87)

*"And they will offer full submission to Allah on that Day."* **Qatādah and ʿIkrimah said: "They will humble themselves and surrender on that Day."** Ibn Kathir draws out the implication: *they will all surrender to Allah; there will not be anyone who does not hear and obey.*

There is something the Arabic makes visible here. One and the same verb — أَلْقَوْا — stands at the centre of two consecutive ayat. In ayah 86 it is rendered "they will **throw** their statement back at them"; in ayah 87 it is rendered "they will **offer** full submission to Allah." The word for the accusation flung at them is the word for the surrender they hand over.

Ibn Kathir illustrates their new clarity with three ayat: *"How clearly will they see and hear, the Day when they will appear before Us!"* (19:38) — meaning, he says, **they will see and hear better than they have ever seen and heard before**; *"if you only could see when the guilty hang their heads before their Lord: 'Our Lord! We have now seen and heard'"* (32:12); and *"all faces shall be humbled before the Ever Living, the Sustainer"* (20:111), which he explains as: they will humble and submit themselves.

The tragedy is not that they lacked the faculties. The faculties work perfectly — on the wrong day.

**"And what they falsely invented will wander away from them."** Ibn Kathir: *the things they used to worship, which were all based on fabrications and lies, will all disappear, and they will have no helper or supporter, and no one to turn to.*

## Punishment upon punishment (ayah 88)

*"Those who disbelieved and tried to obstruct the path of Allah — for them We will add torment on top of the torment."*

Ibn Kathir is exact about why: **one punishment for their disbelief, and another punishment for turning others away from following the truth.** Two separate wrongs, two separate sentences. Disbelief settles on the one who holds it; obstruction reaches into other people's lives.

He cites the portrait in 6:26 — *"And they prevent others from him and they themselves keep away from him"* — explaining it as: *they forbade others to follow him and they themselves shunned him.* And then the same ayah's verdict: *"they destroyed only themselves, while they do not realise it."* The harm they aimed outwards lands on them, and they do not see it.

**A point of doctrine drawn out here.** Ibn Kathir says this ayah is evidence that **there will be varying levels of punishment for the disbelievers, just as there will be varying degrees of Paradise for the believers**, and supports it with *"For each one there is double torment, but you know not"* (7:38). Divine justice is not one flat sentence applied to everyone; it is measured.

## The Prophet ﷺ brought as witness (ayah 89)

Now the scene turns and faces us. *"And on the Day when We resurrect a witness from each nation from among themselves, and We bring you as a witness against these."* Ibn Kathir explains "these" as **your Ummah**, and reads the ayah as a double address: *remember that Day and its terrors, and the great honour and high position that Allah has bestowed upon you.* Terror and honour named together, in one ayah, about one moment.

**How the Prophet ﷺ himself received this.** Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah is like the ayah at which ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd stopped when he recited to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from the beginning of Sūrat al-Nisā'. When he reached *"How will it be then, when We bring from each nation a witness and We bring you as a witness against these?"* (4:41), the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him, **"Enough."** Ibn Masʿūd said: *"I turned to him and saw his eyes streaming with tears."*

That is the whole of the report, and it is enough. The recitation stops, and the tears come. Ibn Kathir does not explain them; the scene itself is the lesson.

## "An explanation of everything"

*"And We revealed the Book to you as an explanation of everything, and a guidance and a mercy and good news for the Muslims."*

**Ibn Masʿūd** said of *tibyānan li-kulli shayʼ*: *"Allah made it clear that in this Qur'an there is complete knowledge and about everything."* Ibn Kathir spells out the range: reports of what happened in the past, information about what is yet to come, what is lawful and unlawful, and what people need to know about their worldly affairs, their religion, their livelihood in this world, and their destiny in the Hereafter. Of *"a guidance"* he says simply: **for their hearts.**

**Al-Awzāʿī** read the phrase more tightly: an explanation of everything **with the Sunnah** — that is, through the Prophet's ﷺ own teaching.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** treats the obvious question head-on. "Everything," it says, means everything about the religion, because that is what Divine revelation and the prophetic mission concern themselves with. It therefore warns that **the very effort to cull out answers to problems of economic science from the Qur'an is an exercise in error** — though it adds that the appearance of some implied hint here or there is not contrary to this.

Then the harder objection: the Qur'an does not carry answers to every problem of the religion itself, so how is it "an exposition of everything"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that **the Qur'an does carry the basic principles concerning all these problems**, and it is in the light of those principles that the aḥādīth of the Messenger of Allah clarify them; some details are then delegated to the principles of *ijmāʿ* (the consensus of the scholars) and *qiyās* (analogical deduction following the norms set by the Sharīʿah). Its conclusion is a valuable one: the religious rulings deduced from the aḥādīth, from *ijmāʿ* and from *qiyās* are also, in a way, stated by the Qur'an itself.

## Why the Book is mentioned right here

This is the most illuminating observation in the commentary on this passage, and it explains the join between the two halves of ayah 89. The mention of *"And We have revealed the Book to you"* comes immediately after *"And We shall bring you as a witness against these."* The meaning — **and Allah knows best**, as Ibn Kathir carefully says — is that **the One who obligated you to convey the Book which He revealed to you will also ask you about that on the Day of Resurrection.**

The witnessing and the Book are one subject. A trust given is a trust asked about. He supports it with: *"Then We shall indeed question those to whom it was sent, and We shall indeed question the Messengers"* (7:6); *"So by your Lord, We question them all about what they did"* (15:92–93); and *"On the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers together and says to them: 'What was the response you received?' They will say: 'We have no knowledge; indeed only You are the Knower of all that is hidden'"* (5:109).

He then mentions 28:85 — *"Verily, He who obligated the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to the return"* — read as: the One who gave you the obligation of conveying the Qur'an will bring you back to Him on the Day of Resurrection and question you about your commission of the duty He gave you. Ibn Kathir is scrupulous here and we should be too: he notes that **this is one of the opinions**, and that it presents a good understanding of it. He does not present it as the settled reading.

## Living it

**Test what you call upon.** Ayah 86 shows people who called upon something besides Allah, and shows what that something says to them on that Day: *"You are lying. We never commanded you to worship us."* And 46:5 asks who is more astray than the one who calls upon what cannot answer him. It is a question worth putting to ourselves about where we actually turn.

**The doors are open now.** Ayah 84 names exactly two things that are withheld there: the chance to offer an excuse, and the chance to return and repent and ask forgiveness. Both are in your hands at this moment. That is the mercy hidden inside a fearsome ayah.

**Watch your influence.** Ayah 88 adds a second punishment for the one who turns others away from the truth. Whatever weight your words carry with a child, a sibling, a friend, a following — that weight is being counted. And 6:26 is the sobering footnote: they forbade others and shunned him themselves, and destroyed only themselves, without realising it.

**Sit with the Prophet's ﷺ tears.** He heard the ayah about standing as witness, said "Enough," and his eyes streamed. The right response to this passage is not analysis but a lowered head.

**Take the Book as it presents itself.** Guidance for the heart, mercy, and good news — the exposition of the religion, whose principles the Sunnah, *ijmāʿ* and *qiyās* unfold, and not a place to go mining for the answers of worldly sciences. Read it looking for what it promises to give.

passages.title: Justice, kindness, and what Allah forbids
passages.tafsir:
**In one sentence.** Ayah 90 gathers six instructions — three things Allah commands and three He forbids — and then tells us why He is saying it at all: *"He admonishes you, so that perhaps you may take heed."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it the most comprehensive verse of the Qur'an, one in which the essence of the entire range of Islamic teachings has been condensed into a few words. The commentaries take those six words to be deliberately broad, and almost all their effort goes into showing how much each one takes in: how far *ʿadl* reaches, how many kinds of *iḥsān* there are, why *baghy* had to be named separately when *munkar* already covered it.

## "The most comprehensive ayah in the Qur'an"

Ash-Sha'bi reported that Shatiyr bin Shakl said: "I heard Ibn Mas'ud say: 'The most comprehensive ayah in the Qur'an is in Surat An-Nahl: *Verily, Allah enjoins justice and kindness...*'" Ibn Kathir notes that this was reported by Ibn Jarir.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records what followed from that judgement: because this single verse condenses the essence of the entire range of Islamic teachings into a few words, the practice has continued from the blessed period of the most righteous early generations to this day of reciting it at the close of the special khutbah of Jumu'ah and of the two Eids.

## Three men who heard this ayah

A large part of what these commentaries preserve here is not argument but *reception* — what happened to people when they first heard these words.

**'Uthman bin Maz'un.** Ibn Kathir records, on the authority of 'Abdullah bin 'Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting in the courtyard of his house when 'Uthman bin Maz'un passed by and smiled at him. The Prophet ﷺ invited him to sit, and sat facing him. While they were talking, the Prophet ﷺ began looking up at the sky for a while, then lowered his gaze to the ground on his right. He turned slightly away from his companion towards where he was looking, and began tilting his head as though trying to understand something. 'Uthman watched. When the matter was finished and he had understood what was said to him, the Prophet ﷺ stared at the sky again, looking at whatever he could see until it disappeared, then turned back to face 'Uthman.

'Uthman said he had never seen him do anything like it. The Prophet ﷺ asked him to describe what he had seen, and 'Uthman described it exactly. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Did you notice that?" — then told him: a messenger from Allah had come to him just then, while 'Uthman was sitting there. And what did he say? The Prophet ﷺ recited: *"Verily, Allah orders justice and kindness..."*

'Uthman said: "That was when faith was established in my heart and I began to love Muhammad ﷺ." Ibn Kathir reports this from Imam Ahmad and grades it a Hasan hadith with a good connected chain of narrators in which their hearing it from each other is clear. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves 'Uthman's own framing of it: at first he had embraced Islam because the people around him said so, and it had not yet taken root in his heart; after this moment his faith was firm and fortified, and love for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ settled there for good.

Pause on what he was given. He saw the signs of revelation coming down in front of him, and then he was told what had come down — *be just, be good, look after your family, and keep away from indecency, evil and aggression.*

**Aktham ibn al-Saifi.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, from Ibn Kathir quoting *Maʿrifatus-Sahabah*, a book by Abu Yaʿla, that Aktham was the chief of his people. Hearing of the Prophet ﷺ, his claim to prophethood and his call, he decided to go himself; his people said that going in person was not appropriate for a man of his rank, so Aktham proposed instead that two men be sent to survey the situation and report back. They came with two questions: "Who are you, and what are you?"

The Prophet ﷺ answered the first with his lineage — "I am Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah" — and the second with his function: "a servant of Allah and His Messenger." Then he recited this ayah. The two men asked him to recite it again; he kept reciting it until they had it memorised.

They came back and reported that their first question had been aimed at his lineage, and that he had given it little attention — he simply thought it enough to give his father's name — though when they checked with others they found him very high in lineage and nobility. Then they recited the ayah. Aktham answered at once: this tells us that he bids morals which are high and forbids morals which are low; embrace his religion as soon as possible, so that you stay ahead of other people and do not lag behind as camp followers. He embraced Islam on the basis of this very verse.

**Walid ibn Mughirah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that when the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse before Walid ibn Mughirah, he went to report his impression to his people, the Quraysh of Makkah: in it there is a special sweetness, and above it a unique halo of light; leaves are going to sprout from its roots and fruit is going to show on its branches — and this can never be the speech of any human being. The commentary records that impression and stops there.

## The three commands

### 1. Al-ʿAdl — justice

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān begins with the root: the real and literal meaning of *ʿadl* is **to make equal**. From that one idea, several meanings branch out.

Because it means making equal, it names the equitable judgement of officials in people's disputed cases — the sense in *"and that when you judge between people, judge with fairness"* (4:58). In view of this, it also names **moderation** (*al-iʿtidāl*) between the two extremes of excess (*al-ifrāṭ*) and deficiency (*at-tafrīṭ*). And some commentators read it here as the equality of a person's outward and inward state: what one says or does through the obvious organs of the body should be compatible with what he believes in and lives by.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's verdict is that the word is used here in its **general** sense, inclusive of all these forms and shades reported from the different authorities — there is no contradiction or divergence between them.

Ibn al-ʿArabi drew out the relationships in which "making equal" applies:

- **Between a person and his Lord.** He gives the right of Allah precedence over the pleasure of his own self, makes the seeking of His pleasure far more urgent than the pursuit of his own desires, obeys His commands and totally abstains from what He has forbidden.
- **Between a person and his own self.** He enters into a deal of justice with his own soul: protecting it from whatever brings physical or spiritual destruction, refusing the desires that are harmful to it in the end, staying content and patient — and *also* avoiding putting unnecessary burden on it without valid excuse. Note that justice here cuts both ways. A person can wrong his own soul by indulging it, and he can wrong it by grinding it down.
- **Between a person and the rest of Allah's creation.** Dealing with the whole creation in a cooperative spirit — wishing well, doing good, having sympathy; never betraying anyone with the slightest breach of trust in any transaction, minor or major; demanding from his own self justice for everyone; and seeing to it that no human being is hurt by anything he says or does, apparent or concealed.

To these Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the justice of the person before whom two parties bring a case, who must decide without any tilt towards anyone and in accordance with what is the truth; and the person who leaves out the extreme options of excess and deficiency in all matters and takes the path of moderation. Abu ʿAbdullah al-Razi preferred exactly this: that *ʿadl* is inclusive of moderation in belief, moderation in deed, moderation in morals — everything. (*Al-Bahr al-Mubit*, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites it.) Imam Al-Qurtubi, who gives all these details to determine the sense of *ʿadl*, also considers this good for the purpose.

Which yields a remarkable result, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: this one word, *ʿadl*, encompasses in itself **adherence to all good morals and deeds, and the avoidance of all bad ones.**

### 2. Al-Iḥsān — doing good, and doing it beautifully

The real and literal meaning is **to make something good**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes two kinds:

1. That a person makes his own deeds, morals and habits good and perfect in his own person.
2. That he deals with another person nicely, decently and favourably. Arabic marks this second sense with the preposition *ilā* ("towards"), as in *"be good as Allah has been good to you"* (28:77).

Imam Al-Qurtubi held that the word is used here in its general sense and is therefore inclusive of **both**. And the first kind is itself general: coming out with acts of worship in their best possible form, making efforts to improve one's own deeds and morals, and seeking betterment in dealings with others.

The Prophet ﷺ himself gave the meaning of *iḥsān* in worship in the famous hadith of Jibra'il. The gist of his blessed statement: worship Allah as if you are seeing Allah — and if you cannot imagine the Divine presence at that level, then have at least this much certitude, that Allah is seeing what you are doing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grounds this in a cardinal part of Islamic faith: not the minutest particle of this universe can remain outside the reach of the knowledge and perception of Allah.

So the second command reaches in three directions at once: *iḥsān* in worship, *iḥsān* in one's own deeds, morals and habits so that they come out right in form and in spirit, and *iḥsān* towards the whole creation of Allah — believer or disbeliever, human or animal.

Imam Al-Qurtubi pressed that last point to a place most of us would not think to look: the person in whose house the cat is not fed and taken care of, and whose caged birds are not attended to as due, is not counted among the *Muḥsinīn* — however devoted to acts of worship he may be.

### 3. Iʿṭā' dhi-l-qurbā — giving relatives their due

*Iʿṭā'* means to give — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes it carries the added sense of giving as a **gift or presentation, in good grace**. *Al-qurbā* means relationship or kinship, and *dhi-l-qurbā* means one's relatives.

What is to be given is not spelled out here. Another ayah names the object: *"And give the relative his due, and the poor, and the wayfarer; and do not spend wastefully"* (17:26), and the same object applies here.
