Ibn Kathir reads this phrase as the command to **uphold the ties of kinship**, citing that same ayah.

That "due" is not only money. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists: serving relatives financially, serving them physically, visiting them when sick, taking care of them when in need — and the giving of verbal comfort and the expression of concern and sympathy. The call that says you were thought of is part of what is owed.

Why single this out when *iḥsān* already covers it? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: it was mentioned separately in order to place stress on its added importance.

## The three prohibitions

**Al-Faḥshā' — shameful acts.** Ibn Kathir: *faḥshā'* refers to all things that are forbidden, and he cites *"Say: the things my Lord has indeed forbidden are the indecencies, whether committed openly or secretly"* (7:33). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines it as the word or deed whose evil is all too open and clear, and which everyone considers bad.

**Al-Munkar — evil deeds.** Here the two commentaries emphasise different things, and both are worth having. Ibn Kathir explains *munkar* as those forbidden deeds committed **openly** by the one who does them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines it as the word or deed whose unlawfulness is **agreed upon** by the well-recognised, authentic exponents of the Shariʿah — and draws an important consequence: in differences that rest on *ijtihād* (reasoned legal effort), **no side can be regarded as *munkar***. On this reading *munkar* includes all sins, outward or inward, done practically or committed morally.

**Al-Baghy — transgression.** Its real meaning is **to cross the limit**: the sense is injustice and excess. Ibn Kathir defines it as aggression towards people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a fine structural observation. Linguistically, *munkar* already includes both *faḥshā'* and *baghy* — so why name them separately? *Faḥshā'* is picked out as a separate entry, and placed first, because of its extreme evil and abomination. And *baghy* is taken up separately because its fallout is **contagious**: it affects others. Sometimes it reaches the outer limits of mutual hostility, even armed confrontation, and sometimes it goes further still and causes international disorder.

**A warning from the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ here — without naming a collection — that there is no sin more deserving of having its punishment hastened in this world, along with what is reserved for its doer in the Hereafter, than **tyrannical aggression** (*baghy*) and **cutting the ties of kinship**.

Notice the correspondence: the two sins named in that hadith stand opposite two of this ayah's own instructions — the command to give relatives their due, and the prohibition of *baghy*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same teaching in its own words: according to a saying of the Prophet ﷺ, there is no sin whose retaliation and punishment comes so quickly as injustice. From this, it says, we learn that the severe punishment due in the Hereafter for injustice has to come anyway, but much before that Allah punishes the wrongdoer in this world as well — even though the man may fail to realise that the punishment he received was for a particular injustice he committed; and Allah has promised to help the one who was wronged.

## Justice is the floor; kindness is the climb

Some commentators, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, draw the line between the first two commands like this. **Justice** means you give the other person his right in full and take what comes to you, neither less nor more; and if someone hurts you, you hurt him only as much as he did, no more. **Iḥsān** means you give the other person more than his real due and, as for your own right, you ignore it to the limit that you willingly accept even less than was due; and when someone hurts you in word or deed, rather than inflicting the equal retaliation you are entitled to, you forgive him — indeed, you return the evil he did with what is good for him.

Hence the crucial distinction Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws: **the command to do justice comes in the form of what is *farḍ* and *wājib*** — obligatory and necessary as a duty; **while the command to be good appears in the status of an act which is voluntary (*nafl*)** — motivated by a well-meaning desire to contribute more in the way of what is good.

Ibn Kathir illustrates the same pairing from three other ayat, and the pattern in them is striking. *"And if you punish them, then punish them with the like of that with which you were afflicted; but if you have patience, it is better for those who are patient"* (16:126). *"The recompense for an offence is an offence the like thereof; but whoever forgives and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah"* (42:40). *"And wounds equal for equal; but if anyone remits the retaliation by way of charity, it shall count as atonement for him"* (5:45). In each of these the Qur'an first fixes the limit of just retaliation, and then in the same breath points beyond it. Ibn Kathir notes that other ayat likewise support the institution of justice in Islam while encouraging a fair and generous attitude.

## "He admonishes you, that you may take heed"

Ibn Kathir explains *yaʿiẓukum* simply: He commands you what He commands you of good, and forbids you what He forbids you of evil. The ayah does not close with a threat but with a **reminder** — *so that perhaps you may take heed.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends with the same conviction: these six commands, imperative and prohibitive, are — if pondered upon — an elixir for the perfect prosperity of man's individual and collective life. May Allah bless us all with the ability to follow them.

## Living it

- **Start where Ibn al-ʿArabi started.** Before justice between you and others, there is justice between you and your Lord — His right ahead of your appetite — and justice with your own soul: neither indulging it into ruin nor burdening it without valid excuse.
- **Meet the floor before reaching for the ceiling.** Give in full, take only what is yours, and if you retaliate, never beyond the like. That is the duty. Forgiving instead — and returning good for evil — is the voluntary climb the Qur'an keeps pointing to.
- **Let *iḥsān* reach the small things.** Qurtubi's unfed cat is the standard: a worship that does not soften how you treat what is under your care has missed something.
- **Kinship is a command, not a mood.** Money, physical help, the visit when they are ill, the word of comfort and the expression of sympathy.
- **Guard against *baghy*** — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, its harm does not stay with the one who commits it, and because on the hadith Ibn Kathir cites, no sin is more deserving of having its punishment hastened in this world.

passages.title: Keep the covenant, never sell it — what Allah has remains
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These seven ayat take one command — keep your word — and follow it down: the pledge itself (91), the person who undoes it and the motive that breaks it (92), the divided humanity in which such pledges are made and the reckoning for it (93), what breaking a pledge costs here and hereafter (94–95), and the answer that dissolves the temptation — what you hold runs out, what Allah holds does not (96–97).

A broken promise is a trade: something was offered for the word you gave. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, adds that these ayat are the explanation and conclusion of the verses just before them, which carried the command to do justice and to be good — and the sense of justice there already includes the fulfilment of pledges.

## Ayah 91 — what "the covenant of Allah" actually covers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the word عهد (`ahd) its full width: it is inclusive of **all transactions, pacts and pledges whose responsibility has been assumed verbally** — whether or not one swears by it, and whether it relates to doing something or to not doing it. So this is not a verse confined to ceremonial oaths; on that definition it reaches the quotation you gave, the delivery date you promised, the contract you signed.

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 91 as one of Allah's plain commands: to fulfil covenants, keep promises, and fulfil oaths after confirming them. The ayah supplies its own reason — **you have appointed Allah as your guarantor**. And it closes: *"Verily, Allah knows what you do"* — which Ibn Kathir calls a warning and a threat to those who break their oaths after confirming them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: after giving a pledge or making a contract, breaking it is a **major sin**, and **no kaffārah (expiation) is fixed for it** — no payment clears the file; instead it brings the punishment of the Hereafter on the offender. The commentary reports that the Prophet ﷺ said a flag shall be planted on the back of the pledge-breaker on the Day of Resurrection, which will become the cause of his or her disgrace there. (Acting contrary to what one has sworn by is likewise a major sin, full of evil consequences in the Hereafter, with particular situations in this world in which kaffārah becomes necessary.)

**"But doesn't the Sunnah allow getting out of an oath?"** Ibn Kathir raises the tension himself. He notes there is no conflict between 16:91 and *"do not use Allah as an excuse in your oaths"* (2:224), nor with *"that is the expiation for oaths when you have sworn; and protect your oaths"* (5:89) — which means, he explains, do not forgo your oaths without offering the penance. Nor is there conflict with the hadith reported in the Two Sahihs, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: *"By Allah, if Allah wills, I will not swear an oath and then realise that something else is better, but I do that which is better and find a way to free myself from the oath"* — according to another report he said, *"and I offer penance for my oath."*

His resolution: there is no contradiction, **because the oaths in 16:91 are the kind that have to do with covenants and promises** — not the kind that have to do with urging oneself to do something or preventing oneself from doing something. A personal vow that proves unwise can be released with penance; a pledge given to someone else is a different thing.

Mujahid said the oath here refers to **oaths made during Jāhiliyyah**. Ibn Kathir notes that this supports the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Jubayr bin Mut'im, also reported by Muslim, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"There is no oath in Islam, and any oath made during the Jāhiliyyah is only reinforced by Islam."* The meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, is that Islam does not need oaths as they were used by the people of the Jāhiliyyah; adherence to Islam is sufficient to do away with any need for them.

## Ayah 92 — the one who unravels her own yarn

Do not be like the one who **undoes the thread she has spun, after it has become strong**.

Who is she? Abdullah bin Kathir and As-Suddi said she was a foolish woman in Makkah who, every time she spun thread and made it strong, would undo it again. Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: this is like the one who breaks a covenant after confirming it. **Ibn Kathir judges the second view more correct and more apparent** — and it stands, he says, whether or not there really was a woman in Makkah who undid her thread after spinning it.

**A note on the Arabic.** Ibn Kathir gives two possible readings of أنكاثًا (ankāthan): it could refer back to the word translated "undoes", reinforcing the meaning; or it could be the predicate of the verb "to be" — meaning, *do not be ankāthan*, the plural of nakth (breach, violation), from the word nākith (perfidious).

*"By taking your oaths as a means of deception among yourselves"* means, says Ibn Kathir, for the purposes of cheating and tricking one another.

## The real temptation: switching to the stronger side

Ayah 92 names the motive: *"when one group is more numerous than another group."* Ibn Kathir spells out the scenario: you swear an oath with some people if they are more in number than you, so that they can trust you — but when you are able to betray them, you do. He draws out the logic: **Allah forbids this by showing a case where treachery might be expected or excused, and forbidding it even there.** If treachery is forbidden in such a case, then in cases where one is in a position of strength it is forbidden more emphatically.

Mujahid described the practice: they used to enter into alliances and covenants, then find other parties who were more powerful and more numerous, so they would cancel the alliance with the first group and ally with the second. This is what they were forbidden to do. Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said something similar.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: Muslims are ordered not to break a pact for the sake of worldly interests and gains — the party you are bound to may look weak and few, while another abounds in numbers, strength or wealth. **Being tempted to switch to the powerful and wealthy party in hope of better gains is not permissible.** Rather, stay by the pledge you gave, and let all gains and losses rest with Allah.

There is one exception, with a condition attached. If the party you are bound to commits or commissions acts contrary to the dictates of Islamic religious law, then it is necessary to break that pledge — **subject to the condition that they be clearly forewarned that Muslims will not be bound by that pact anymore**, as stated in *"then throw [the treaty] towards them, being right forward"* (8:58).

*"Allah only tests you by this."* Sa'id bin Jubayr said this means you are tested **by the large numbers** (reported by Ibn Abi Hatim); Ibn Jarir said it means you are being tested **by His command to you to adhere to your covenants**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies the whole situation as a device by which Allah tests Muslims — to determine whether they will obey the desires of their self and break the solemn pledge, or sacrifice their selfish motives in obedience to the command of Allah. And ayah 92 closes: on the Day of Resurrection He will clarify what you differed over, and everyone, says Ibn Kathir, will be rewarded or punished in accordance with his deeds, good or evil.

## Ayah 93 — why we are not one community

The whole problem of covenants exists **because** people are divided into groups with competing interests — and ayah 93 places that division under Allah's will. Ibn Kathir reads *"Had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation"* alongside *"had your Lord willed, all of those on earth would have believed together"* (10:99) — meaning He could have created harmony among them, with no differences, conflicts or hatred between them — and alongside 11:118–119, *"they will not cease to disagree, except him on whom your Lord has bestowed His mercy."* And here, similarly: *"but He allows whom He wills to stray and He guides whom He wills."*

The ayah refuses to let that become an excuse: *"you shall certainly be called to account for what you used to do."* Then on the Day of Resurrection, Ibn Kathir writes, He will ask them all about their deeds, and will reward or punish them even to the equivalent of the scalish thread in the long slit of a date stone, or the size of a speck on the back of a date stone, or even a thin membrane of the date stone.

## Ayah 94 — the foot that slips after standing firm

Ayah 94 repeats the prohibition, and attaches a consequence: *"lest a foot should slip after it was firmly planted."* Ibn Kathir: this is an analogy describing one who **was** on the right path but then deviated and slipped from the path of guidance because of an unfulfilled oath that involved hindering people from the path of Allah. Because if a disbeliever were to find that, after having agreed to a covenant, the believer betrayed him, then **the believer will have hindered him from entering Islam**. Hence: *"and you taste the evil of having hindered from the path of Allah, and you will suffer a terrible punishment."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, presses to the worst case: the person who **at the very time of taking the oath** harbours other ideas and intentions, already set to act counter to the oath, going through the exercise of oath-taking merely to deceive the other party. That is far more dangerous than breaking a common oath. The danger is that such a person may end up deprived of the very asset of īmān (faith) — which, Qurtubi says, is exactly what *"lest a foot should slip after it is firmly placed"* means.

## Ayah 95 — the paltry price, and the ruling on bribery

Ibn Kathir: do not neglect an oath sworn in the Name of Allah for the sake of this world and its attractions, **for they are few** — and even if the son of Adam were to gain this world and all that is in it, that which is with Allah is better for him: the reward of Allah, better for the one who puts his hope in Him, believes in Him, seeks Him, and fulfils his oaths in the hope of what Allah has promised.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses on the word "paltry": as compared with the gains of the Hereafter even the entire world and its entire wealth is nothing but paltry. Whoever opts for the gains of the mortal world at the cost of the far superior returns of the Hereafter has struck a deal that will bring nothing but utter loss.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a ruling out of this ayah. **Ibn 'Atiyyah** said: if doing something is obligatory on a person, then it is a covenant of Allah due against him, and he is responsible for it — so charging wages or something in return for fulfilling that duty, and not doing what duty calls for without being first paid off in cash or kind, **amounts to breaking the covenant of Allah**. Similarly, if not doing something is obligatory on a person, and he does it against returns received from someone, that too constitutes breaking the covenant of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this statement of Ibn 'Atiyyah also accommodates the comprehensive definition of bribery (rishwat) given in Tafsīr Al-Bahr al-Muhit: **taking money for doing what it is obligatory on you to do, or for doing what it is obligatory on you to leave.**

The commentary concludes that all prevailing kinds of bribery are unlawful. The example: a government servant who receives a salary has virtually given a pledge to Allah that he will perform the job assigned to him for that salary. If he goes about asking for some return from someone in order to do that job, hedging and postponing the required action until he has it, **he is breaking the covenant of Allah** — and likewise if he does something the department never empowered him to do, by accepting a bribe for it.

## Ayah 96 — the arithmetic that settles it

*"Whatever you have will be exhausted, and what is with Allah will remain."* Ibn Kathir: what is with you will come to an end and vanish, because it is only there for a certain, limited time; and what is with Allah — His reward for you in Paradise — will remain, without interruption or end, because it is eternal.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a widening of this ayah from its author's revered teacher, **Maulana Sayyid Asghar Husain of Deoband**, may the mercy of Allah be upon him. A casual look at *"what is with you"* leads one to think of wealth and possessions only. But the word **مَا (mā, "what") is general lexically**, and there is nothing prohibiting us from taking it in a general sense. So included under it are the wealth and possessions of this world **and all the states and matters one experiences in it**: happiness and sorrow, pain and comfort, sickness and health, gain and loss, someone's friendship or enmity. All of these are transitory and must perish. **What remains is the after-effect** — what these states bring by way of reward or punishment on the Day of Judgment. So any reckless pursuit of things that must perish, staking one's life and energies on that altar while neglecting the eternal reward and punishment, is something no sane person should elect to do.

Ayah 96 closes with a promise to the patient. Ibn Kathir points out the **Lām of affirmation** in this promise — here the Lord swears that He will reward the patient for **the best** of their deeds, which, Ibn Kathir explains, means He will forgive them for their bad deeds.

## Ayah 97 — the good life, promised to man and woman alike

Ayah 97 makes it explicit: *whoever does righteous deeds, male or female, while he or she is a believer.* Ibn Kathir sets out what that means — deeds in accordance with the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ, with a heart that believes in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, while believing that these deeds are commanded and enjoined by Allah.

The promise has two halves: **a good life in this world**, and reward according to the best of their deeds in the Hereafter. On the good life, Ibn Kathir gathers the early views:

- feeling tranquillity in all aspects of life;
- good, lawful provisions — reported from Ibn 'Abbas and a group of scholars;
- contentment — 'Ali bin Abi Talib, and also Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Wahb bin Munabbih;
- happiness — recorded from Ibn 'Abbas by 'Ali bin Abi Talhah;
- "none gets this good life except in Paradise" — Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah;
- lawful provisions and worship in this life; and working to obey Allah and finding joy in that — Ad-Dahhak.

**Ibn Kathir's verdict: the correct view is that a good life includes all of these things.** He supports it with the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, also recorded by Muslim, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"He who submits has succeeded, is given sufficient provisions, and is content with Allah for what he is given."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that according to the majority of commentators, "good life" here means a pure and pleasing life in the present world, while some Tafsir authorities have taken it to mean life in the Hereafter. It does **not** mean such a person will never encounter poverty or sickness. It means that when he does, two things shield him from becoming disturbed — first, his habit of remaining content with what is available (qanā'ah), which works in straitened circumstances as well; and second, his belief that he will receive the great and eternal blessings of the Hereafter in return for whatever poverty or pain he has suffered. Poised against that is the disbeliever and sinner: facing poverty and pain, he has nothing to hold him together or give him solace — in that state he is likely to lose his sanity, even think of committing suicide. And if he is affluent instead, his greed will not let him sit peacefully: when the drive for more wealth makes him a millionaire, dreams of becoming a billionaire keep spoiling his peace.

As for righteous believers, says Ibn 'Atiyyah as quoted there, Allah blesses them with a life full of pleasure, contentment and gracefulness **right here in this world as well** — something that never changes whatever the condition. And if they face lean days or sickness, they always have a strong support to fall back on: they are perfect believers in the promises made by Allah, with strong hopes of ease after hardship and comfort after pain. The farmer takes any amount of pain over his crops and welcomes it, certain of the return coming; the businessman and the wage earner brave hardship, believing the business will bring profit and the job a salary. The believer too believes he is getting a return for every hardship, except that when the Hereafter comes his return arrives as blessings great and everlasting. That, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is the good life the believer is blessed with in cash, on the spot, right here in this world.

## Living it

- Every verbal commitment falls under ayah 91 on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's definition, and in giving it you have appointed Allah as your guarantor.
- The test in ayah 92 arrives precisely when the party you are bound to is weak or few and a stronger, wealthier offer appears; and if you must exit a pact because they act contrary to Islamic law, the condition is clear forewarning that you are no longer bound (8:58).
- When something is offered for your word, run ayah 96 on it. What you have will be exhausted. What is with Allah remains.

passages.title: Seek refuge from Satan when reciting
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are a single instruction with its explanation attached. Ayah 98 commands the believer to seek Allah's protection from Satan when reciting the Qur'an; ayat 99 and 100 immediately tell us where the enemy's reach lies and where it does not — he has no power over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord, and his power is only over those who take him as their patron and who join partners with Allah. Command first, then reassurance: you are told to ask for shelter, and then told where that enemy's authority actually ends.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the thread from what came just before. The preceding verses laid emphasis on the fulfilment of the covenant with Allah, and after that on the importance and desirability of acting righteously in one's life. Why does a person neglect to follow such commandments? Because of Satanic instigations. So this verse teaches us to seek protection against Satan, the accursed — and Maʿārif notes that this is "something needed in every good deed."

Which raises the obvious question the commentary then answers: if it is needed in every good deed, why has it been mentioned particularly with the recitation of the Qur'an?

## Why recitation in particular

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers more than one reason.

**Because Satan himself runs from this act.** The recitation of the Qur'an, Maʿārif says, is an act so unique that Satan himself runs away from it. It quotes a line of verse: *"Shaitan bolts from people who recite the Qur'an!"* There are also specified verses and chapters that have been tested and produce the desired result in removing the traces of Satanic input in particular; that they are effective and beneficial stands proved from definite textual authorities (*nuṣūṣ*) — this from Bayān al-Qur'ān. And yet, despite all that, the command to seek protection came attached precisely to recitation. Maʿārif's conclusion: it "becomes all the more necessary with other deeds."

**Because there is danger inside the recitation itself.** There is always the danger, Maʿārif says, of Satanic instigations intruding into the recitation of the Qur'an itself. One may fall short in observing the etiquette due during the recitation, or the recitation may remain "devoid of the essential spirit of deliberation, thinking, submission and humbleness." So for this too it was deemed necessary that protection from Satanic instigations be sought. (Ibn Kathir, Mazharī and others.)

Ibn Kathir states the purpose of seeking refuge in the same spirit: the reason for seeking refuge with Allah before reading is that the reader should not get confused or mixed up, and that Satan should not confuse him **or stop him from thinking about and pondering over the meaning of what he reads**. That last clause is worth sitting with. What is being asked for is not only protection over the tongue, but over the reader's engagement with the meaning.

On that basis, Ibn Kathir notes, the majority of scholars said that refuge should be sought with Allah **before starting** to read.

## The words themselves

**"Seek refuge" (fa-sta'idh).** Maʿārif's rulings give the wording that has come down for this: *a'ūdhu bi'llāhi min ash-shayṭān ir-rajīm* — "I seek protection with Allah from Shaitan, the accursed" — and Maʿārif calls the saying of it *ta'awwudh*. Ibn Kathir, pointing back to the hadiths on this subject that he gathered at the beginning of his Tafsir, uses the term *Isti'ādhah*, seeking refuge with Allah.

**"The outcast," "the accursed."** Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah gives "Shaytan, the outcast"; Maʿārif's rendering of the ta'awwudh gives "Shaitan, the accursed." Either way, the one you are asking to be kept clear of is described as already cast out and already cursed.

**"When you recite."** Ibn Kathir explains the command as addressed to the servants "when they want to read Qur'an," and the majority position he reports is that refuge is sought before starting to read. So the ta'awwudh belongs at the doorway into the recitation, not somewhere halfway through it.

## Ibn Kathir on the two enemies

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes a passage from the preface of Ibn Kathir's Tafsir that explains why the defence prescribed against this particular enemy is a request for protection rather than a fight.

Human beings, Ibn Kathir says, have two kinds of enemy. The first come from their own kind, like the general run of disbelievers. The other kind is that of the jinn who are diabolic and disobedient. Against the first, Islam commands defence through jihad involving fighting and killing; for the other kind, **the command is limited to the seeking of protection from Allah only.**

The reason is the nature of the enemy. The first kind is homogeneous — the same sort of creature you are — and its attack comes openly, visibly; therefore fighting in jihad against such an enemy was made obligatory. The Satanic enemy is not visible, and its attack on humankind does not take place frontally. Therefore, as a measure of defence against such an enemy, what has been made obligatory is seeking the protection of a Being whom no one is able to see — neither humankind, nor Satan.

Then Ibn Kathir adds what Maʿārif calls a subtle expediency in entrusting this defence to Allah. Consider what is at stake on each side. One who stands subdued by Satan is, in the sight of Allah, rejected and deserving of punishment. Quite contrary to this is the case of the human enemy, the disbelievers: if someone is subdued or killed while confronting them, he becomes a martyr (*shahīd*), deserving of reward from Allah (*thawāb*). So when one confronts a human enemy with all his strength, it turns out to be nothing but beneficial, no matter what the circumstances — either he prevails over the enemy and puts an end to his power, or he himself attains *shahādah* and deserves the best of returns with Allah.

Against Satan there is no such second outcome. That is precisely why, on Ibn Kathir's reasoning, the response commanded here is to take shelter with Allah.

## What the ta'awwudh asks of you in practice

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the rulings.

**It is Sunnah, not obligatory.** Reciting *a'ūdhu bi'llāhi min ash-shayṭān ir-rajīm* before initiating the recitation of the Qur'an stands proved from the Holy Prophet ﷺ, so that the command given in this verse is carried out. But not doing it occasionally also stands proved from authentic (*ṣaḥīḥ*) aḥādīth. Therefore the majority of Muslim scholars have not classed this injunction as obligatory (*wājib*) but have declared it Sunnah — a position on which Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī has reported a consensus (*ijmāʿ*) of the scholars of the Muslim community. The narratives carrying the word and deed of the Prophet ﷺ on both sides — reciting *a'ūdhu bi'llāh* under most conditions, and not reciting under some — have been mentioned exhaustively by Ibn Kathir at the beginning of his Tafsir.

**In ṣalāh, the jurists differ.** Should the ta'awwudh be recited only at the beginning of the first rakʿah, or at the beginning of every rakʿah? Views of leading Muslim jurists differ in this matter. According to the great Imām Abū Ḥanīfah it should be recited only in the first rakʿah, while Imām al-Shāfiʿī declares its recitation at the beginning of every rakʿah commendable (*mustaḥabb*). The arguments given by both have been presented in Tafsīr Mazharī with full elaboration.

**One ta'awwudh covers a sitting.** While reciting the Qur'an — whether in ṣalāh or out of it — saying *a'ūdhu bi'llāh* is Sunnah, and the rule applies to both situations equally. Once it has been said, one may go on reciting as much as one wishes; the same single ta'awwudh said at the beginning is sufficient. But if one abandons the recitation in the middle, gets busy with some mundane chore and then resumes it, one should begin again by saying *a'ūdhu bi'llāh* and *bismillāh* at that time.

**Not before other books.** Saying *a'ūdhu bi'llāh* before reading any word or book other than the Qur'an is not a Sunnah; there one should recite only *bismillāh* (Al-Durr al-Mukhtār, Shāmī).

**But the ta'awwudh has a life outside recitation.** The Ḥadīth teaches the saying of ta'awwudh in other situations too. When someone gets very angry — so says the Ḥadīth — the heat of the anger goes away by saying *a'ūdhu bi'llāhi min ash-shayṭān ir-rajīm* (cited by Ibn Kathir). And it also appears in Ḥadīth that before going to the toilet it is commendable (*mustaḥabb*) to say *Allāhumma a'ūdhu bika min al-khubuthi wa'l-khabā'ith* — "O Allah, I seek protection with You from the foul and the impure" (Shāmī). The same instinct, in other doorways: before something sacred, and before something vulnerable.

## Ayah 99: "he has no power over them"

Now the reassurance. The key word is *sulṭān* — rendered "power" and "authority." Ibn Kathir records more than one reading of what exactly is being denied to Satan:

- **Ath-Thawrī** said: "He has no power to make them commit a sin they will not repent from." Notice what this does and does not say. It does not say the believer will never slip; it says Satan has no power to make him commit a sin he will not repent from. The way back is not closed off.
- **Others** said it means that he has no argument for them.
- **Others** said it is like the ayah *"Except Your chosen servants amongst them"* (15:40).

The ayah names two qualities together, and both are load-bearing: **those who believe** and **who put their trust only in their Lord**. Maʿārif explains the second: these are people who, rather than trust their own will power in their states and actions, place their ultimate trust in Allah — "for He is the One who gives us the ability to do everything good and also the One who shields us from everything evil." Such people, Maʿārif says, Satan cannot possess and dictate.

That is a striking way to put it. On Maʿārif's reading, what keeps a person out of Satan's grip is not confidence in his own will power but the transfer of trust away from it and onto Allah — and the ta'awwudh commanded in the previous ayah is that same reliance put into words.

## Ayah 100: where his power does reach

Ayah 100 names the two groups over whom Satan does have *sulṭān*.

**"Those who take him as a patron."** Ibn Kathir reports **Mujāhid**: "Those who obey him." Others said: "Those who take him as their protector instead of Allah." Maʿārif's language points the same way: these are people who *elect* to befriend none but Satan because of their selfish motives and who particularly like things about him — a relationship entered into, not an ambush suffered.

**"And those who join partners with Him."** This, says Ibn Kathir, means those who associate others in worship with Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what ayat 99 and 100 together establish: Allah has **not** given Satan the kind of power that would disarm any human being and compel him to become helpless and take to evil. So if a person opts not to use his capability of choice and control — out of sheer carelessness or some selfish motive — this would be his own fault. As for those who elect to befriend none but Satan because of their selfish motives, and who go about associating others in the pristine divinity of Allah: over such people "the Shaitan is all over them, in possession, in control, and would not let them go towards anything good while, in every evil, they are right in front."

Maʿārif points to the same subject taken up elsewhere, in Sūrat al-Ḥijr, where Allah has Himself refuted the claim of Satan: *"Surely, My servants — you have no power over them, except the one who follows you from among the astray"* (15:42).

Put simply, on the reading these two commentaries give: Satan's authority is not seized from a person; it belongs over those who obey him, take him as their protector instead of Allah, and associate others in worship with Allah.

## Living it

**Say it, and know what you are asking for.** Before you open the Qur'an, the *a'ūdhu bi'llāh* is not a throat-clearing formula. On Ibn Kathir's explanation you are asking that nothing confuse you and nothing stop you from thinking about and pondering over the meaning of what you read. Ask for that specifically, and your reading changes.

**Take it as an offered shelter, not a burden.** The consensus reported by Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī is that this is Sunnah, not obligatory (*wājib*).

**Renew it after a real break.** One ta'awwudh carries a whole sitting; but if you leave off in the middle for some mundane chore and come back, begin again with *a'ūdhu bi'llāh* and *bismillāh*.

**Refuse both excuses.** These ayat close two doors at once. "I couldn't help it" — Maʿārif says plainly that no such compelling power was given to Satan, and that failing to use your own capability of choice and control is your own fault. "I can handle it" — ayah 99 names safety for those who believe *and* put their trust in their Lord, and Maʿārif contrasts that trust precisely with trusting one's own will power.

**And when you fall, do not let him keep you.** Ath-Thawrī's reading of ayah 99 is the gentlest sentence in this passage: over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord, Satan has no power to make them commit a sin they will not repent from.

passages.title: Answering the charge that Muhammad invents revelation
passages.tafsir:
## One question running through five ayat

These five ayat take up the sharpest accusation the idolators of Makkah levelled at the Prophet ﷺ: that he was making the Qur'an up. The passage does not answer it once and move on. It works through the accusation in stages — it names who actually brought the revelation down (ayah 102), it takes apart the two forms the charge took, that changed rulings prove invention (ayah 101) and that a human being was feeding him the words (ayah 103), and it closes by taking the word *liar* and fixing it where it belongs (ayat 104–105). One question runs through the whole unit: whose speech is this?

## The whisper this passage answers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the sequence. Three ayat earlier, in ayah 98, came the instruction to say *aʿūdhu bi'llāh* — "I seek protection with Allah" — while reciting the Qur'an. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out what that instruction indicates: Shayṭān puts scruples in the heart when a person recites the Qur'an. And it reads the ayat before us as a refutation of exactly those satanic instigations.

That reading holds the five ayat together. This is not only the record of a quarrel in Makkah. The doubts being answered here — *is this really from Allah? why does it change? where did he get it?* — are the kind of scruple a reciter is taught to seek protection from, and what follows is Allah's reply to them.

## The first charge: "You are only a forger"

Ibn Kathir opens his comment by saying that Allah is telling us here of the weak minds of the idolators and their lack of faith and conviction, and that it is impossible for them to have faith when He has decreed that they are doomed. That frame matters for everything that comes after: the objection was not an honest difficulty waiting for an answer.

**What set them off.** Ibn Kathir gives the occasion plainly. When they saw that some rulings had been changed by being abrogated, they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, *innamā anta muftar* — "You are but a forger," which Ibn Kathir glosses simply as "one who tells lies." A ruling had been set aside and another put in its place, and from that they drew their conclusion about the man reciting.

**What "replacing a verse" means.** The ayah says *baddalnā āyatan makāna āyah* — "when We change a verse in place of another." Mujahid explained the phrase to mean, "We remove one and put another in its place." Qatadah connected it to the ayah of Sūrat al-Baqarah, "Whatever verse We change (abrogate) or omit…" (2:106). This is abrogation — *naskh* in Arabic — where Allah, who gave the ruling in the first place, sets it aside and gives another.

Ibn Kathir's reply to the whole objection is one sentence, and it carries everything: "But Allah is the Lord Who does whatever He wills, and rules as He wants." Sovereignty is the answer. The One who sends a ruling owns that ruling.

## The answer arrives before the charge

Look at where the reply sits in the sentence. "And when We change a verse in place of another — **and Allah knows best what He reveals** — they say: 'You are but a forger.'" The answer is placed inside the ayah before the accusation has even been quoted. The reader is handed the reply before hearing the charge.

And then the ayah closes: "Rather, most of them do not know" — *lā yaʿlamūn*. The charge is bracketed by two statements about knowledge. Allah knows best what He sends down; most of them do not know. They are not called wicked at this point; they are called ignorant — and the thing they lack is precisely the knowledge the ayah has just said belongs to Allah.

## Who actually brought it down

**"Say."** The Prophet ﷺ is not left to defend himself in his own words. Ibn Kathir introduces ayah 102 as what "Allah said, in response to them" — and what Allah says is *qul*, "Say." Even the answer is revealed to him. The defence against the charge of inventing revelation is itself revelation.

**Rūḥ al-Qudus.** Ibn Kathir identifies *Rūḥ al-Qudus*, rendered "the Holy Spirit," as Jibril. So the chain is laid out: from your Lord, by way of Jibril, to you. The man they accuse of forgery is the last link in that chain, not its source. He did not compose it; he received it.

**"From your Lord with truth."** Ibn Kathir explains *bi'l-ḥaqq* here as "with truthfulness and justice." The charge on the table was forgery. The word given to describe the descent of the Qur'an is truthfulness.

**And then what it is for.**

*To make the believers firm* — *li-yuthabbita alladhīna āmanū*, rendered "for the conviction of those who believe." Ibn Kathir explains it: so that they will believe what was revealed earlier and what was revealed later, and humble themselves towards Allah. This is the quiet marvel of the passage. The same fact — that some ayat replace others — draws the word "forger" from one man and firmness from another, because the believer takes the earlier and the later as coming from one Lord and lowers himself before Him. The evidence has not changed; the heart receiving it has.

*A guide and good news for the Muslims* — Ibn Kathir: He has made it a guide and good news to the Muslims who believe in Allah and His Messengers. Guidance is for the road ahead; good news is for the heart that has to walk it.

## The second charge: "A man is teaching him"

The accusation returns in ayah 103 in a more concrete form, and Ibn Kathir tells the story behind it. There was a foreign — that is, non-Arab — man living among the Quraysh as the servant of some of their clans, who used to sell goods by aṣ-Ṣafā. Ibn Kathir says the Messenger of Allah ﷺ may have sat with him sometimes and talked with him a little. But, he adds, the man was a foreigner who did not know much Arabic, only enough simple phrases to answer questions when he had to.

That was the whole basis of the claim: *innamā yuʿallimuhu bashar* — "It is only a human being who teaches him."

**The refutation is a single line of the ayah.** "The tongue of the man they refer to is foreign, while this — the Qur'an — is in a clear Arabic tongue." Two tongues, set side by side. Ibn Kathir puts the point as a question: how could this Qur'an, with its eloquent style and perfect meanings — more perfect, he says, than any Book revealed to any previously sent Prophet — have been learnt from a foreigner who hardly speaks the language? "No one with the slightest amount of common sense would say such a thing."

Notice how Ibn Kathir classifies what they said. He does not call it an argument to be weighed. He calls it lies, allegations and slander. And notice how the ayah opens: *wa-laqad naʿlamu* — "and We surely know that they say…". Allah is not being informed of the rumour. The rumour is being lifted into the open and set beside the Book itself, where its own absurdity finishes it.

## Why proof this clear did not land

If the refutation is that plain, why did they not believe? Ayah 104 answers, and with it the passage stops arguing and starts explaining. Ibn Kathir writes that Allah does not guide those who turn away from remembering Him and who are heedless of what He revealed to His Messenger ﷺ — those, he says, "who have no intention of believing in that which he has brought from Allah." This kind of people, he continues, will never be guided to faith by the signs of Allah or by the Message He sent through His Messengers in this world, and in the Hereafter they will suffer a painful and severe punishment.

Read carefully, this is not a statement that evidence is worthless. It is a statement about what evidence needs in order to work. Guidance is withheld from those who turned away first, from those who had no intention of believing. The signs remain signs; the eye has been shut.

## The word "liar", returned to its owner

Ayah 105 does something unexpected. Instead of continuing to defend, it defines: fabricating falsehood belongs to those who do not believe in Allah's ayat — "and it is they who are liars." Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion out. Here Allah informs us that His Messenger ﷺ is not a forger nor a liar, because the one who fabricates falsehood about Allah and His Messenger ﷺ is the most evil of creatures.

Then he sets the two parties beside each other. On one side, the disbelievers and heretics who were known to the people as liars. On the other, Ibn Kathir writes, the Messenger Muhammad ﷺ — the most honest and righteous of people, the most perfect in knowledge, deeds, faith and conviction; known among his people for his truthfulness, with no one among them having any doubt about it, to such an extent that they always addressed him as **al-Amīn**, the Trustworthy.

**Testimony from outside.** Ibn Kathir closes with the exchange between Heraclius, the king of the Romans, and Abu Sufyan, whom Heraclius questioned about the attributes of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. One of the things Heraclius asked was: "Did you ever accuse him of lying before he made his claim?" Abu Sufyan said, "No." Heraclius drew the conclusion himself: "He would refrain from lying about people and then go and fabricate lies about Allah?"

The reasoning is simple enough that a foreign king reached it from the answers he was given: a man never accused of lying about people does not suddenly become a liar about Allah. And this is where the five ayat arrive. The question they opened with was whose speech this is. The answer given is that it came down from your Lord by way of Jibril — and that the accusation of fabrication describes the accusers, not the accused.

## Living it

**Take the doubt to Allah rather than around in circles.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's link back to ayah 98 is the practical key to this passage. Scruples arriving during recitation are expected — the instruction to seek protection with Allah assumes them. So the response to the whisper is not private argument but *aʿūdhu bi'llāh*, and then the answer Allah Himself has already given in these ayat.

**Let "Allah knows best what He reveals" settle the questions of wisdom.** Where a ruling is not transparent to us, ayah 101 locates the missing piece precisely: it is knowledge, and it is His. Ibn Kathir's line is worth carrying — Allah "does whatever He wills, and rules as He wants."

**Expect the same fact to divide people.** Ayah 102 shows one reality producing firmness in one heart and accusation in another. Do not assume that someone unconvinced by clear evidence simply needs more evidence; ayah 104 says what is missing in that case, and it is not information.

**Guard your own truthfulness.** Ayah 105 makes fabrication the mark of the one who does not believe in Allah's ayat. And when Ibn Kathir defends the Prophet ﷺ against the charge, the thing he reaches for is his character — the most honest of people, called al-Amīn by his own people. Ordinary honesty is not a minor virtue. In this passage it is doing the work of an argument.

passages.title: Disbelief after faith and hearts sealed
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat pass judgement on one figure: the person who had faith, understood it, and then walked away from it — and in the same breath they carve out an exception for the believer whose tongue was forced while his heart never moved. Ayah 106 gives the ruling and the exception; ayah 107 names the motive behind the fall; ayah 108 speaks of hearts, ears and eyes sealed; ayah 109 states where it ends. One arc: a choice, its cause, its consequence, its outcome.

## The people this passage came down about

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports (citing Qurtubi and Mazhari) that ayah 106 was revealed about the noble Sahabah who were arrested by the Mushriks. Their disbelieving captors told them plainly: return to disbelief, or you will be killed.

Those arrested were Sayyidnā ʿAmmār, his father Sayyidnā Yāsir and his mother Sayyidah Sumayyah, along with Sayyidnā Suhayb, Bilāl and Khabbāb (may Allah be pleased with them all).

Yāsir and Sumayyah refused outright to utter any word of disbelief. Yāsir was killed. Sumayyah was tied between two camels which were then made to run, and she was torn apart. That, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, was how she met her shahādah (martyrdom in the way of Allah) — and these two blessed souls were the first to meet their shahādah for the sake of Islam. Khabbāb likewise refused completely, and it was in perfect peace that he accepted being killed by the disbelievers.

ʿAmmār took the other road. With his life immediately at stake he made a bare verbal declaration of disbelief — while his heart, in his own words, stayed perfectly satisfied and firmly set on his faith. When the enemy released him he went straight to the Prophet ﷺ and told him what had happened, in great pain over it. The Prophet ﷺ asked him one question: **when you were making that statement, what was going on in your heart?** ʿAmmār answered that his heart was at peace and firmly set on his faith. The Prophet ﷺ put him at rest by telling him he was not to face any punishment for that — and it was in confirmation of that verdict, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, that this ayah was revealed.

Notice the shape of this. A man arrives crushed by what he said under torture; the Prophet ﷺ does not interrogate his words, he asks about his heart; and then the ayah comes down confirming exactly that ruling. The ayah opens with a severe warning, but the exception inside it is a mercy with a face and a name.

## The exception, word by word

The clause is *illā man ukriha wa-qalbuhu muṭmaʼinnun bil-īmān* — "except one who was forced while his heart is at peace with the faith."

Ibn Kathir explains it as covering "one who utters statements of disbelief and verbally agrees with the Mushrikin because he is forced to do so by the beatings and abuse to which he is subjected, but his heart refuses to accept what he is saying, and he is, in reality, at peace with his faith in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ." The tongue is captured; the heart is not.

Now hold that phrase — *his heart is at peace with the faith* — against the way Ibn Kathir describes the other man in the very same ayah, the one who opens his breast to disbelief. He uses the language of peace for both: the forced man is "in reality, at peace with his faith in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ"; the condemned ones "open their hearts to disbelief finding peace in that." The ayah sets the two hearts side by side so that we can see the difference between them is not the words on their lips — both may have said the same sentence — but **where the heart has come to rest**. One finds its rest in faith while the words are being wrung out of it under blows. The other makes room inside itself for disbelief and settles down there.

And Ibn Kathir is precise about who is condemned. He begins the passage by saying that Allah "is angry with them who willingly disbelieve in Him after clearly believing in Him... because they understood the faith yet they still turned away from it." That matches the ayah's own words — *on them is wrath from Allah, and theirs will be a terrible torment*. This is not the ignorance of someone who never heard. It is informed, unforced rejection.

## Ikrah: what actually counts as compulsion

From ayah 106 the jurists derive the ruling on someone compelled to utter a word of disbelief under threat of death. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets it out: if he judges that in all likelihood his threateners are fully capable of carrying it out, this is a state of duress; and if he then utters a word of disbelief verbally while his heart stays firm on faith — a heart that shuns saying what is false and evil — there is no sin on him, nor will his wife become unlawful for him (Qurtubi, Mazhari).

*Ikrah* literally means using threat or violence to force a person to act against his or her will. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes two degrees:

**1. Ikrah ghayr muljiʼ** — compulsion that is not absolute. The person is unwilling at heart, but is not so stripped of choice and volition that he cannot say no. Under this degree, uttering a word of disbelief or doing something unlawful does **not** become permissible. (Some supplementary rulings do release certain adverse effects even here; the relevant details, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, appear in the books of fiqh — the works of the Muslim jurists.)

**2. Ikrah muljiʼ** — compulsion that leaves no choice at all: if he refuses to do what his coercers order, he will be killed or lose a limb. Here, the mere verbalisation of the word of disbelief is permissible — on the express condition that the heart remains firm and at peace with faith. Likewise, short of killing another human being, if a person is coerced into some other unlawful deed, no sin attaches to him for it.

Both concessions carry a further condition: the one making the threat must actually be capable of carrying it out, and the coerced person must have the overwhelming likelihood that if he refuses, the coercer really will do what he threatens. Fear on its own is not duress; the threat has to be one he can genuinely deliver.

## A permission, not a demand

This is the point the commentaries handle with great care. Ibn Kathir states that the scholars agreed: a person forced into disbelief may either go along with his captors in the interests of self-preservation, **or** refuse. The concession is genuine — and so is the higher road, and Ibn Kathir gathers three witnesses to it.

**Bilāl** (may Allah be pleased with him) refused, while they inflicted all sorts of torture on him, even placing a huge rock on his chest in the intense heat and telling him to admit others as partners with Allah. He answered only: *"Alone, Alone."* And he said, "By Allah, if I knew any word more annoying to you than this, I would say it."

**Habīb bin Zayd al-Ansārī**, questioned by the Liar Musaylimah: "Do you bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah?" — "Yes." "Do you bear witness that I am the messenger of Allah?" — "I do not hear you." Musaylimah kept cutting him, piece by piece, and he remained steadfast, insisting on his words.

**ʿAbdullah bin Hudhāfah al-Sahmī** — here Ibn Kathir says outright that it is better and preferable for the Muslim to remain steadfast in his religion even if that leads to him being killed, and cites Al-Hāfiz Ibn ʿAsākir's biography of this Companion. Taken prisoner by the Romans and brought before their king, he was offered a share of the kingdom and the king's daughter in marriage if he would become a Christian. He replied that if he were given everything the king possessed and everything the Arabs possess to make him give up the religion of Muhammad ﷺ even for an instant, he would not do it. Threatened with death: "It is up to you." He was crucified while archers shot near his hands and feet; he still refused. A copper vessel was heated and a Muslim prisoner thrown into it before his eyes until only scorched bones were left; he still refused. Brought back to be thrown in himself, he wept — and the king, hoping he would respond, called him over. ʿAbdullah said: *"I only weep because I have only one soul with which to be thrown into this vessel at this moment for the sake of Allah; I wish that I had as many souls as there are hairs on my body with which I could undergo this torture for the sake of Allah."*

Two details at the end of that account illuminate the ruling itself. According to some reports, he was imprisoned and deprived of food and drink for several days, then sent wine and pork, and he would not come near them; asked why, he said, "It is permissible for me under these circumstances, but I did not want to give you the opportunity to gloat." He knew a concession applied to him — and still declined to use it. And when the king said, "Kiss my head and I will let you go," he answered, "And will you release all the Muslim prisoners with me?" The king said yes; he kissed his head, and he and every Muslim captive the king held were released. Back home, ʿUmar bin al-Khattāb said that every Muslim should kiss the head of ʿAbdullah bin Hudhāfah, and that he would be the first — and he stood up and did it (may Allah be pleased with them both).

## Ayah 107: the reason anybody falls

*"That is because they preferred the life of this world over that of the Hereafter."* Ibn Kathir: they will suffer severe punishment in the Hereafter "because they preferred this life to the Hereafter, and they left the faith for the sake of this world."

The Qur'an does not say they were out-argued or that a proof defeated them. It says they made a trade. They had understood the faith — they had believed — and they exchanged the lasting for the immediate. Then: *"and Allah does not guide the people who disbelieve"* — which Ibn Kathir glosses as Allah "did not guide their hearts and help them to stand firm in the true religion." In his wording, standing firm on faith is not self-generated; it is guidance and help from Allah.

## Ayah 108: hearts, hearing and sight sealed

*"They are those upon whose hearts, hearing and sight Allah has set a seal."* Ibn Kathir: "He put a seal on their hearts so that they would not be able to understand what is beneficial for them, and He sealed their ears and eyes so that they would not benefit from them. Their faculties did not help them at all, so they are unaware of what is going to happen to them."

Two things are worth holding together here. First, the ayah attributes the sealing to Allah, and Ibn Kathir restates it in exactly those terms — *He* put a seal on their hearts, *He* sealed their ears and eyes. Second, notice where the sealing falls in Ibn Kathir's own sentence. The order he narrates runs: they understood the faith yet turned away from it; they preferred this life to the Hereafter and left the faith for the sake of this world; Allah did not guide their hearts or help them stand firm; He put a seal on their hearts. The seal arrives at the end of that sentence, not at its beginning.

And then the terrible last word of the ayah: *and they are the heedless* — the *ghāfilūn*, rendered here as "the heedless." The organs of perception are still in the head; the man still hears sound and sees light. What is gone is the benefit — Ibn Kathir says the seal is on the ears and eyes "so that they would not benefit from them," and that "their faculties did not help them at all." And the state carries no alarm with it: they are "unaware of what is going to happen to them." That is precisely what makes it dangerous.

## Ayah 109: lā jarama

*Lā jarama* — "No doubt" — "means, it is inevitable, and no wonder," says Ibn Kathir, "that those who are like this" will, in the Hereafter, be the losers. It is the tone of a conclusion that no longer needs arguing. And *"in the Hereafter, they will be the losers"* means, in his words, "they will lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."

That is the trade of ayah 107 finally priced out. They preferred this world and got it; on the Day it is settled, what they lose is not a portion of their wealth or standing but, as Ibn Kathir puts it, their own selves and their families.

## Where else "compulsion" reaches — and where scholars differed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān extends the principle to two classes of transaction, and the contrast is instructive.

**Transactions that require heartfelt consent** — sale, gift and the like. The Qur'an itself is the definitive authority here: *"Do not eat up the wealth of others, unless there is a trade with mutual consent"* (4:29), and it appears in Hadith that the wealth and property of a Muslim does not become lawful unless it be with a whole-hearted pleasure from the person. So a sale or gift executed under duress has no validity in the sight of the Shariah; once the person is out of the state of compulsion he has the option to reassess it and freely retain or cancel it.

**Transactions that hinge on the words alone** — marriage, divorce, revocation of divorce, freeing a slave. Here intention and inward willingness are not binding conditions of the transaction. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the hadith that there are three things in which not only the serious words but also the non-serious words are counted as serious (reported by Abū Dāwūd and by al-Tirmidhī, who graded it *hasan*) — so that even words said in jest bring marriage, divorce or revocation into effect.

On whether this extends to **divorce pronounced under duress** (*talāq mukrah*), the scholars genuinely differed, and the sources report both sides:

- **Imam Abū Hanīfah, al-Shaʿbī, al-Zuhrī, al-Nakhaʿī and Qatādah** (may Allah's mercy be upon them) held that it does take effect, since the actualisation of divorce is connected with nothing but the pronouncing of the words, and the intention and will of the heart is not a condition here.
- **Imam al-Shāfiʿī and Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās** held that it does not take effect, on the strength of the hadith *"Removed away from my Ummah are mistake, forgetting, and what they are compelled to under coercion"* (reported by al-Tabarānī from Sayyidnā Thawbān).

Imam Abū Hanīfah's answer to that hadith, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains it, is that it concerns the rulings of the Hereafter: what is said or done contrary to the Shariah by mistake, forgetfulness or under duress brings no sin. Worldly consequences, however, still follow, because the act itself really occurred. His illustration: a man who kills by accident incurs neither the sin of it nor the punishment of the Hereafter — yet the loss of life has genuinely happened, so its legal effects follow too: after the prescribed waiting period (*ʿiddah*) the widow may enter a second marriage contract, and the estate is distributed to the legal heirs. Likewise, once words of divorce, marriage or revocation have been said verbally, their legal effects follow (Mazhari, Qurtubi). *Wa Allāhu subḥānahu aʿlam* — and Allah, Glorified is He, knows best.

Two things are worth noticing here. Note what Abū Hanīfah's own answer concedes: on his reading, what is said under duress brings no sin, and his disagreement with the other view is about whether the words carry their worldly legal effect. And note where this entire body of ruling is anchored — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens its commentary by saying that it is "from the first verse (106)" that the religious ruling on the compelled person comes, and the whole discussion of duress unfolds from there.

## Living it

**The measure is where your heart rests.** The ayah does not weigh a person by the worst sentence extracted from him under duress, nor absolve one whose mouth is clean while his breast has been opened wide to disbelief. That is a mercy and a warning in one clause.

**A concession from Allah is not a disgrace.** ʿAmmār came to the Prophet ﷺ in anguish and was told he faced no punishment for what he had said — and the ayah came down confirming it. At the same time the sources plainly honour those who refused, and Ibn Kathir says outright that it is "better and preferable" to remain steadfast even if it leads to being killed. Both are true; one is a permission, the other is a summit, and it is not for anyone to shame a person for taking the permission Allah gave.

**Ayah 107 is the question to bring home.** Most of us will never be ordered to renounce our faith under threat of death. But the mechanism the ayah names — preferring this life to the Hereafter — operates in small trades. Ask what is being exchanged, and for how long a return.

**Take the heedlessness in ayah 108 seriously.** The most frightening thing described there is not pain but the absence of any signal — hearts, ears and eyes that bring their owner no benefit, and no awareness of what is coming. And notice what Ibn Kathir names as the alternative: that Allah guide a person's heart and help him stand firm in the true religion. That is the thing to keep asking for.

passages.title: Mercy for the tried, then each soul's reckoning
passages.tafsir:
Two ayat, one movement. In ayah 110 Allah promises forgiveness and mercy to believers who were compelled to renounce their faith, and who afterwards rebuilt that faith with costly action — emigration, struggle, patience. In ayah 111 the scene shifts to the Day of Judgement, where every soul arrives pleading its own case and is paid in full for exactly what it did. The first ayah tells you where mercy comes from; the second tells you why you will need it, and why nobody else can supply it for you.

## Where these ayat sit in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the sequence. The verses just before this carried warnings of punishment against disbelief — *kufr* — "whether original or apostacy (*irtidād*)", that is, whether someone never believed at all or turned away after having believed. Then ayah 106 makes a striking point: faith, an honest and true declaration of belief, is a wealth that could work wonders for a disbeliever (*kāfir*) or an apostate (*murtadd*) — come to Allah with real *īmān* and all his past sins would stand forgiven. Ayah 107 brings up the last day of Qiyāmah, because the whole phenomenon of reward and punishment has to occur after it. Ayah 108 adds a qualification: the real punishment of disbelief and sin comes after Qiyāmah, yet there are some sins whose punishment is faced to a certain degree already, within the present world.

That is the ground on which our two ayat stand. Faith can wipe out a past; the Day is where accounts are finally settled; some of the reckoning arrives early. Ayah 110 now takes the hardest case imaginable — a believer who was forced into renouncing Islam — and shows the road back. Ayah 111 then places that same person, and everyone else, on the Day itself.

## The people ayah 110 is about

Ibn Kathir titles this passage plainly: *The One who is forced to renounce Islam will be forgiven if He does Righteous Deeds afterwards.*

He describes a specific group. They were oppressed in Makkah, and their position with their own people was weak. So when those people tried them, they went along with them. That is the unvarnished truth the ayah itself states: they emigrated *after they were put to trials*.

Then they managed to escape. Ibn Kathir lists what that escape cost them: they left their homeland, their families and their wealth behind, seeking the pleasure and the forgiveness of Allah. They joined the believers, fought with them against the disbelievers, and bore hardship with patience.

And Allah's verdict on them: *after this* — Ibn Kathir stresses the words, meaning after their giving in when put to the test — He will forgive them and show mercy to them when they are resurrected.

Two honesties are worth sitting with here. First, the Qur'an does not tidy up their record. It says out loud that they were tried and that they gave in. Second, it does not leave them defined by that moment. The verse names their collapse and then names their return, and the sentence ends not on the collapse but on Allah being Forgiving, Most Merciful.

## What was done to them, and what they then did

**فُتِنُوا (*futinū*).** The rendering here is "after they were put to trials"; the other translation of the ayah puts the same thing from the other side — "after being compelled ˹to renounce˺". Either way, what the words describe is something that happened *to* these people, at the hands of those who tried them. This is not a verse about people who drifted or sold their faith cheaply.

**هَاجَرُوا (*hājarū*) — they emigrated.** This is the first thing they themselves did, and Ibn Kathir has already told us what it meant in practice: homeland, family and wealth left behind.

**Then they struggled, and then they were patient.** Ibn Kathir's reading of the verse runs: those who emigrated after they were put to trials, *and then* performed jihād, *and were patient*. The list arrives in that order. Trial, then departure, then fighting alongside the believers, then bearing hardship with patience. Their return was not a sentence they said; it was a sequence they lived.

And patience is named last, after the fighting. The dramatic act of leaving Makkah is not the end of the story. What comes after — enduring, staying, bearing the hardship of the new life — is folded into what Allah is forgiving them for.

## "Your Lord" — said twice

Ibn Kathir's rendering holds these broken, recovering believers inside a phrase that appears at both ends of the verse: "Then, verily, **your Lord** for those who emigrated… after this, **your Lord** is indeed Forgiving, Most Merciful." The people in question could not have felt further from safety; the verse locates them squarely inside that relationship, and then seals the sentence with two of Allah's Names: the Forgiving, the Most Merciful.

The placement matters. A verse that began with people failing a test ends with Allah describing Himself. That is the direction the passage wants your eye to travel.

## Ayah 111: the Day every soul comes pleading

Then the scene changes entirely. Ibn Kathir explains ayah 111 phrase by phrase.

**"The Day when every person will come pleading" (*yawma taʾtī kullu nafsin tujādilu*)** — Ibn Kathir glosses it: *making a case in his own defence*. Picture a courtroom where every single soul is simultaneously its own advocate, pressing its own argument, trying to speak for itself.

**"for himself" (*ʿan nafsihā*)** — and here is the weight of it. Ibn Kathir: *no one else will plead on his behalf; not his father, not his son, nor his brother, nor his wife.* He names four of the closest relationships a person has and removes them one by one. Every soul is pleading — but only for itself. The word for "soul" or "self" — *nafs* — stands in both halves of the phrase: each self, pleading about its own self. There is no one else in the sentence.

**"and every one will be paid in full for what he did"** — Ibn Kathir: *meaning whatever he did, good or evil.* Not a selection, not a summary. Whatever he did.

**"and they will not be dealt with unjustly"** — Ibn Kathir spells out precisely what that guarantee covers: *there will be no decrease in the reward for good, and no increase in the punishment for evil. They will not be dealt with unjustly in the slightest way.*

Read that carefully and notice the shape of it. The floor is absolute justice: nothing you earned will be shaved off, and nothing will be added to what you deserve. But justice is only the floor. Above it stands what ayah 110 just established — that Allah forgives, that He shows mercy. Ayah 111 tells you the scales are perfectly true. Ayah 110 tells you Who is holding them.

## Why these two ayat belong together

The link is not decorative. Ayah 110 describes people whose only real hope, on the Day of ayah 111, is that Allah forgives — because their own file contains a moment of collapse, and on that Day no father, son, brother or wife will be pleading their case for them. So Allah gives them the promise *before* He describes the Day. He tells them the ending first.

And He does not give it as a bare pardon. He attaches it to what they did after the failure: they emigrated, they fought, they endured. Ibn Kathir's heading says it exactly — the one who is forced to renounce Islam will be forgiven *if he does righteous deeds afterwards*.

## Living it

**Being forced into a moment of weakness is not a verdict.** The people of ayah 110 went along with their persecutors when they were tried, and the Qur'an still frames them inside "your Lord… Forgiving, Most Merciful." Whatever a person has been forced into, despair of Allah's forgiveness is not what these ayat teach.

**But the way back is action.** The verse does not record that Allah forgave them because they felt terrible about it. It records what they did: they emigrated, they fought, they bore hardship with patience. If something has gone wrong in your religion, the pattern here is to put distance between yourself and whatever pressured you, to make an effort in Allah's cause that costs you something, and then to hold that position patiently over time.

**Count the price honestly.** Homeland, family, wealth — Ibn Kathir names what they gave up. The passage does not pretend the return journey is cheap.

**Prepare for a Day when no relationship will help you.** Not your father, not your son, not your brother, not your wife — Ibn Kathir removes them by name. Everyone you would instinctively turn to will be occupied pleading their own case. What comes with you into that scene is what you actually did, paid out in full — and Allah's forgiveness, which is exactly what ayah 110 holds out.

passages.title: The parable of the secure, ungrateful town
passages.tafsir:
Allah does not argue here; He paints. A town is put before us with everything a town could want — safety, calm, provision arriving from every place — and it answers all of it by denying the One who gave it. So it is clothed in hunger and fear instead. Ayah 112 shows the reversal; ayah 113 names the sin that caused it: a Messenger came to them from among their own people, and they called him a liar. Together the two ayat are one case study in what gratitude and ingratitude do to a people's life.

## Four strokes of a blessed life (ayah 112)

Allah describes the town in a short stack of words, and each one is a distinct favour:

- **آمِنَة (āminah) — secure.** In a land where, as Ibn Kathir puts it, men were being snatched away from everywhere outside it, whoever entered this town "was safe, and he had no need to fear."
- **مُطْمَئِنَّة (muṭma'innah) — peaceful.** Ibn Kathir's fuller phrase for the place is "secure, peaceful and stable" — not merely unattacked, but settled.
- **يَأْتِيهَا رِزْقُهَا رَغَدًا — its provision coming to it in abundance.** Ibn Kathir glosses *raghadan* as "with ease and in plenty" — not scraped for, but arriving.
- **مِنْ كُلِّ مَكَان — from every place.** And in the verse Ibn Kathir cites alongside it, "fruits of all kinds" were brought to it (28:57).

Notice that the town itself is the grammatical subject of what follows: *fa-kafarat* — "so **it** denied the favours of Allah." Ibn Kathir's rendering makes the sense explicit: "it (its people) denied the favors of Allah."

## Which town is this?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports two readings. **According to leading Tafsir authorities, the similitude is general and universal** — it does not relate to a particular habitation. **Others connect it to what happened in Makkah**, and this is the reading Ibn Kathir adopts firmly: "This is what we say about the example that was given of the people of Makkah." He notes it was also the opinion of Al-'Awfi and Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, and that Malik narrated it from Az-Zuhri as well — may Allah have mercy on them all.

The two readings are not in conflict: one states the principle, the other identifies a case in which it played out.

Ibn Kathir's ground for the Makkan reading is the sheer strangeness of that town's security: "a secure sanctuary while men were being snatched away from everywhere outside of it." And he sets beside it the excuse Allah quotes from its people in another passage: *"If we follow the guidance with you, we would be snatched away from our land"* — answered there by Allah, *"Have We not established a secure sanctuary for them, to which are brought fruits of all kinds, a provision from Ourselves"* (28:57). Read together, the two halves of that verse show people offering Allah's own gift as their reason for refusing the Giver.

## The favour they denied

We hear "the favours of Allah" and think of the fruit and the safety. Ibn Kathir says they denied the blessings of Allah towards them, **the greatest of which was Muhammad ﷺ being sent to them**. That is why he sets beside this ayah the verse about those who "have changed the favors of Allah into disbelief, and caused their people to dwell in the abode of destruction; Hell, in which they will burn — and what an evil place to settle in!" (14:28–29), and then a series of verses that call the sending of the Messenger a *blessing*: "Indeed, Allah blessed the believers when He sent a Messenger from among themselves to them" (3:164); "Allah has indeed revealed to you a reminder… (and has also sent to you) a Messenger" (65:10–11); and "We have sent a Messenger to you from among you, reciting Our Ayat to you, and purifying you, and teaching you the Book and the Hikmah" — a passage that runs on to the very command this town broke: **"and do not be ungrateful"** (2:151–152).

That last line is where Ibn Kathir's chain of citations lands. The town's failure was not a difference of opinion about a claim; it was a refusal to acknowledge the greatest thing it had been given.

## "So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear"

The words of the punishment are deliberately strange: *fa-adhāqahā-llāhu **libāsa**-l-jūʿi wal-khawf*. Ibn Kathir's rendering gives the sense — "So Allah made it taste extreme hunger (famine) and fear" — but the word *libās* in the Arabic literally means a garment, and a garment is not a thing one tastes.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, stops right there. The word "garment" is used "with the force of a similie denoting something being wide-spread and all-enveloping." Fear and hunger were cast over them the way a garment or dress is put on and "becomes an integral part of the body" — that is how the two "were released and set all over them."

Two senses are fused on purpose. *Tasting* is the most intimate kind of knowing: not hearing about hunger, but having it on your tongue. A *garment* is total coverage: it goes wherever you go and touches every part of you. And the reversal is exact. Provision had come to them *from every place*; now hunger and fear covered them from every side.

## What the famine looked like

Ibn Kathir places this concretely in the Prophet's ﷺ life. It came "when they defied the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and insisted on opposing him, so he supplicated against them, asking Allah to send them seven years like the seven years of Yusuf" — that is, seven years of famine. They were then stricken with a year in which everything they had was destroyed, and they ate *'Alhaz*: the hair of the camel mixed with its blood when it is slaughtered.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, reporting the same Makkan connection, describes an acute famine of seven years, in which people were compelled to eat animal carcass, dead dogs and filth.
