Read together, the two sources agree on its shape: a town to which "fruits of all kinds" had once been brought from every place was reduced to eating what no one eats.

## And what the fear looked like

Ibn Kathir is precise about the second half of the "garment." Their sense of security was replaced with fear of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions after they had migrated to Al-Madinah. "They feared the power and the attack of his armies, and they started to lose and face the destruction of everything that belonged to them, until Allah made it possible for His Messenger ﷺ to conquer Makkah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it in a phrase: they were "virtually gripped with the awe of Muslims."

The place that had been *the safe place* now lived in fear.

## Mercy in the middle of the punishment

Two reports preserved in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān keep this passage from hardening into mere triumph.

The first (from Mazhari): the chiefs of Makkah came to the Holy Prophet ﷺ with the plea that those who had committed disbelief and disobedience against his call were all grown men — the women and children were innocent. Thereupon the Prophet ﷺ arranged to have food supplies sent to them from Madinah.

The second (from Qurtubi): Abu Sufyan, **while still in his state of kufr**, came and said in effect: you teach kindness to relatives, and mercy, and forgiveness — here are your people standing on the brink of destruction; please pray to Allah for the removal of this famine from us. Thereupon the Prophet ﷺ prayed for them, and the famine was gone.

Sit with that. The same tongue that had supplicated against them supplicated for them the moment they asked. The man they had rejected sent food to their children from the city he had migrated to. The punishment described in ayah 112 was never a locked door.

## Ayah 113: the charge stated plainly

Ayah 112 gave the sentence; ayah 113 reads out the indictment: *"There has come to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him, so the torment seized them while they were wrongdoers."*

**"From among themselves."** Two of the verses Ibn Kathir brings in repeat that same phrase — "a Messenger from among themselves" (3:164), "a Messenger to you from among you" (2:151–152) — and he introduces them by saying that Allah "reminded them of this blessing." So the phrase carries the *size of the favour*: what was sent to them was, in Ibn Kathir's words, the greatest of the blessings they denied.

**"So the torment seized them."** Not a slow drift — a grip closing.

**"While they were wrongdoers" (ẓālimūn).** This closing clause forecloses any thought that the calamity was arbitrary. Ibn Kathir sums the episode up in exactly those terms: "This happened because of their evil deeds, their wrongdoing and their rejection of the Messenger ﷺ that Allah sent to them from among themselves."

## The reversal ran both ways

Ibn Kathir draws out the symmetry that makes this passage more than a warning. Allah "changed the situation of the disbelievers and made it the opposite of what it had been, so they lived in fear after being secure, they were hungry after having plenty of provisions." And at the same time: "after the believers lived in fear, Allah granted them security, giving them ample provisions after they lived in poverty, making them rulers, governors and leaders of mankind."

One law, two directions. The very things withdrawn from the town — security and provision — were granted to the believers who until then had lived in fear and poverty. Security and provision are not properties a place owns; they are gifts.

## Living it

**Audit the blessings you have stopped noticing.** Ayah 112 does not list gold or empire. It lists safety, a settled home, and provision that arrives with ease — precisely the blessings we only see once they are gone. Naming them is where gratitude begins.

**Know which favour is the greatest.** Ibn Kathir's key move is to say that the blessing they denied above all others was the Messenger ﷺ sent among them. The Book and the Sunnah are that same favour, still in our hands. Gratitude for it looks like following him, not admiring him.

**Ingratitude is not a small matter.** Ibn Kathir explains "they denied the favors of Allah" as denying His blessings, the greatest of which was the Messenger ﷺ — and the chain of verses he cites ends on the command *"and do not be ungrateful"* (2:151–152). That is the practical takeaway of the whole passage.

**Answer people the way the Prophet ﷺ did.** He sent food to a city that had denied him, and prayed for relief for a man who had not yet believed. Being wronged did not shrink his mercy.

passages.title: Lawful food and inventing forbidden things
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat circle one question: **who has the right to say what a human being may and may not eat?** Allah tells the believers to eat freely from the lawful, good things He has provided and to thank Him (114); states what He has forbidden, with an allowance for the one forced by necessity (115); forbids the tongue that declares its own "lawful" and "forbidden" and names that an invention of lies against Allah (116), whose enjoyment is brief and whose end is painful (117); recalls what was forbidden to the Jews (118); and closes by holding the door of repentance open to anyone who has already done wrong (119).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties the passage to what came before it: the preceding verses said that disbelievers will be punished for their ungratefulness to Allah, whose blessings they had been enjoying. Now, it explains, Muslims are instructed to stay away from ungratefulness and instead be grateful for the ḥalāl (lawful) things Allah has given them — and then they are told how the disbelievers and polytheists had become ungrateful: by declaring what Allah had made ḥalāl to be ḥarām (forbidden), and what Allah had called ḥarām to be ḥalāl. Muslims are warned never to do that. That is the thread of the passage: gratitude and its opposite; receiving Allah's provision with thanks, and refusing to tamper with His law.

## "So eat … and be grateful" (114)

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 114 as a direct order: Allah orders His believing servants to eat the good and lawful things that He has provided, and to give thanks to Him for that, "for He is the Giver and Originator of all favors, Who alone deserves to be worshipped, having no partners or associate."

Two things are worth slowing down for.

First, the food is described twice over — **ḥalāl** (permitted) and **ṭayyib** (good, wholesome). Ibn Kathir keeps both words in his paraphrase: "the good and lawful things that He has provided." The provision is lawful, and it is good; and it is *provision*, traced back to the One who gave it.

Second, the ayah ends by hooking gratitude onto worship itself: *and be grateful for Allah's favour, if it is He Whom you worship.* On Ibn Kathir's reading, the two belong together — He is the Giver and Originator of all favours, and He alone deserves to be worshipped, with no partner or associate. Thanking Allah for a meal is the natural act of someone who actually holds that to be true.

## What Allah has forbidden (115)

Ayah 115 names four things: dead flesh, blood, the flesh of swine, and *mā uhilla li-ghayri llāhi bihi* — "any animal which is slaughtered as a sacrifice for other than Allah." Ibn Kathir glosses that last phrase precisely: it means "it was slaughtered with the mention of a name other than that of Allah." By that gloss, what puts this animal outside the lawful is the name pronounced over it.

Of the forbidden things Ibn Kathir writes that Allah "mentions what He has forbidden — things which harm them in both religious and worldly affairs" — naming dead meat, blood and the flesh of pigs.

Then comes the concession: **"But if one is forced by necessity, without willful disobedience, nor transgressing, then Allah is Pardoning, Most Merciful."** Ibn Kathir explains *fa-man iḍṭurra* as "if one needs to do it, without deliberately disobeying or transgressing" — the door is opened for real need, and the words that follow it rule out deliberate disobedience and transgression. He adds that he has already discussed a similar ayah in Sūrat al-Baqarah and there is no need to repeat it here; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise points readers to its own detailed treatment of these four prohibitions in its commentary on Sūrat al-Baqarah, under verses 173–174.

Two divine names close the ruling: **Ghafūr** (Pardoning) and **Raḥīm** (Most Merciful). A law about what enters the mouth ends on the One who gave the law. Commenting on ayah 118, Ibn Kathir will describe this very allowance for cases of necessity as "part of making things easy for this Ummah, because Allah desires ease for us, not hardship." (*Ummah* here means the community of Muslims.)

## The word "only" — and a problem it raises

Ayah 115 begins with **innamā** ("He has *only* forbidden you…"). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here on a real difficulty. *Innamā* is a restrictive particle — it fences a statement off, as if to say *this and nothing else* — and it "seems to give the impression that things Haram are no more than the four mentioned in the verse." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the same impression emerges even more clearly from another verse: *"Say, I do not find, in what has been revealed to me, anything prohibited…"* (al-Anʿām 6:145).

Yet, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly, "according to clarifications of the Qur'an and Sunnah and by the Consensus of the Muslim Ummah, there are many more things rated as Haram." (*Sunnah* here means the Prophet's ﷺ way as transmitted; *consensus* means the agreement of the Muslim scholars.)

The answer, it says, "comes through deliberation into the context of these very verses." The purpose in this place "is not to describe Halal and Haram as they are commonly understood." The purpose is to point out what the *mushrikīn* — the idolaters — of the period of Jāhiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) had done: "They had made many things Haram on their own although Allah Taʿālā had never ordered them about their unlawfulness." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the sense of the ayah like this: *out of the things you have (arbitrarily) made out as Haram, only that which is really Haram is being mentioned here.*

That is a lesson in reading, not only a solution to one verse. A restrictive statement is read inside the frame of the argument it is answering — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own statement of what the Qurʼān, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Ummah establish is the fixed point that keeps the reading honest.

## The tongue that legislates (116)

Ibn Kathir fills in what those invented prohibitions looked like. Allah forbids us to follow the ways of the idolaters "who declare things to be permitted or forbidden based upon their own whims and whatever names they agree on," and he lists the famous categories of Jāhiliyyah livestock:

- **Baḥīrah** — a she-camel whose milk was spared for the idols, and nobody was allowed to milk it.
- **Sāʾibah** — a she-camel let loose for free pasture for their false gods and idols, on which nothing was allowed to be carried.
- **Waṣīlah** — a she-camel set free for idols because it gave birth to a she-camel at its first delivery and then again at its second.
- **Ḥām** — a stallion camel freed from work for the sake of their idols, after it had finished a number of acts of copulation assigned for it.

"All of these," Ibn Kathir concludes, "were laws and customs that were invented during jahiliyyah." An elaborate system of prohibitions — with no revelation behind a single one of them.

**The wording of the prohibition is striking.** Allah does not merely say "do not lie." He says *wa lā taqūlū li-mā taṣifu alsinatukumu l-kadhib* — "And do not describe what your tongues have lied about, saying: 'This is lawful and this is forbidden.'" Ibn Kathir's gloss on *li-mā taṣifu* is: "do not speak lies because of what your tongues put forth." The lie is located in the speaking itself — in the verdict the tongue puts forward.

Why so severe? Because of the clause that follows: *li-taftarū ʿalā llāhi l-kadhib* — "to invent lies against Allah." As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, making things ḥalāl and ḥarām is the exclusive right of the Creator; doing it on one's own "amounts to interference in Divine prerogatives, in fact, amounts to attributing lies to Allah Taʿālā." To pronounce a thing lawful or forbidden is to speak in Allah's name, whether or not one means to.

**Ibn Kathir then widens the ayah past camels.** He says it includes:

- everyone who comes up with an innovation (*bidʿah*) for which he has no evidence from the Sharīʿah (the revealed law);
- whoever declares something lawful that Allah has forbidden;
- whoever declares something unlawful that Allah has permitted —

and in each case the motive he names is the same: "only because it suits his opinions or whim to do so."

Both directions are named, and that deserves emphasis: declaring ḥarām what Allah permitted stands alongside declaring ḥalāl what Allah forbade, in one list, under one verse.

Then the verdict: **"Verily, those who invent lies against Allah will never succeed."** Ibn Kathir: they will not succeed "either in this world or the Hereafter."

## "A brief enjoyment" (117)

Ayah 117 is short and cold: *matāʿun qalīl* — a passing, brief enjoyment — "but they will suffer a painful torment." Ibn Kathir spells out both halves: "As for this world, it is transient pleasure, and in the Hereafter, theirs will be a severe punishment." He brings two parallels from elsewhere in the Qurʼān: *"We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We will drive them into an unrelenting punishment"* (31:24), and *"Verily, those who invent a lie against Allah will never be successful. A brief enjoyment in this world! and then to Us will be their return, then We shall make them taste the severest torment because they disbelieved"* (10:69–70).

Whatever such inventing yields, the Qurʼān measures it with one word — *qalīl*, little — and sets what follows it beside it.

## What was forbidden to the Jews (118)

Ibn Kathir explains the placement of ayah 118 carefully. After mentioning what He has forbidden us to eat, "and after making allowances for cases of necessity — which is part of making things easy for this Ummah, because Allah desires ease for us, not hardship" — Allah then mentions what He forbade for the Jews in their laws before they were abrogated, "and the restrictions, limitations and difficulties involved therein."

"What We related to you before" refers, Ibn Kathir says, to Sūrat al-Anʿām: *"And unto those who are Jews, We forbade every animal with undivided hoof, and We forbade them the fat of the ox and the sheep except what adheres to their backs…"* through to *"We are indeed truthful"* (6:146).

Then the crucial clarification. **"And We did not wrong them"** — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, "in the restrictions that We imposed upon them." **"but they wronged themselves"** — meaning "they deserved that." He cites the parallel: *"Because of the wrong committed of those who were Jews, We prohibited certain good foods which had been lawful for them — and also for their hindering many from Allah's way"* (4:160).

Notice the contrast Ibn Kathir himself draws in framing this ayah: on one side, an allowance for necessity that he calls part of making things easy for this Ummah, because Allah desires ease for us and not hardship; on the other, restrictions, limitations and difficulties in the earlier law. Read that back against ayah 114 — a short list of prohibitions, an allowance for necessity, and the good and lawful things Allah has provided, to be eaten with thanks.

## The door left open (119)

The passage has just said that those who invent lies against Allah will never succeed, in this world or the next. Then ayah 119: **"Then, your Lord — for those who did evil out of ignorance and afterward repent and do righteous deeds — verily, after that, your Lord is Pardoning, Most Merciful."**

Ibn Kathir introduces it as Allah telling us this "honoring and reminding believers who have sinned of His blessings, that whoever among them repents, He will accept his repentance." On "those who did evil out of ignorance," he reports that **some of the Salaf** — the early generations of Muslims — **said this means that everyone who disobeys Allah is ignorant.** On "and afterward repent and do righteous deeds," he explains: "they give up the sins they used to commit and turn to doing acts of obedience to Allah." And "after that" means, he says, after that mistake.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the key word.** The ayah says *bi-jahālah*, not *bi-jahl*. **Jahl** is employed as the antonym of *ʿilm* (knowledge) and "releases the sense of a lack of knowledge or understanding." **Jahālah** "denotes acting ignorantly — even if done knowingly."

The consequence is enormous, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: this tells us that the forgiveness of sins through *tawbah* (repentance) "is not restricted to a situation where a sin is committed with lack of understanding or volition. Rather, a true taubah or repentance may forgive all sins, even though committed deliberately."

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies this to the passage's own subject: even those who have committed such evil deeds through ignorance should not lose hope in the mercy of Allah Taʿālā; should they repent and believe honestly and truly, Allah will forgive all sins committed by them.

Note the two names that close ayah 119 — **Ghafūr, Raḥīm**, Pardoning and Most Merciful — the same pair that closed the allowance for necessity in ayah 115. Mercy stands at both ends, with the warning held between them.

## Living it

**Eat, and give thanks.** Ayah 114 is a command in two halves, and most of us keep only the first. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the whole passage as an instruction to stay away from ungratefulness and to be grateful instead for the ḥalāl Allah has given.

**Guard the sentence "this is ḥarām."** To say it is to speak about Allah's ruling — that is the force of ayah 116 and of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's comment that making things ḥalāl and ḥarām is the exclusive right of the Creator. Ibn Kathir's condition is evidence from the Sharīʿah; "I don't know, ask someone who does" costs nothing.

**The error runs both ways.** Ibn Kathir places banning what Allah permitted and permitting what Allah banned in the same list under this ayah, and names the same motive for both: "only because it suits his opinions or whim to do so." When a ruling lands exactly where your preference already was, that is a moment to look again at the evidence.

**Take the allowance Allah gave.** He built necessity into the ruling Himself, and Ibn Kathir reads that as part of making things easy for this Ummah — Allah desires ease for us, not hardship. Use it when the need is real; the ayah's own words fence it off from deliberate disobedience and transgression.

**Read "only" in context.** These four are not the whole of what Allah forbade. Ayah 115 is answering what the idolaters of Jāhiliyyah had invented, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains — and by the Qurʼān, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Ummah, many more things are ḥarām.

**And do not write yourself off.** Ayah 119 is placed where it is. Whatever the sin, and however knowingly it was done — *jahālah* covers acting ignorantly even when done knowingly — the terms remain what Ibn Kathir stated: give up the sins you used to commit, turn to acts of obedience to Allah, and your Lord, after that, is Pardoning, Most Merciful.

passages.title: Abraham the ḥanīf, and the command to follow his way
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat bring the long argument of this sūrah to rest on a single man. Allah praises Ibrāhīm (Abraham) — his leadership, his obedience, his pure monotheism, his gratitude — then commands the final Prophet ﷺ to follow his way, and finally removes the last prop from under those who invent prohibitions in the name of religion. What holds the passage together is a quiet, devastating piece of reasoning: the people who most loudly claimed that everything they did was in accordance with Ibrāhīm's teachings are answered out of what they themselves already believed.

## The argument these ayat are winning

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the sequence. The verses just before this refuted the root of shirk and kufr — the rejection of Allah's Oneness and the rejection of the mandate He gave His Prophet ﷺ — and also refuted an offshoot of that same disease: legalising the illegal and illegalising the legal, "a virtual reversal of Divinely ordained arrangements." Now, the first direct addressees of the Qurʼān were the mushriks of Makkah, and for all their idol-worship they claimed that they were adherents of the great community of Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm and that what they did was all in accordance with his teachings. So, as Maʿārif puts it, the rejection of their position came on the basis of what they already believed in.

Read the five ayat as five steps of that refutation, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays them out:

- **120** — Ibrāhīm was the foremost universal leader of nations, with the high station of a prophet and messenger of Allah; and the added words "and he was not among the mushriks" confirmed him a torch-bearer of the most perfect belief in the Oneness of Allah.
- **121** — he was grateful to Allah and on the straight path. A warning signal to adversaries who claimed to be his followers: how could people as ungrateful as they were have the cheek to call themselves his adherents?
- **122** — he was successful in the Dunyā and the Ākhirah.
- **123** — the prophetic mission of Sayyidnā Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ is true and he was truly committed to the ideal of the authentic community of Ibrāhīm. Conclusion: your claim cannot be correct without faith in and obedience to the Prophet ﷺ.
- **124** — the hint here is that the good things you have, on your own, made unlawful for yourselves were really not unlawful in the community of Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm.

## "Ibrāhīm was an *ummah*" (ayah 120)

Ibn Kathīr heads his comment on these ayat **"The Khalīl (Close Friend) of Allah,"** and opens: Allah praises His servant, Messenger and close friend Ibrāhīm — *the Imām of the Ḥanīfs, the father of the Prophets* — and declares his innocence of the idolaters, Jews or Christians.

Four words carry the praise.

**Ummah.** The word has a few meanings, but the well-known sense is community, nation, or group of people — which is exactly why calling one man an *ummah* stops the reader. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that this is what it means here, as reported from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, and then unfolds that sense: Ibrāhīm is, in his person, a community, a nation, almost a compendium of their perfections and merits. Mujāhid said plainly, "*Ummah* here means that he was a nation on his own." There is another recognised meaning of *ummah* — the leader of a community, someone imbibing in his person many perfections — and Maʿārif notes that some commentators have taken exactly this meaning at this place. Ibn Kathīr is one who reads it so: "*Ummah* here means the leader who is followed." One reading looks at what he was in himself; the other at what he was to everyone who came after him.

Maʿārif points out how visible that leadership is: people from all famous faiths of the world believe in him and consider it an honour to be the followers of his community. The Jews, the Christians and the Muslims revere him. Even the mushriks of Arabia, despite their idol-worship, felt proud to believe in him and in supposedly following his way — the way of someone who was the foremost idol-breaker in human annals. The irony is the whole argument in miniature.

**Qānitan li-llāh — devoted to Allah.** Ibn Kathīr glosses *qānit* as humble and obedient; Maʿārif as obedient to the command of his Creator. And Maʿārif does something valuable here: it shows you what that obedience cost. It "becomes crystal clear from the trials this khalīl of Allah has gone through. Imagine the fire of Namrūd (Nimrod), the Command to go elsewhere leaving behind his family in a wilderness, and then, his being ready to sacrifice his very dear son." *Qānit* is not a temperament. It is a word tested by fire, by a wilderness, and by the readiness to give up a beloved son.

**Ḥanīfan.** Ibn Kathīr's definition is precise and worth memorising: a *ḥanīf* is "one who deliberately steers clear of shirk in favour of tawḥīd." Note the deliberateness. A ḥanīf has not merely avoided idols by accident of birth or culture; he has turned away from them on purpose and turned towards Allah alone on purpose. That is the man being held up in front of idol-worshipping Makkans who claimed to be walking his road.

**"And he was not one of the idolaters."** The denial is placed right beside the praise, and it is exactly the clause Maʿārif leans on: it confirms Ibrāhīm as a torch-bearer of the most perfect belief in Allah's Oneness, so the name cannot be borrowed without the substance. Ibn Kathīr reads it as Allah declaring Ibrāhīm's innocence of the idolaters, Jews or Christians.

## Grateful, chosen, guided (ayah 121)

**"Thankful for His favours."** Ibn Kathīr explains simply that he gave thanks for the blessings Allah gave him — and then defines what that thanks looked like by citing another ayah about him: *"And of Ibrāhīm, the one who fulfilled"* (53:37), which Ibn Kathīr explains as meaning that **he did everything that Allah commanded him to do.** That is the measure of gratitude this passage works with: not a phrase on the tongue but a life that carries out in full what it was given to carry. Set that beside the Makkans, and Maʿārif's warning lands: ingratitude and a claim of discipleship cannot live in the same chest.

**"He chose him."** *Ijtabāhu* means He selected him, says Ibn Kathīr, quoting *"And before, We indeed gave Ibrāhīm his integrity, and We were indeed most knowledgeable about him"* (21:51). Ibrāhīm's standing is a gift of divine choosing — and the ayah cited adds that the One who chose him was "most knowledgeable about him."

**"And guided him to a straight path."** Ibn Kathīr defines the straight path here with two halves that must both be present: to worship Allah alone, without partners or associate — *and* in the manner that He prescribed and which pleases Him. Sincerity in the object of worship, and conformity in the manner of it.

## Given both houses (ayah 122)

"And We gave him good in this world" — Ibn Kathīr: 'We granted him all that a believer may require for a good and complete life in this world.' Mujāhid gave a more particular reading of that "good": **"This means a truthful tongue."**

Then the ayah does not stop at this world: "and in the Hereafter he shall be of the righteous." Maʿārif sums the verse up in a line — Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm was successful in the Dunyā and in the Ākhirah both.

## "Follow the way of Ibrāhīm" (ayah 123)

Ibn Kathīr connects this to everything before it: *because of his perfection, greatness, and the soundness of his tawḥīd and his way,* Allah revealed to "the Seal of the Messengers and Leader of the Prophets ﷺ" the command to follow the *millah* (the way, the religious community-path) of Ibrāhīm, the ḥanīf who was not one of the idolaters. He points to the parallel in Sūrat al-Anʿām: *"Say: Truly, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a right religion, the religion of Ibrāhīm, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters"* (6:161).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question. The Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ is the most distinguished (*afḍal*) of all the blessed prophets and messengers — so why is the *afḍal* asked to follow one who is, in this context, *mafḍūl*? It offers two wise considerations:

1. **The shape of the law was already known.** When Ibrāhīm appeared, Allah blessed him with a Sharīʿah and its injunctions. When the Last of the Prophets ﷺ appeared, his Sharīʿah too — with the exception of some particular injunctions — was laid out in accordance with it. Since that earlier Sharīʿah had come into the world first and was already known and recognised, this similarity was expressed through the word *ittibāʿ*, "following."
2. **The command is itself a tribute to Ibrāhīm.** Maʿārif cites ʿAllāmah al-Zamakhsharī (author of *Tafsīr al-Kashshāf*): this command to follow is itself a special tribute among the many honours attributed to the khalīl of Allah, and that it is so special has been hinted at through the use of the word **thumma ("then")** in the ayah. The sense being conveyed, Maʿārif says: certainly great are all the merits and perfections of Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm as they are, but the most superior of all of them is that Allah has asked His preferred-most and dearest messenger ﷺ to follow his way.

## The Sabbath was only for those who disputed about it (ayah 124)

Ibn Kathīr opens with the principle: there is no doubt that for every nation Allah prescribed one day of the week for people to gather to worship Him. For this Ummah He prescribed **Friday**, because it is the sixth day, on which Allah completed and perfected His creation; on this day He gathered and completed His blessings for His servants.

Then the history, which Ibn Kathīr reports with the caution of "it was said." It was said that Allah prescribed this day for the Children of Israel through His Prophet Mūsā, but they changed it and chose Saturday, because it was the day on which the Creator did not create anything, as He had completed His creation on Friday. Allah then made observance of the Sabbath obligatory for them in the laws of the Tawrāh — and at the same time told them to follow Muḥammad ﷺ when he was sent, and took their promises and covenant to that effect. Mujāhid's comment on the ayah is exactly this: **"They observed the Sabbath (Saturday) and ignored Friday."**

Ibn Kathīr continues: they kept Saturday until Allah sent ʿĪsā bin Maryam. Here the reports differ, and he presents them as differing — it was said that ʿĪsā told them to change it to Sunday, and it was also said that he did not forsake the laws of the Tawrāh except for a few rulings which were abrogated, and that he continued to observe the Sabbath until he was taken up. Afterwards, the Christians at the time of Constantine were the ones who changed it to Sunday in order to be different from the Jews, and they started to pray towards the east instead of facing Jerusalem. Ibn Kathīr closes the discussion the way a careful scholar should: **"And Allah knows best."**

That account is what stands behind the ayah's phrase "those who differed concerning it": on this report the Sabbath was not the original prescription, but a ruling settled upon a people after they had changed their day. And the ayah ends by handing the whole quarrel over: *your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection about what they differed over.* The final verdict on that dispute is not ours to pronounce.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why this closes the passage: the hint given to the Makkans is that the good things they had, on their own, made unlawful for themselves were really not unlawful in the community of Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm. The prohibitions they invented cannot be traced back to him.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathīr cites here a report in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs from Abū Hurayrah, who heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that we are the last but will be the first on the Day of Resurrection, even though they were given the Book before us; that this is the day Allah obligated upon them but they differed concerning it, and Allah guided us to it; and that the people observe their days after us — the Jews on the following day and the Christians on the day after that. Ibn Kathīr notes that this version was recorded by **al-Bukhārī**.

He then cites a report from Abū Hurayrah and Ḥudhayfah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah let the people who came before us stray from Friday, so the Jews had Saturday and the Christians had Sunday; then Allah brought us and guided us to Friday — so there are Friday, Saturday and Sunday, and thus they will follow us on the Day of Resurrection: we are the last of the people of this world, but will be the first on the Day of Resurrection, and will be the first to be judged, before all of creation. Ibn Kathīr states this was reported by **Muslim**.

In both reports the same words recur: others were given the Book first, they differed, and Allah guided this Ummah to the day.

## Living it

**Be a ḥanīf on purpose.** Ibn Kathīr's definition asks for a deliberate turn: know what shirk is, steer clear of it knowingly, and direct worship to Allah alone. A claimed attachment that has never actually chosen anything is precisely what these ayat take apart.

**Let gratitude be measured in obedience.** If thankfulness for Allah's favours means, as Ibn Kathīr explains, doing everything He commanded, then the honest audit of our shukr is our compliance, not our vocabulary.

**Take the straight path in both its halves.** Worship of Allah alone without partners, in the manner He prescribed and which pleases Him. Sincerity without conformity, or conformity without sincerity, is not what Ibrāhīm was guided to.

**Don't claim a way you won't walk.** The whole passage turns on people who honoured a name and abandoned its content. Maʿārif makes the test concrete at ayah 123: their claim to Ibrāhīm cannot be correct without faith in and obedience to the Prophet ﷺ.

**Don't invent prohibitions.** Ayah 124's quiet lesson, as Maʿārif reads it, is that making unlawful for yourself what Allah made good is not extra piety — it is the very disorder this sūrah has been correcting.

**Value your Friday.** Ibn Kathīr says Allah prescribed this day for this Ummah, and the reports he cites say Allah guided us to it after others differed and strayed. That is a favour — and this very passage has already told us what gratitude for a favour looks like: doing what Allah commanded.

passages.title: Call with wisdom; restrain and be patient
passages.tafsir:
**These four ayat close Sūrah an-Naḥl** by turning from the disbelievers to the Prophet ﷺ himself. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, he "is being taught how to fulfill the rights of his mission" — and the teaching, though addressed to him, "includes and covers all true believers." Ayah 125 is the *method* of the call. Ayat 126–128 are what to do when the call is answered with cruelty.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī that when Haram ibn Ḥayyān (may Allah have mercy on him) neared death, his relatives asked for his parting testament. He answered that a will is what people make for wealth, and he had none — "But, I would still make a wasiyyah, that of the ayat of Allah, particularly that of the last verses of Sūrah an-Naḥl — and I order you to stand firm on them."

## Ayah 125: a whole curriculum in a few words

**"Call to the way of your Lord."** *Daʿwah* literally means *to call*, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this is the first duty of every prophet; everything else they taught unfolds from it. The Qur'an names the Prophet ﷺ by this very quality — "one who invites towards Allah with His permission whilst being a lamp, lighted" (33:46) — and passes the duty on to his community (3:104).

Notice which name of Allah is chosen: not "the way of Allah" but **"the way of your *Rabb*."** *Rabb* is the One who nurtures, raises, provides and trains, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the hint — the work of daʿwah "is connected with the attribute of nurture, raising, training and education." The Prophet ﷺ is being told, in effect: *the way your Lord has raised you, raise others*. The word *daʿwah* carries this too: a prophet's task is not merely to make people hear the commands but to *invite* them to live by them — and nobody inviting another to Allah would frame it in a way that repels, maligns or mocks him.

**Ḥikmah (wisdom).** The scholars read this word variously: some took *al-ḥikmah* as the Qur'an, some the Qur'an and the Sunnah, some the conclusive proof; Ibn Jarīr (cited by Ibn Kathīr) said it is "what was revealed to him from the Book and the Sunnah." Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, quoting al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, offers a definition Maʿārif ul Qurʼān considers to gather up the rest: *sound speech which goes into one's heart* — words that are true **and** find their way in.

Rūḥ al-Bayān unpacks the practical side: ḥikmah is "the insight through which one finds out the dictates of circumstances and talks as appropriate," employing "lenience where lenience is called for and firmness where firmness is in order," and where a frank word would embarrass someone, communicating by hint — so the listener is neither shamed nor pushed into digging in on his prejudice. Wisdom here is not softness; it is *accuracy*.

**Al-mawʿiẓah al-ḥasanah (good counsel).** *Mawʿiẓah*, per al-Qāmūs and al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's *al-Mufradāt*, is to speak in the spirit of genuine well-wishing, in a way that softens the heart and makes it receptive; only then is it useful to speak of the reward of accepting and the harm of refusing. Ibn Kathīr gives its Qur'anic texture: exhortation, and the stories of what befell earlier peoples, told to warn of Allah's punishment.

Why add **al-ḥasanah, "good"?** Because, Rūḥ al-Maʿānī notes, people wishing others well still manage to be hurtful while doing it. The word rules that out: good counsel settles the listener's heart, removes his doubts, and leaves him certain you have no personal motive.

**"And argue with them in the best manner."** Ibn Kathīr: if any of them wish to debate, "let that be in the best manner, with kindness, gentleness and good speech." Rūḥ al-Maʿānī adds that arguments must be pitched so the listener can follow them and built on premises he already grants, so they dissolve his doubts rather than harden him. Nor is this reserved for fellow Muslims: "do not argue with the People of the Book except in a manner which is best" (29:46).

**Two principles, or three?** Some commentators matched the three to three audiences: wisdom for people of knowledge, good counsel for the general public, debate for those carrying doubts or refusing out of hostility. Maulānā Ashraf Thānawī (may Allah have mercy on him), in *Bayān al-Qurʼān*, held it a stretch to read three separate audiences into the wording; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows him, taking all of it as etiquette for everyone.

Rūḥ al-Maʿānī adds a grammatical observation. Had all three been principles, the ayah would have listed them in one series joined by conjunctions. Instead ḥikmah and mawʿiẓah ḥasanah are joined together, while *jādilhum billatī hiya aḥsan* stands as a fresh sentence. So debate is not a foundation of the call — it is guidance for something that *arises* on the road of daʿwah, much as ayah 126 will address the harm that arises on that road. Two principles, then, never to be dispensed with; and a licence for argument only when someone forces it, hedged so tightly by *"in the best manner"* that argument without that condition "has no place and status in the Sharīʿah."

## How the prophets actually did it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grounds this in the hardest case: Allah sent Mūsā and Hārūn (peace be upon them) to Pharaoh — a tyrant who claimed divinity and would die a disbeliever — with the instruction **"And speak to him mildly, perhaps he may accept admonition or fear Allah"** (20:44) — a verse Ibn Kathīr cites for the same point. The commentary presses it home: those we call today are not further astray than Pharaoh, and none of us is Mūsā or Hārūn — so where did we acquire a right Allah withheld from two of His prophets?

Nūḥ (peace be upon him), told after nine hundred and fifty years of this work "Indeed we see you in obvious error," answered only: "O my people, there is no error in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds" (7:60–61); Hūd (peace be upon him), called a liar and a fool, replied in the same register (7:66–67). And the long exchange between Mūsā and Pharaoh in Sūrah ash-Shuʿarā' is, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, "a masterpiece of prophetic manners": Mūsā admits plainly what he did (26:20), corrects the record about the "favour" of being raised in that house — it was Pharaoh's own decree of killing Israelite children that put him in the river (26:22) — and when Pharaoh calls him a madman before an audience, he does not answer the insult at all. He carries on describing his Lord (26:28). No emotion betrayed, no blow returned.

## From the Sunnah

The Prophet ﷺ never let the call become a burden. A narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of al-Bukhārī records that he held his sessions of exhortation only on certain days of the week, lest the Companions grow weary, and told others to do likewise. Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) reports that he ﷺ said: **"Make (things) easy and do not make (things) difficult and give (people) the good news (of mercy from Allah) and do not disappoint or alienate (them)"** (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Kitāb al-ʿIlm).

Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) urged people to become *rabbānī* — reported in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, where the word is explained as one who, keeping the principles of teaching and training in view, begins with simple matters and only once people are settled in them moves to what would have been too hard at the start. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān blames much of the ineffectiveness of modern preaching on this very failure: long lectures, unasked-for sermonising, demands made without learning what the listener faces.

He ﷺ also shielded people from public embarrassment. Seeing someone in the wrong, he would not address him directly but beam the remark at the gathering: *"What has happened to people that they do so?"* — and the one concerned would hear, feel it in his heart, and set about ridding himself of the fault. And because daʿwah means calling someone *closer*, not cataloguing his defects, the prophets' calls so often open with **"O my people"** — the bond of brotherhood first, the correction after. Writing to Heraclius, the Prophet ﷺ addressed him as "the Great Man of Byzantium" and led with common ground: "O people of the Book, come to a word common between us and you that we worship none but Allah" (3:64).

## The danger hidden inside "winning"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is severe here, because argument corrodes the arguer. Imām al-Ghazālī likened it to liquor as *umm al-khabāʼith*, "the mother of evils": once overpowering your opponent and demonstrating your intellectual superiority becomes the goal, it breeds envy, malice, arrogance, backbiting, spying on others' faults, delight at their discomfort, and haughty rejection of truth. Imām al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) said knowledge is a brotherhood of the learned, and asked how those who have turned knowledge into enmity can invite anyone to follow their religion. His rule: correct someone privately and politely and that is *advice*; disgrace him publicly and that is *vice*.

The Prophet ﷺ warned that on the Day of Judgement the person most severely punished, of all human beings, will be a scholar from whose knowledge Allah has given him no benefit; and he said, "Do not learn the ʿilm (of dīn) to compete with the learned in pride and prestige nor to challenge the incompetent with it nor to make the faces of people turn towards you therewith. So whoever will do that, will be in the fire" (Ibn Mājah, from the ḥadīth of Sayyidnā Jābir, may Allah be pleased with him, with sound chains of authority as in Takhrīj al-ʿIrāqī ʿalā al-Iḥyāʼ). Imām Mālik (may Allah have mercy on him) said that altercation and confrontation in knowledge "drives away the light of knowledge from the heart of a servant"; asked whether one who knows the Sunnah may debate to defend it, he said: "No. But, he should inform the addressee about the Sunnah. Then, should he accept it, good — otherwise, let him observe silence." None of this excuses silence at home, though — Allah says, "Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire" (66:6).

## "Your Lord knows best who has strayed"

The closing clause of ayah 125 is mercy for the caller. Ibn Kathīr: Allah already knows who is doomed and who is blessed; it is written and the matter is settled — so call them, "but do not exhaust yourself with regret over those who go astray, for it is not your task to guide them." He is a warner; conveying is his duty, and the reckoning is Allah's — hence "You cannot guide whom you love" (28:56) and "It is not up to you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills" (2:272). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as comfort against the shock of refusal after you have done everything right. *Do not lose hope. Do not despair.*

## Ayat 126–128: Uḥud, and the choice not to answer in kind

**The occasion.** According to the majority of commentators these verses are Madanī. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, from Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī, a narration of al-Dāraquṭnī from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him): after Uḥud, when the idolaters marched back, the bodies of seventy leading Companions were found — among them Ḥamzah (may Allah be pleased with him), the revered uncle of the Prophet ﷺ, whose body they had mutilated in their rage, cutting his nose, ears and other parts and slitting open his abdomen. The very sight of it shocked the Prophet ﷺ, and he said that to avenge Ḥamzah he would have seventy of the idolaters subjected to the same. It was against that scene that these three ayat came down. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the narration in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī accords with this, and that other Companions too were mutilated (as reported by al-Tirmidhī, Aḥmad, and Ibn Khuzaymah and Ibn Ḥibbān in their Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him).

The right of retaliation was confirmed but *capped* — seventy for a few, irrespective of number, is not the justice and equity Allah intended to establish in the world through him; and the higher road was commended to him as befitting a model of morals at their best. And so, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates (from al-Mazharī, from al-Baghawī), the Prophet ﷺ said: **"Now, patient we shall be. We shall not take any revenge from anyone"** — and he paid a kaffārah (expiation) for his oath. Years later at the Conquest of Makkah, with those same people under his control, that was certainly the moment to carry out what he had declared at Uḥud. He did not; he had forsaken that intention the day these verses came.

**Justice, measured.** Ibn Kathīr: Allah here commands justice in punishment and equity in settling the cases of rights. ʿAbd al-Razzāq recorded from Ibn Sīrīn, "If a man among you takes something from you, then you should take something similar from him" — also the opinion of Mujāhid, Ibrāhīm, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others, and the one Ibn Jarīr favoured. Ibn Zayd read it differently: the Muslims had been commanded to forgive the idolaters, and when strong and powerful men entered Islam and asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to deal with them, this ayah was revealed — then, he said, it was abrogated by the command to engage in jihād.

Because the standard is *likeness*, the jurists derived the law of even retaliation: a killer is killed, one who inflicts injury has an even injury inflicted on him; and where exact equivalence cannot be reckoned — a killing by repeated blows with a rock or by arrows — al-Jaṣṣāṣ holds the execution is by the sword instead. The ayah's wording is general enough to cover financial loss too: one whose property is usurped may take back its like, the jurists differing over whether what he takes must be of the same kind as what was taken from him, some permitting it unconditionally.

**"But if you are patient, it is better."** The permission is real; the counsel points past it.

## Ayah 127: patience is itself something given

Ayah 126 addresses the believers in the plural; **ayah 127** narrows to the Prophet ﷺ alone: *waṣbir* — "And be patient." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the shift as station-appropriate: in view of his great dignity and high station, patience was more becoming for him than for others — "As for you, you just do not even contemplate a revenge. Take to ṣabr as your only option."

Then the clause: **"and your patience is only by Allah."** Ibn Kathīr says this both emphasises the command and tells us patience "cannot be acquired except by the will, help, decree and power of Allah." The very thing demanded of you is the thing you must ask Him for.

**"And do not grieve over them"** — over those who oppose you, says Ibn Kathīr, for Allah has decreed that this should happen. **"And do not be distressed by their plots"** — do not be worried or upset by the efforts they are putting into opposing you and causing you harm, "for Allah is protecting, helping, and supporting you." Note the order: first the hands are restrained (126), then the heart is settled (127). The Qur'an does not merely forbid revenge; it removes the grief and anxiety that make it feel necessary.

## Ayah 128: the promise that makes it possible

**"Indeed Allah is with those who are mindful of Him and those who do good."** Ibn Kathīr explains this being-with (*maʿiyyah*) as one of supporting them, helping them and guiding them, and marks it as a *special* kind. The general kind of being-with, he says, is by means of seeing, hearing and knowing: "And He is with you wherever you may be. And Allah sees whatever you do" (57:4); "There is no secret counsel of three but He is their fourth... but He is with them wherever they may be" (58:7); "You will not be in any circumstance, nor recite any portion of the Qur'an, nor having done any deeds, but We are witnessing you" (10:61). But the withness promised here is what He said to the angels — "Verily, I am with you, so support those who believe" (8:12) — and to Mūsā and Hārūn: "Fear not, verily I am with you both, hearing and seeing" (20:46). It is what the Prophet ﷺ said to Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) when they were in the cave: **"Do not worry, Allah is with us."**

Who qualifies? Ibn Kathīr: **those of taqwā** keep away from what is forbidden, and **the doers of good (muḥsinūn)** do deeds of obedience to Allah — "These are the ones whom Allah takes care of, He gives them support, and helps them to prevail over their enemies and opponents." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a shade to the second: *iḥsān* here is being good to Allah's creation — so the pairing is people bound to righteous deeds who are also particular about dealing with others nicely. That is the note the sūrah ends on — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, "if someone is blessed with the 'company' (help) of Allah, who can touch him!"

## Living it

- **Read the person before you speak,** and let them feel you are on their side — *al-ḥasanah* was added precisely because well-meant advice so often wounds.
- **Correct privately, and start small:** the *rabbānī* teacher begins with what people can carry.
- **Do not go looking for the argument.** It is a concession, not a principle — and, as al-Ghazālī warned, the surest way for a caller to lose his own heart.
- **When wronged, cap yourself — then consider letting it go,** and ask Allah for the patience you are commanded to have. Measure success by faithfulness, not results.
